#5535. 5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

Real estate investing apps show the average return first. Amanda Neely, CFP, shares five questions on fees, payouts, liquidity and more.

Investing in real estate used to mean buying a building. Now it can mean tapping a button. Crowdfunding platforms, fractional-ownership apps and private lending marketplaces let you put $500 or $50,000 into real estate without ever signing a deed. Plenty of agents use them for their own money, and clients ask agents about them too.

Access is a good thing. But the app puts the friendliest number front and center … an average rate of return. It rarely shows you your actual annualized return after fees and defaults or how far your balance could drop in a bad year.

This fall, I sat down with several people who had all invested through the same program. Each of them had a different understanding of where their money was going.

One had stopped going to the program’s update calls years ago, because nobody on them would tell her whether she was making money or losing it. Every one of them could tell me, to the dollar, what landed in their account each month.

I haven’t put my own money into these platforms, and most of the reasons why are on this list.

Here are five questions to ask before you, or a client, put money into any real estate investing platform.

Some platforms are marketplaces. They connect you to deals that someone else runs. Others steer your money into funds they manage themselves. The second setup isn’t automatically bad, but it means the company can get paid more than once: a platform or membership fee up front, then a management fee inside the fund.

How to check: Find the fund’s name on your statement and look up who manages it. If it’s the same company that recommended it (or a close affiliate), ask for every layer of fees in writing.

Real estate funds on these platforms usually pay monthly or quarterly distributions, and part of each payment is often classified as return of capital. In plain English, part of what you’re paid is your own money coming back.

In real estate, some return of capital is normal. Depreciation lets a property fund pay out cash that isn’t taxed as income yet, and that gets labeled return of capital, too. The warning sign is return of capital paired with a sliding share value.

If the distributions hold steady while the fund’s value per share (often called NAV) keeps dropping, the income is coming out of your principal. You still feel paid every month, and the account is getting smaller.

How to check: In the app, compare the fund’s value per share on the day you bought with today’s. Then look at your year-end tax forms, which show return of capital separately from dividends.

Say you put $20,000 into a private loan that pays you $400 a month for five years. That’s $24,000 back. Spread over five years, it looks like about 4 percent a year. But because part of every payment is your own principal coming home, the annualized return is actually closer to 7.4 percent. The payout made it look worse than it was.

Now flip it. That 7.4 percent only holds if the borrower pays every month. Lending platforms spread your money across many borrowers, and some of them won’t pay. A platform advertising 10 percent that loses 4 percent of its loans to default each year is paying you closer to 6 percent.

How to check: Ask the platform for the annualized return after fees and defaults, not the payout rate. Then ask what that number was in its worst year.

Many of these platforms are newer than the last real estate downturn. A platform that developed when money was cheap hasn’t shown you how it behaves when money is expensive. The company running the app is also a business, and businesses fail. WeWork, the shared-office company, was valued at $47 billion in 2019 and filed for bankruptcy in November 2023.

How to check: Find the platform’s launch date and look for at least one stretch of rising rates or falling prices in its history. Then ask where your investment actually sits. Many platforms hold each property or fund in its own legal entity, separate from the company itself, so your share can survive if the platform doesn’t. If neither answer is clear, size your investment like the experiment it is.

Many platforms expect you to stay in for five years or more. Some charge a penalty to leave early, others limit how much can come out each quarter, and many reserve the right to pause withdrawals entirely. In spring 2020, Fundrise, one of the best-known real estate investing apps, suspended redemptions from its mature funds “until further notice.”

The lockup is part of why these investments can pay more than a savings account, so it isn’t automatically a problem. It becomes one when money you might need in a slow month ends up somewhere that can tell you “not yet.”

How to check: Read the redemption section of the offering documents. Then ask one blunt question: “If I wanted all of it back next month, what would happen?”

When a client asks whether an app is a good idea, try:

“I can’t tell you whether it’s right for you, but here are the five questions to get answered first.”

You come across as the agent who thinks clearly about money without crossing into advice you’re not licensed to give.

Commission income doesn’t arrive on a schedule, so the money you can reach in a slow month matters more than the money that pays the most. Before your own dollars go into a platform, make sure your cushion lives somewhere you can actually reach. Liquidity first, then growth. Treat the app as the growth layer of your plan, not the floor under it.

The average return will always be the number they show you first. Make it the last one you trust.

Amanda Neely is a Certified Financial Planner and the CEO of Counterflow. Connect with her on LinkedIn and Substack.

#5534. Anthropic's IPO puts AI liability risks that may be uninsurable before investors

Free daily briefing on global business news.

MarketWatch says Anthropic could face legal claims from catastrophic AI misuse that no insurance company could underwrite

Anthropic could face “significant and unpredictable” legal claims arising from an AI misuse event so catastrophic that insurers would be unable to underwrite the exposure, the company said in its IPO filing, according to MarketWatch.

The risk is one of several that investors must weigh in Anthropic’s IPO, according to MarketWatch, which called the offering a first for a lab devoted solely to frontier AI and said investors are being pushed to evaluate kinds of risk unlike any they have faced previously.

AI developers have previously revealed episodes of their autonomous software behaving unpredictably, according to MarketWatch. The examples it cites include OpenAI agents that broke into a startup's systems, an Anthropic model that fed a false lead on a homicide to local police, and a Meta $META Platforms model that breached a different firm while undergoing security evaluations.

Anthropic executives have publicly warned about the dangers of advanced AI. Evan Hubinger, who leads the company's alignment science team, wrote on X $TWTR that he thinks the chance AI kills all humans within the next decade is greater than 10%.

CEO Dario Amodei put the chance that AI's future goes "really, really badly" at 25% during the Axios AI+ DC Summit in September 2025. He has also written that the world is "considerably closer to real danger in 2026 than we were in 2023."

Anthropic has a scaling policy meant to keep it from building a model it cannot control. On Feb. 24, the company softened that policy to commit to delaying a model in narrow cases, with the decision depending on how far ahead it is of rivals and on the safety measures those rivals have in place.

#5533. Leaving VMware starts as a cost decision, but day-two operations decide whether it works

Enterprises leaving legacy hypervisors are finding that moving virtual machines is only half the job, and that a portable data management layer often decides whether a Kubernetes migration succeeds. Rising license costs are pushing teams to run containers and VMs on one platform.

That shift is playing out at Mouser Electronics Inc., one of the world’s largest electronic components distributors. After running Red Hat Inc.’s OpenShift for containers for five to six years, the company is now building a production OpenShift Virtualization cluster to move workloads off Broadcom Inc.’s VMware, according to Ronald Waller (pictured, left), systems engineer at Mouser.

“It doesn’t matter if we’re running containers or VMs, we’re running it on the same foundation, which really works well,” Waller said. “Because we can manage those things with the same tool sets and same skill sets.”

Waller and Jon Owings (right), assistant vice president of global technical presales, cloud and data services, at Portworx by Everpure, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how the data management layer helps run VMs and containers on OpenShift. (* Disclosure below.)

Kubernetes already serves as a common control plane for containerized AI workloads, and pulling VMs onto it extends that standard to older applications. Everpure Inc., which rebranded from Pure Storage Inc. this year as part of a data-centric pivot, positions Portworx as the matching abstraction for storage.

“Kubernetes provides that ubiquitous control plane for all of them, and that’s what customers are asking us for,” Owings said. “The one thing that was missing was the same thing but for data.”

The learning curve for VMware administrators moving to Kubernetes is steep, and Waller has climbed it over the last year. Storage turned out to be the easy part when he built Mouser’s proof-of-concept cluster, he explained.

“I asked the storage guy what I needed from him, and he handed me a user ID and an API key. I went to Portworx Central. I configured my spec for the operator and the storage cluster, created my secret, and boom, Portworx Enterprise did everything else on the backend,” Waller said. “I didn’t even have to think about it.”

Portworx keeps building for that use case. It made data management native to OpenShift in May and unveiled new AI and VM capabilities at KubeCon. For teams following Mouser’s path, Owings sees the exit from a legacy hypervisor as a chance to rethink day-two operations on a data management layer that travels across clouds and Kubernetes distributions.

“What can we change that we didn’t like about the last 15 years? … Were we dependent on a vendor? Were we dependent on shell scripts or PowerShell?” Owings said. “We have this great opportunity to do something new, and Kubernetes has that open API that allows you to be creative.”

#5532. Mapped: Where the Most Homeowners Own Their Homes Outright With No Mortgage

Roughly 3 in 5 American homeowners pay a mortgage every month, yet the share of those who own their property outright is steadily growing—with at least half of all homeowners in three states now completely mortgage-free.

According to a new Realtor.com® data analysis of the recently released 2025 American Community Survey 1-Year Estimates, 59% of homeowners carried a mortgage last year, while 41% owned their homes free and clear.

That marks a major shift from 2010, when fewer than a third of homes (32.8%) were owned outright while 67% carried home loan debt.

Mortgaged homeownership has shrunk across all four regions, though reliance on financing still varies significantly by geography. The West had the highest mortgage debt rate at 63.8%, while the South recorded the lowest at 56.8%. The Northeast and Midwest tied at 58.7%.

At the state level, West Virginia led the nation with 56.6% of its homeowners living mortgage-free, followed by Mississippi (52.7%) and New Mexico (50%).

On the other side of the spectrum, Washington, DC, in 2025 logged the lowest share of outright homeownership, at just 26.5%, trailed by Maryland (30.6%) and Colorado (31.6%).

Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu explains that the balance between mortgaged and free-and-clear homes meaningfully shapes housing market dynamics, especially at a time when mortgage rates are high.

"Areas where owners rely more heavily on mortgages are more sensitive to rate changes, because monthly payments and the cost of moving both rise with borrowing costs," says Xu. "Areas with a higher share of outright ownership are less exposed and may feel smaller effects from rate shocks because residents who own their homes outright are likely indifferent to changes in borrowing costs."

Ultimately, those market forces sway inventory levels, home prices, and whether first-time buyers can access homeownership.

With mortgage rates stuck above 7% and the Federal Reserve all but certain to raise interest rates in December—and possibly again in January 2027—to combat inflation, the lock-in effect is poised to chill the market again.

Homeowners sitting on low mortgage rates are reluctant to give them up, keeping much-needed inventory off the market. That supply squeeze, in turn, puts upward pressure on prices and makes it harder for renters to access homeownership.

Free-and-clear owners, however, are not bound by borrowing costs and can list whenever they choose.

"A mortgage-free owner isn’t watching interest rates to decide when to move," Christie Goldman, a real estate agent with Better Homes and Gardens Real Estate Central in Charleston, WV, tells Realtor.com. "They can buy their next home with cash, which makes their offer stronger, and they can close on their own timeline without a lender, an appraisal contingency, or rate risk."

Across the 50 states and the District of Columbia, West Virginia stands out with the lowest share of mortgaged homes, at 43.4%, and conversely the highest share of outright ownership, at 56.6%.

Two main forces drive this dynamic: relatively low median home prices and an older population that tends to hold on to properties longer than residents in many other states.

"In West Virginia, a paid-off home isn’t a someday goal. It's how people here live," says Goldman. "When people put down roots here, they stay."

It is common for a local family to purchase a home, raise their children there, and pay it off, often with the next generation buying property in the same community.

According to Goldman, affordability is what makes that cycle possible.

In October 2026, the median asking price in West Virginia was $259,999, well below the national median of $415,000.

"At those prices, owning your home free and clear is a realistic goal here, not a distant dream," says the agent, pointing to the 2025 United Van Lines’ national study that ranked West Virginia as the second-leading inbound destination for movers.

"Many of those buyers sell a higher-priced home elsewhere and can pay cash here," says Goldman. "Once they discover the mountains, the community, and the pace of life, they don’t want to leave."

Xu also attributes West Virginia's high share of mortgage-free owners to the state's slow population growth, particularly among young adults, which has kept new borrowers from entering the market in large numbers.

Between 2015 and 2025, the population aged 18–34 fell 5% in West Virginia, while the same age group in the U.S. grew 3.8%.

Owning one's home outright offers many perks, sharply reducing monthly expenses and creating a buffer against economic headwinds.

"Mortgage-free homeowners have more financial flexibility, especially with today's higher interest rates and rising living costs," Thomas O’Shaughnessy, vice president and real estate broker at Clever Real Estate, tells Realtor.com. "They don't have monthly mortgage payments, which makes it easier to manage expenses, save money, and handle unexpected repairs or emergencies."

In theory, a high percentage of debt-free homeowners can also help unlock inventory for the next wave of buyers.

"They may be more willing to list, downsize, move elsewhere, or buy again," says O'Shaughnessy. "All of these can improve inventory and help move the market in your community."

In West Virginia, however, Goldman notes that high levels of mortgage-free ownership does not necessarily flood the market with fresh listings because people put down deep roots and tend to stay in their homes for decades.

On the flip side, Washington, DC, and Maryland log the highest shares of mortgaged homes in the nation, at 73.5% and 69%, respectively—a trend Xu links to the region's job market.

"Federal, professional, and contracting employment draws midcareer workers, who buy homes and borrow soon after arriving," she notes.

In 2025, nearly 45% of DC homeowners and 36% of Maryland homeowners were aged 35 to 54. Elevated housing costs also force many buyers to finance: The median listing price in DC was $549,000 and $424,894 in Maryland last month.

Given that local homeowners carry so much mortgage debt, rate hikes hit markets like DC and Maryland particularly hard.

"Many buyers there need loans, so fewer can afford to buy, and homeowners with low-rate mortgages are less likely to sell," says Xu.

The latest ACS data from the U.S. Census Bureau shows that in 2025, homeownership among households aged 75 and up rose to 78.3%, up from 75.7% in 2010.

During the same period, the mortgage-free share among this demographic fell from 79.7% to 71.3%. In other words, most baby boomers still own outright, but the share with a loan rose from 20.3% to 28.7%.

Xu says the two trends—more seniors owning their homes, and more of those owners carrying a mortgage—together shape when senior sellers are likely to list.

"A senior with a low-rate loan faces a lock-in effect in today’s high-rate environment," says Xu. "Selling means giving up that cheap financing for a more expensive loan on the next home, which can keep the house off the market longer and slow the handoff to the next generation."

Meanwhile, seniors who own outright can sell on their own schedule, whether for health, care, or downsizing, so their home is more likely to pass to the next generation when the owner’s circumstances change.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5531. Compass follows through on Reffkin’s threat, sues 15 MLSs

The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.

Several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules. Now, the brokerage giant is taking another 15 of them to federal court.

The company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

The announcement marks a major escalation in a fight that has been building since September, fueled by demand letters, legal threats and increasingly pointed public messaging from Compass execs. Eight of the 15 MLSs targeted Thursday are already suing Compass in two separate federal cases, adding another layer to an increasingly complicated legal battle.

A Compass spokesperson described the latest lawsuits to Inman as a follow-through on Reffkin’s warnings at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale in late September, noting that some MLS organizations had filed their own lawsuits before Compass took legal action.

The lawsuits target six MLSs in California, three in North Carolina and six others across the country.

At the center of the lawsuits are MLS rules that require agents to submit listings to the MLS once they begin publicly marketing a property.

Sellers can generally keep their homes off the MLS through an office-exclusive arrangement. But advertising a property on a brokerage website, social media or other public channels typically triggers a requirement to share the listing with the MLS.

Compass argues that those rules unfairly limit competition and prevent agents from offering alternative marketing strategies, even when homeowners want to advertise their properties outside the MLS first.

“Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson said in a statement shared with Inman. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”

The brokerage also rejected warnings from MLS leaders that allowing public marketing without requiring listings to be shared through the MLS would harm buyers, sellers or competing agents.

Compass pointed to seven of the nation’s 25 largest MLSs that it said already allow agents to publicly market office-exclusive listings without fines. Those MLSs cover approximately 340,000 agents across 12 states, according to the company.

“If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30 percent of the country?” the spokesperson said.

MLS leaders counter that their rules are intended to ensure that publicly marketed homes are available to other brokers and their buyers. They argue that agents who benefit from access to shared MLS listings should also contribute their own publicly marketed properties.

California Regional MLS CEO Art Carter, who spent months negotiating with Reffkin before the dispute reached federal court, emphasized that point in a recent interview with Inman.

“At some point, you’ve got to say, this is a cooperative,” Carter said.

Carter also warned that withholding listings from MLS databases could leave appraisers and lenders with incomplete information about home sales, making it harder to determine accurate property values.

The new complaints largely echo arguments Compass made in its Oct. 16 antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, accusing MLS organizations of restricting competition through their listing rules. In the complaints filed Thursday against MLSs, Compass seeks triple damages and court orders blocking enforcement of the challenged rules.

On Sept. 8, Compass attorneys sent California Regional MLS a demand letter calling on the organization to stop fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings. The brokerage gave CRMLS until Oct. 6 to comply, warning that it was prepared to spend millions of dollars on litigation if its demands weren’t met.

Similar letters went to other MLS organizations across the country.

On Sept. 23, Compass International Holdings sent a separate letter demanding that MLS organizations stop sharing its agents’ production and listing data with third-party companies that help competing brokerages recruit agents. The letter specifically identified vendors Courted, BrokerMetrics and Brokerkit as examples of companies using MLS data for recruiting.

Compass argued that information provided to MLS organizations for real estate transactions shouldn’t be used to help competitors recruit its agents. It sought greater control over how that data was distributed, including the ability to exclude information associated with its brokerage brands from feeds used by recruiting companies.

Industry experts who recently spoke to Inman questioned parts of Compass’ argument, noting that MLS data serves purposes beyond recruiting and that access is often governed by agreements with brokerages and technology vendors.

Compass later raised the issue in its October antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging it lost millions of dollars in commissions after agents were recruited away using data the MLS allegedly sold to competing brokerages.

On Sept. 30, Reffkin took his fight over private listings directly to MLS executives at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale. During a contentious session that drew pushback from attendees, Reffkin warned that Compass would begin filing antitrust lawsuits in mid-October against MLSs that continued fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings.

Photo by Michael Roberts of AJ Canaria Creative Services

He said Compass wanted to display listings on its own website without agents facing penalties, while some MLS executives questioned whether the company’s demands went further and could undermine cooperation.

The dispute reached federal court Oct. 5, when CRMLS sued Compass. Compass filed its own antitrust complaint against CRMLS on Oct. 16.

Amid the escalations, tensions and litigation in recent weeks, MLS organizations have also begun raising money to defend their rules in court. CRMLS announced plans for an MLS Cooperation Legal Defense Fund on Sept. 30, while CMLS subsequently announced a separate legal action fund to be run by an independent nonprofit.

In an Oct. 27 interview with Inman, CMLS CEO Jessica Edgerton said the organization had received preliminary financial commitments and was developing a process for reviewing requests for assistance.

The growing dispute has also coincided with changes to how Compass employees participate in industry leadership. On Nov. 9, Inman broke the news that Compass International Holdings had adopted a policy restricting salaried employees from serving in Realtor association leadership positions. The directive came after brokerage managers and other employees were instructed to step down from association leadership roles, including positions some had spent years working toward.

Compass confirmed the policy change, saying it was extending a similar approach previously adopted by Anywhere Real Estate, which merged with Compass earlier this year. The company did not clarify whether exceptions were permitted or whether the restrictions also applied to MLS boards and committees.

Below is one of the 15 federal antitrust complaints filed by Compass against MLS organizations on Thursday. The lawsuits make similar legal arguments challenging restrictions on publicly marketing listings outside the MLS.

#5530. Uber started offering Amazon's Zoox robotaxis to riders in Las Vegas

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Riders who request UberX and other ride types may be matched with a Zoox vehicle at no additional cost, the companies said

Uber $UBER Technologies began offering robotaxis from Amazon $AMZN-owned Zoox through its app in Las Vegas on Monday, the companies said. It is the first time Zoox has partnered with a third-party platform.

Riders who book UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric or Wait & Save could be paired with a Zoox car without paying extra. Riders can raise the odds of landing a Zoox by opting in through "Ride Preferences" in the app settings. Zoox will keep operating its own app in Las Vegas.

Uber and Zoox signed a multi-year agreement with MGM Resorts International under which the two are the official providers of rideshare and robotaxi service at MGM's Las Vegas properties. The companies said they will work with MGM on pickups and drop-offs, on-property wayfinding, in-app guidance and infrastructure changes meant to ease traffic flow.

Samarth Kejriwal, Uber's global head of autonomous mobility, said in a statement that the launch is "another step toward making autonomous transportation part of everyday life." Zoox co-founder and CTO Jesse Levinson said in a statement that the company is seeing "more riders choosing to ride with Zoox" as it expands service in Las Vegas.

Uber and Zoox plan to bring their partnership to Los Angeles in 2027. Zoox is due to begin initial operations there by the end of 2026, through its own app.

The launch adds to competition with Waymo, which has begun operating in Las Vegas, according to Bloomberg. Uber has offered rides in Motional vehicles in Las Vegas since March, but a human safety driver still sits at the controls of those cars. Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, speaking in this month's earnings remarks, predicted the Motional cars will go fully driverless "soon" once Zoox is live, according to Bloomberg.

Khosrowshahi said on the company's earnings call for the third quarter that Uber plans to give its app a separate autonomous ride choice and increase vehicle supply in the months ahead, according to TechCrunch. Customers have no means of requesting a Zoox vehicle specifically at launch.

The Nevada Transportation Authority voted unanimously this year to approve a permit under which Uber can put as many as 1,000 robotaxis on the road in Clark County, using vehicles from its Motional and Zoox partnerships, according to TechCrunch. Uber told TechCrunch it will not handle upkeep or other support for Zoox's vehicles in Las Vegas.

#5529. Sovereign or not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide

BREAKING ANALYSIS by David Vellante and Amit Eyal Govrin

Sovereignty is everywhere right now, and most people still can’t agree on what it means and, just as importantly, what it all means to them.

This week theCUBE Research releases its new market report, Sovereign or Not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide. In this Breaking Analysis, we’re joined by its author, Amit Eyal Govrin, lead analyst for sovereign AI at theCUBE Research and CEO of Agentcy Labs, to talk about why he wrote it, what sovereignty is and what it isn’t, and what surprised him most in the findings.

The full scores are in the report. Read the full report online: Sovereign or Not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide https://siliconangle.com/sovereign-or-not

Dave: As someone who’s been leading the thought leadership in this domain, how did you come up with the inspiration to research this topic and write the report?

Amit: To understand the how, it helps to understand the why. I’ve been thinking about this subject for a while now. It hasn’t always been called “sovereignty,” but the tenets have always been the same.

It all started around four years ago, as I’ve been a builder in this space for that long. First with Kubiya, one of the industry’s first agentic implementations, deploying agents in enterprise production environments as early as September 2023, before agents were even an industry term.

We were deploying as a software-as-a-service company, and many of those concerns were legitimate. As a software company, we got to keep our intellectual property and license it out. If we were successful, we would create dependency, which effectively meant customers lost control of their crown jewels.

When we started Agentcy Labs earlier this year, customers familiar with our work approached us, and many of these points crystallized for us. What they told us: We’re relieved you are no longer at Kubiya. It’s not that we ever doubted your technology or the value it brings. Quite the opposite. That was what they were afraid of. Kubiya creates a dependency, adoption balloons, and they lose control of their costs. Or a vendor changes the meter on them because of shareholder pressure or regulatory controls.

What clicked for us is that their resistance was never about Kubiya or our technology. It was about the loss of control of their alpha. Namely, the Agentic Operating System, the key driver of their artificial intelligence transformation, which falls under our technological pillar.

It doesn’t matter if the vendor is a startup, an AI lab or a hyperscaler. No enterprise can afford to mortgage its entire business on an external dependency on such a key issue. It’s far too strategic not to own outright.

That finding forced us to rethink the model behind software, dig deeper into sovereignty as an issue of control, and help the industry define it in a more standardized way.

Dave: So control is the heart of it. But when most people hear sovereignty, they think about where the data sits. Is that the wrong way to look at it?

Amit: Sovereignty goes well beyond territory, which is often the most misunderstood aspect. People hear sovereignty and immediately revert to the sovereign state: government initiatives, national security, on-premises air-gapped environments. That can be true in some cases. But by and large, our sovereignty discussions involve enterprises and regulated industries that have sovereignty as a core tenet of their AI initiatives.

It goes beyond buzzwords and sovereign-washing claims. Think back to the explosive Alex Karp interview on CNBC claiming enterprises are losing their alpha to frontier labs. I largely agree with that claim, by the way. Only he finished his pitch by offering customers to move it over to Palantir. In other words: Stop mortgaging your alpha to Anthropic and OpenAI, come rent it from us.

That interview was my trigger point to take up arms and educate the industry on sovereignty: what it is, what it isn’t, and most importantly, what you, as a buyer of AI, can do about it.

Dave: And you’ve been out in the field with buyers ever since. What did those conversations teach you, and how did that shape the framework?

Amit: Since then, we’ve been included in dozens of engagements with enterprises, governments and policymakers around the world, from Washington to Brussels, New Delhi, Sydney and even Riyadh. We are in the room when sovereignty discussions happen. That helped us shape our view, tease out the concerns, and focus on what really matters and why. From those discussions came the 5 Pillars of Sovereignty framework. We use it today to assess all vendor relationships, policy and regulation, and geopolitical events.

Dave: Which brings us to the report. You started with the hyperscalers. Walk us through how you approached it.

Amit: In our first edition, Sovereign or Not? The Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide, we take the buyer’s lens and assess each hyperscaler by its sovereignty posture.

Hint: By definition, working with any hyperscaler means ceding a good portion of control over your Operational, Technological, Legal and Financial pillars. Oftentimes that’s the reality in the real world.

My view: Sovereignty is not a purity test. It’s perfectly acceptable to go with a hyperscaler, as long as it’s a known dependency you priced in as an acceptable risk. If that’s the case, let us guide you through these considerations to the best path forward for your organization.

Dave: OK, let’s get to the part everyone wants to know. Who scored what, and why?

Amit: We looked at seven hyperscalers and 40 of their offerings, from the point of view of buyers in five regions: the U.S., Europe, Asia-Pacific, Latin America and the rest, including the Middle East and Africa. Everything is scored out of 5.

The short version: The most sovereign product a hyperscaler sells is the one the hyperscaler itself can’t reach.

On these tests, sovereignty often runs inverse to how a hyperscaler is built. A shared global control plane and services the vendor runs for the customer make a cloud easy to adopt, but every layer the vendor runs is a layer the buyer does not control. Amazon Web Services and Google built their platforms around that abstraction, which becomes a hindrance once a buyer needs to run the stack without them. The grades measure how much control a buyer can take back, not the quality of the cloud.

Who came out on top, who came in last, and by how much, is in the report. And every score is backed by a source. Don’t like your grade? Publish the document and we’ll re-score it.

Fair is fair, though. Every one of the seven owns some ground:

Dave: What surprised you most when you went through the findings?

Amit: None of the hyperscalers has a practical solution for the U.S. CLOUD Act, and that alone has created a real legal clawback on non-U.S. companies.

In plain English: The U.S. government can ask an American cloud company for data it controls, no matter which country the data sits in. A sovereign cloud in Brandenburg, run by a German subsidiary, doesn’t change the answer. It’s still owned by an American company.

The vendors aren’t hiding it. AWS told us as much on the record. Microsoft’s own lawyer in France told the French Senate he couldn’t guarantee French data would never reach U.S. authorities. That’s honesty, and we don’t penalize honesty. It’s the law, and it applies to every American cloud the same way.

The fixes buyers are being sold, like keeping data local, holding your own encryption keys, or a contract promise to fight requests, don’t change who the government can go to.

Dave: So what’s a non-U.S. buyer supposed to do about that?

Amit: There’s no perfect answer today, only partial ones.

Going with a hyperscaler is fine, as long as you know the risk and priced it in. What’s not fine is believing a data center in Brandenburg, on its own merits, solved your sovereignty problem.

Dave: And this is just the first of several. Where do you go from here?

Amit: This is the first of a series: neoclouds, OEMs, telcos and specialized sovereign initiatives, wherever you happen to be, whether you’re a U.S., EU, Latin American, APAC or Middle Eastern buyer. Every edition covers the 5 Pillars, plus security, regulation and exit costs. Readers will be surprised by how deep we got, including quotes from the hyperscalers themselves and surveys of actual buyers. I truly think this will be valuable to everyone listening and reading.

Dave: That’s phenomenal, Amit. This is a cutting-edge report on a truly important and timely subject. If previously you were building on the frontier, you’re now squarely on the frontier of research. The scores, the vendor answers and the buyer data are all in the full report.

Read the full report online: Sovereign or Not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide

Amit Eyal Govrin is lead analyst for sovereign AI at theCUBE Research and CEO of Agentcy Labs, which designs and builds sovereign AI platforms for enterprises and governments. #5528. Contractor at Site of Brooklyn Building Collapse Was Previously Sued for Negligence

The general contractor overseeing the construction site adjacent to a deadly building collapse in Brooklyn was previously accused in a lawsuit of compromising the structural integrity of nearby properties during an excavation project, court records show.

Signage at the construction site at 2625 Bedford Ave., as well as planning documents filed with the Department of Buildings, show that Townhouse Builders, Inc, doing business as Promont, was the general contractor overseeing the construction project.

Building records show that the project involved excavation work directly adjacent to the three-story mixed-use building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. that fully collapsed on Wednesday, killing eight people, including two children, and leaving 18 others injured.

The construction project had a documented history of safety concerns flagged by DOB inspectors, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani says there will be a full investigation into whether any issues at the Bedford Ave. construction site contributed to the collapse.

"If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them accountable," the mayor said.

Now, court records reviewed by Realtor.com® show that Townhouse Builders was accused in a 2020 lawsuit of causing "a breached wall, substantial shifting, settlement and cracking" to an adjacent property during a separate construction job.

New York state records list Mordachai Waisbrod as the CEO of Townhouse Builders. The company and an attorney listed as representing the Townhouse in the 2020 lawsuit did not respond to requests for comment from Realtor.com.

Townhouse Builders has worked on numerous projects across New York, including a retail location on Atlantic Ave., a residential tower on Delancey St. in the Lower East Side, and the redevelopment of a residential tower on Park Row.

In 2016, Townhouse Builders was hired by developer Moris Yeroshalm to serve as general contractors on the construction of a six-story hotel at 1200 Broadway in Brooklyn's Bed-Stuy neighborhood.

In a lawsuit filed in Kings County Supreme Court in 2020, Yeroshalmi alleged that "the construction activity performed by Townhouse at the Project caused damage and compromised the structural integrity of Plaintiff's property and adjacent properties."

The suit alleges that "the construction caused, among other things, a breached wall, substantial shifting, settlement and cracking of Plaintiff's property and the adjacent properties, in addition to broken footing of the adjacent properties and structural destabilization of Plaintiff's property and the adjacent properties."

The suit lists the allegedly damaged properties as 1196 Broadway, and 15 and 17 Patchen Avenue, all located in Brooklyn.

The lawsuit further alleges that 1196 Broadway "was severely damaged by the excavation activity" and that 15 and 17 Patchen Ave. "were severely damaged by the pile driving activities."

In the suit, Yeroshalmi alleges Townhouse "breached their duty and were negligent…by allowing construction activities to compromise and destroy the structural integrity of Plaintiff's property and adjacent properties."

Further, the lawsuit accuses Townhouse of "failing to perform a physical inspection and prepare a proper pre-construction survey of Plaintiff's property prior to performing excavation and underpinning, failing to support the premises walls and by allowing the excavation and underpinning to compromise the structural integrity of Plaintiff's property and adjacent properties."

Yeroshalmi sued for damages totaling more than $1.1 million. The suit remains open with the next hearing in the case to be held in January 2027.

A review of Department of Buildings complaints and violations related to 1200 Broadway show that Townhouse Builders received a Class 2 or "major" violation in 2016 for "failure to monitor adjoining structures for movement in all directions during excavation-related activity that may adversely affect adjoining structures."

That same year, it received a Class 1 violation for "failure to safeguard all persons and property affected by construction operations," noting that the excavator's bucket damaged the brick foundation wall of an adjoining building during excavation. Class 1 violations are "Immediately Hazardous violations" that "must be corrected immediately."

In 2017, it received another Class 2 violation for failure to monitor cracks on adjacent buildings during excavation.

In total, the DOB fined Townhouse Builders $10,400 for those three violations.

Court records show Townhouse Builders, under their own name and Promont, have been sued 67 times since 2012. Thirteen of those cases, including the one mentioned above, remain open. It appears the bulk of those cases have to do with injuries on job sites.

On Wednesday, the Brooklyn district attorney's office announced it was opening a criminal investigation into the cause of the collapse.

“We are working closely with the Department of Buildings and our law enforcement partners to determine whether any criminal conduct contributed to this tragedy,” District Attorney Eric Gonzalez said in the statement.

On Thursday afternoon, Mamdani announced the city would be sweeping 100 other sites associated with five "entities" involved in a construction project adjacent to the collapsed building. Mamdani and Department of Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani declined to name the five companies they would be focusing their investigation on.

She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. #5527. ULA's Vulcan rocket failed mid-flight, destroying 40 Amazon internet satellites

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The failure on Amazon Leo's first Vulcan mission is the first for ULA and is expected to lead to a lengthy investigation

United Launch Alliance, the Boeing $BA-Lockheed Martin $LMT venture, lost 40 Amazon $AMZN Leo internet satellites on Sunday when its Vulcan rocket broke down roughly 10 minutes into its climb from Cape Canaveral, Florida, according to Reuters. The failure is the first in the company's history.

The rocket lifted off at 12:40 p.m. ET, according to Bloomberg.

Amazon had targeted a Nov. 15 liftoff for the mission, called Leo Vulcan 1 (LV-01), the company said. It was the first of 38 launches Amazon has contracted with ULA, and it was to carry 40 satellites to low Earth orbit.

ULA said the vehicle "suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," according to Reuters. The cause was unclear, and ULA said it had no specific data yet on what occurred.

"There is risk with any launch, and that's especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01," Amazon said in a statement, according to Reuters. Amazon said it believes ULA will take lessons from the flight and follow through on its longer-range goals for Vulcan.

The failure is expected to trigger a long technical probe that would sideline the rocket from commercial service for months, according to Reuters. Blue Origin, which supplies Vulcan's BE-4 engines, is working with ULA on the investigation. Reuters said it was unclear whether the engines played a role.

Sunday's flight was only the fifth for Vulcan since it debuted in 2024, and it followed a nine-month gap between launches, according to Reuters. Amazon has placed 398 Leo satellites in orbit over 14 launches since 2025, roughly 12% of the 3,236 required to offer service worldwide.

Before the launch, Amazon said its second Vulcan mission, LV-02, was being prepared and was expected to launch within weeks of a nominal LV-01 mission. The company also said its next Arianespace mission, Leo Europe 4, was targeting no earlier than Nov. 23 from Kourou, French Guiana.

#5526. Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

Turn closings into case studies. Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.

I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.

We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.

I don’t think there’s anything wrong with celebrating a closing. But I’ve always felt that the story behind the sale is often more interesting than the sale itself, especially when you consider what a prospective client is trying to figure out when deciding who to hire.

Most sellers probably assume any experienced agent can put their home on the market. What they don’t necessarily know is how that agent approaches marketing, how much effort they’ll put into a listing or how they’ll respond when something doesn’t go according to plan. Those are difficult things to communicate in a listing presentation when every agent is promising some version of the same thing.

For years, I’ve tried to give people a better understanding of our work by creating case studies of the homes we’ve sold. Initially, that meant compiling listing footage into a Reel with a longer caption explaining the transaction. More recently, I’ve been experimenting with carousels that tell those stories across multiple slides using footage we already created to market the property.

What I like about this approach is that people can see what working with us might actually look like, rather than simply taking our word for it.

We recently sold a property in San Pedro where we hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. We found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and we had to start again.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein)

We eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when we shared the case study, we didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing we’d done. We opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

I liked that opening because it put the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, we explained how we responded, got the property back in front of buyers, and ultimately closed.

We’ve used the same approach to tell different stories, including a transaction in Hesperia, California, where we coordinated a sale for sellers who had moved out of state, and a humorous carousel about a San Diego transaction that generated 15,741 views.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein)

Not every transaction needs an extraordinary twist. Sometimes the interesting part is a problem you solved, a decision you made, or the work that went into making the experience easier for your client. The challenge is recognizing those moments and figuring out how to communicate them.

The storytelling portion generally takes me about 15 minutes, although gathering information and designing the finished post take additional time.

Before writing, I go through the transaction and take inventory of everything we’ve done. I want to know how many open houses we hosted, how many people attended, how many postcards we mailed, how much content we published and how many views our videos generated. I’ll also look at offers received and anything else that helps explain how the sale unfolded.

This has made me more conscious of documenting our work as we’re doing it. It’s difficult to communicate the effort behind a sale if you can’t remember the specifics, and having those numbers also makes it easier to evaluate what worked.

I then gather content we’ve already created, whether that’s property videos, walkthroughs, open house footage, or photographs. Repurposing footage gives that content another life, but agents could create something similar using listing photos.

Once I have everything together, I open ChatGPT Voice and talk through the transaction. I’ll explain the sellers’ circumstances, our approach, the decisions we made and anything unexpected. I don’t organize my thoughts beforehand because I find it more helpful to get everything out and work through the story conversationally.

What I’ve found particularly useful is having ChatGPT ask follow-up questions to identify the most compelling angle. Sometimes what I initially find interesting isn’t what another homeowner would care about, and that back-and-forth helps me consider their perspective.

Once we’ve found the angle, we work on the writing, particularly the opening two slides because Instagram can serve both to your audience. Lately, I’ve preferred carousels with moving video backgrounds, but we’ve also created Reels and experimented with humor. I’ve shared an editable version of our Canva template for anyone who wants to try the format.

If you want to try this with one of your transactions, open ChatGPT Voice and use this prompt:

“Interview me about [Address] I recently closed. Ask me one question at a time about the seller’s goals, our marketing strategy, the decisions we made, challenges we encountered and the outcome. Help me identify the most compelling part of the story and why another homeowner would care. Once we’ve found the angle, help me write a seven-slide Instagram carousel with a strong opening and a natural narrative. Use specific details and results, avoid generic sales language, and don’t invent anything.”

We’ve also been sharing these case studies in emails to our database, giving us another opportunity to demonstrate our experience to homeowners and agents who may eventually refer us business.

If you’ve been in the business for any length of time, you probably have dozens of transactions worth revisiting, with interesting stories buried in them. You don’t need a new closing every week to share those experiences, and you don’t need to make every transaction sound more dramatic than it was.

There’s tremendous value in helping people understand the work we do, particularly when so much happens behind the scenes. If we’re already investing all this time and effort into helping our clients, it seems like a missed opportunity not to share more of it.

Use this FREE Canva template to replicate these results.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#5525. NeuralSat raises $3.2M to bring high-speed data connectivity and compute to space

German startup NeuralSat GmbH announced Thursday that it has raised €2.9 million, about $3.2 million, in pre-seed funding to develop a 72-satellite data-relay processing network aimed at speeding up the flow of data from space.

Capnamic and Bayern Kapital co-led the round. Other investors participating in the round included ZOHO.VC, Robin Capital, BAB – Die Förderbank für Bremen und Bremerhaven, Mission E and KIEMIS Holding.

Founded in early 2026, NeuralSat’s satellite constellation will allow operators to offload computing and communications. According to the company, its network will deliver up to 50 gigabits per second via optical and high-frequency radio links.

The network will support real-time edge processing, hosted workloads for commercial and defense clients and provide for time-critical missions like Earth observation and signals intelligence.

“We believe the next major evolution in space will… come from connecting satellites to shared infrastructure that enables them to communicate, access computing resources, and operate together,” Chief Executive Mohd Bilal said in a statement. “Just as the internet transformed how computers interact on Earth, we intend to transform how intelligence is connected and delivered in space.”

The company said the funding will help it accelerate plans to launch its first in-orbit demonstration node, planned for October 2027. After that, NeuralSat plans to begin rolling out commercial operational satellites.

The race to develop and build better connectivity and compute capabilities in space is on. Canadian startup Kepler Communications Inc. launched its first commercial space data relay service in January, allowing resilient data transfer and onboard computing, with a next-gen optical relay network announced in August. Skyloom, acquired by quantum computing firm IonQ Inc. in early 2026, deployed 84 optical terminals and a relay architecture in low Earth orbit.

Space is not the optimal place to run processors because heat dissipation becomes a major issue with no air to carry it away. But space technology firms have developed solutions to radiate it from giant sails and other surfaces. Space-based compute may not replace terrestrial data centers, but it can enable edge compute given payload weight restrictions for orbital launch.

Starcloud Inc., formerly known as Lumen Orbit, raised $250 million in August at a $2.3 billion valuation. The company has already tested an Nvidia H100 graphics processing unit in orbit in late 2025, proving that it can scale to multi-satellite AI “data centers.” The company is now collaborating with Nvidia Corp. on upcoming space-grade chips.

Currently, data relay and compute processing in space reduce the need for other satellites to send data to Earth to complete workloads. Talking to a nearby satellite for edge compute can shave significant time off data transfers. Sending data down to Earth can take a round trip of four to more than 30 milliseconds; satellite-to-satellite is slightly faster, at three to 30 milliseconds.

The real boost comes from relaying between satellites rather than routing long distances on the ground to a data center and back, often via optical cable ground networks, which add additional lag. Over long distances across the globe, inter-satellite links are around 30% to 50% faster than sending signals down to Earth for processing.

Companies such as NeuralSat hope to use the advantage of being right there, near the data production, to provide processing capabilities, or swift relay to a satellite closer geographically to terrestrial data center processing to reduce delays.

#5524. U.K. drugmaker is in talks with the FDA to supply estrogen patches to the U.S.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The company has expanded manufacturing as U.S. prescriptions containing estradiol, a form of estrogen, doubled in two years

Theramex, a London-based drugmaker, is in talks with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration about selling its estrogen patches in the U.S., CEO Robert Stewart told Bloomberg.

Theramex has scaled up production because it anticipates the FDA could let the sales proceed, Stewart said.

"We've been in dialogue with the FDA," Stewart said, according to Bloomberg. "They have the information that they would need to be able to issue a special import, and if they do, we'd be able to immediately respond."

Theramex has no approved products in the U.S., according to Bloomberg. In exceptional cases, the FDA has leeway to let drug companies market medications it hasn't approved for a limited time. An FDA spokesperson would not discuss details or the timing of any step the agency might take regarding Theramex. The spokesperson added that when patients struggle to get their medications, the agency can turn to a number of options, temporary importation among them.

Theramex markets Evorel, an estrogen patch, in the U.K. for relief of menopause and perimenopause complaints like night sweats and hot flashes. If the FDA permits U.S. sales, the number of patches sent each month would be "substantial," Stewart said. He said customers elsewhere would not be impacted by the move.

U.S. women have had trouble finding estrogen patches while demand climbs, according to Bloomberg. Prescriptions that include estradiol, an estrogen type, have doubled over a two-year span to 4 million monthly, according to Bloomberg, citing Symphony Health data. The increase gathered pace once the FDA, a year ago, began softening its warnings on risks of heart problems, breast cancer and dementia linked to the drugs.

The FDA does not classify estrogen patches as being in short supply nationwide, the agency spokesperson said, citing company data on supply, demand and expected future demand. The American Society of Health-System Pharmacists has listed the patches as being in shortage since January, according to Bloomberg. Unless a shortage has been declared, it is uncommon for the FDA to let a firm market an unapproved drug in the U.S.

"We know for some patients these past few months have been frustrating," Sarah Ibrahim, deputy director for regulatory programs at the FDA's drug center, said Oct. 30 on a call with reporters, according to Bloomberg. She said the agency is working to address the problem.

Stewart said Theramex has contacted the FDA since the summer. He said conversations have become more specific and higher level in the past month as it became clearer that demand would outstrip manufacturers' capacity.

Theramex intends to seek FDA approval for its estrogen patches during the first six months of 2027, Stewart said. The company is in early discussions with a business partner about U.S. distribution, in case it is cleared to sell the patches sooner. Stewart declined to name the partner.

Stewart was previously CEO of Amneal Pharmaceuticals, a top U.S. seller of estrogen patches along with Viatris and Sandoz Group, according to Bloomberg.

#5523. A former professional athlete on selling real estate to other athletes

While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he said.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

Sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

Sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A big part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

Athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” said Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively new sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

You have to be patient when working with athletes, he said, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move quickly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

What you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he said.

But you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

Often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré said. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

But that can be a long road. Sangaré said it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

And when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré said; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

#5521. Stubborn input inflation pressures builders despite energy pullback

NAHB’s analysis of the October Producer Price Index shows total inputs to new residential construction up 0.3% on the month and 10.4% year over year, outpacing overall PPI inflation. Goods costs were flat in October, but building materials rose 0.5% and 5.8% annually, with diesel, plywood and board products elevated. Service inputs climbed 0.7% in October and 11.3% year over year, led by double-digit gains in trade services and transportation. The data underscores ongoing pressure on bids, budgets and pro formas, even as headline energy prices ease.  AI Summary

Residential construction input costs continued to outpace overall inflation in October, as gains in building material and service prices offset a monthly decline in energy, according to a National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) analysis of this morning’s Producer Price Index (PPI) release.

The price index for inputs to new residential construction — which combines goods and services — rose 0.3% in October and is 10.4% higher than a year ago, NAHB economist Jesse Wade said. By comparison, the PPI for final demand overall increased 0.3% in October and 6.5% year over year.

For builders, that gap underscores a persistent cost squeeze even as some headline inflation measures appear to cool.

Goods make up roughly 60% of the residential construction inputs index. Overall, the price of input goods used in new residential construction (including energy) was unchanged in October, following a 1.7% jump in September, and is up 9.8% over the past 12 months.

That stability at the top line masks diverging trends beneath the surface:

Key product categories continue to move higher:

For single-family and multifamily builders, the mix of slightly moderating year-over-year gains in some materials and still-elevated levels in others complicates bid setting, option pricing and value-engineering decisions heading into 2027 build cycles.

Service inputs to residential construction, which cover distribution margins, transportation and a range of other services, rose 0.7% in October and are 11.3% higher than October 2025, according to NAHB.

The services side of the index is split into three major components:

All three are running well above general inflation:

Because services often adjust more slowly than commodity prices, this side of the index tends to be “stickier.” For builders, that means even if some material categories ease, fully loaded installed costs can remain elevated due to freight, storage and distribution charges.

The October PPI data reinforces several themes for homebuilders, land developers and their capital partners:

Heading into 2027 selling and construction seasons, the NAHB analysis suggests that homebuilders should not assume relief in headline energy prices will translate directly into lower house costs. Instead, monitoring both material and service-side inflation — and baking higher contingencies into pro formas — will remain critical as the industry navigates persistently high input inflation alongside tighter capital markets and cautious buyers.k

#5520. Agent fleets drag the messaging layer from afterthought to AI’s coordination core

Data center telemetry, sandboxed AI workloads and fleets of agents are pushing more machine-to-machine traffic through infrastructure than ever before, exposing the limits of messaging systems built for steadier demand.

That shift is drawing attention to the Neural Autonomic Transport System, an open-source messaging system that lets applications and services exchange messages by topic. Created in 2010, NATS graduated from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation in November 2026. Its simple design suits AI workloads, according to Andrew Connolly (pictured, left), NATS project maintainer at Synadia Communications Inc., a provider of managed NATS services. When AI tools like Lovable can turn a plain-language prompt into a working web app, the messaging layer has to keep updates flowing as sandboxes come and go.

“What’s changed in the current context, or landscape, is everything is really ephemeral. If you take the Lovable example, connections coming and going really fast, tons of churn, tons of sandboxes, all these things spinning up, spinning down,” Connolly said. “Not every technology can handle that.”

Connolly and Waldemar Quevedo (right), project maintainer of NATS at Synadia, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how NATS handles traffic from short-lived sandboxes, carries data center telemetry and helps AI agents hand off work. (* Disclosure below.)

The demands go well beyond app sandboxes. The project itself has grown from single-cluster deployments into a system that spans data centers, regions and clouds, with one AI app builder recently rebuilding its real-time service on NATS to serve millions of subscriptions, Quevedo noted.

“NATS has evolved to be able to communicate multiple data centers with a super cluster topology with the gateways,” Quevedo said. “It is smart [at routing] the interest graph out to multiple regions, multiple availability zones, multi-cloud.”

Some data center operators use NATS to carry power and cooling telemetry, and Nvidia Corp. built its AI factory event bus on the system as part of its DSX reference architecture, Connolly said. NATS can also route messages across fleets of AI agents, with its JetStream persistence engine and key-value store preserving the state agents need to hand off work.

“In some sense, agentic systems are just microservices systems, but at a bigger scale,” Connolly said. “NATS was good for microservices. It’s going to be great for AI agents.”

#5519. Tyson Foods sees its beef losses easing as plant closures and cattle imports help

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Tyson projects a fiscal 2027 beef result of a $300 million loss to a $100 million profit, versus a $654 million adjusted loss in fiscal 2026

Tyson Foods projected a smaller beef loss for fiscal 2027 on Monday, forecasting adjusted segment operating results between a $300 million loss and a $100 million profit. The segment reported an adjusted operating loss of $654 million in fiscal 2026.

An annual profit would mark the segment's first positive year since 2023, according to Bloomberg. Tyson projected companywide adjusted operating profit between $1.7 billion and $2.15 billion for fiscal 2027, versus the $1.98 billion it posted in fiscal 2026.

Beef remained a drag in the fourth quarter ended Oct. 3. The segment lost $514 million on an operating basis, against $277 million a year earlier, as volume fell 6.0%.

Tyson expects fiscal 2027 sales to drop 3.5% to 5.5%, mainly reflecting reduced beef volumes as it reshapes its plant network and contends with scarce cattle. The company cited U.S. Department of Agriculture projections that domestic beef production will decrease about 2% in fiscal 2027.

Margins are improving because the shuttered plants need fewer cattle and because foreign shipments of live animals and ground beef are adding supply, according to Bloomberg. Live cattle shipments from Mexico have resumed, with more than 80,000 head entering the U.S. since late August.

Tyson cut its fiscal 2026 profit forecast in September for the second time in about a month as beef losses widened. The company said at the time that the restructuring should begin reducing operating cost pressures as it enters fiscal 2027.

In August, Tyson announced plans to close its Joslin, Illinois, beef plant and its Eagle Mountain, Utah, case-ready facility and to pursue the sale of its Pasco, Washington, plant. The moves followed the earlier closure of its Lexington, Nebraska, plant and a cutback to one shift at Amarillo, Texas.

Last week, Tyson began restoring second-shift operations at its Amarillo plant ahead of a planned long-term partnership with Allied Beef Company, a consortium of ranchers. The company expects the shift to reach full operation by summer 2027.

The industry outlook remains uncertain. Typical retail prices for ground beef have stopped climbing near $7 a pound, and drought could force ranchers to send more animals to slaughter, according to Bloomberg.

#5517. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

Want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

A sold comp tells us where a buyer said yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

One of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”

When I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

This is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”

Twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.
