#5516. FDA declined to approve Summit Therapeutics' lung cancer drug

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The agency said ivonescimab lacks a statistically significant overall survival benefit; Summit said it will continue development

Summit Therapeutics announced on Sunday that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration issued a complete response letter declining to approve ivonescimab, its lung cancer drug, in its present form. Summit sought approval of the drug with platinum-containing chemotherapy for patients with locally advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer who had received prior EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy.

The FDA determined that substantial evidence of effectiveness is not established without a statistically significant improvement in overall survival, the company said. The agency also indicated that a progression-free survival benefit without a significant overall survival benefit does not support a positive benefit-risk profile. Summit included the announcement in an SEC filing.

The application rested on HARMONi, a global Phase 3 trial that compared ivonescimab plus chemotherapy with placebo plus chemotherapy. The trial had two primary endpoints, progression-free survival and overall survival. It met the progression-free survival endpoint. In the primary overall survival analysis, the ivonescimab combination showed a positive trend that fell short of statistical significance, Summit said.

In a post-hoc analysis of longer-term follow-up, the overall survival hazard ratio was 0.76 in the full population, in Asian patients and in western patients, according to the company. Summit said no FDA-approved regimen has shown a statistically significant overall survival benefit in this patient setting.

On safety, 16 patients (7.3%) stopped ivonescimab because of treatment-related adverse events, compared with 11 patients (5.0%) who stopped placebo. Four patients (1.8%) in the ivonescimab arm and five patients (2.3%) in the chemotherapy-only arm died of treatment-related adverse events. Summit said the trial showed no new safety signals.

“We are disappointed for patients and their families awaiting additional treatment options in this setting,” Robert W. Duggan, chairman and co-chief executive of Summit, said in a statement. He said the company’s belief in ivonescimab is unchanged and that it will continue its clinical development program.

Summit is developing ivonescimab in lung, colorectal, urothelial and renal cell cancers. The company said ivonescimab is not approved by any regulator in its license territories, including the U.S. and Europe, and that no PD-1 x VEGF bispecific antibodies are approved in the U.S. Akeso invented the drug, which was first approved in China in May 2024.

Summit obtained ivonescimab from Akeso in 2022 through an agreement valued at as much as $5 billion, which covers the U.S., Canada, Europe and Japan, according to MarketWatch.

AstraZeneca $AZN completed a $2 billion equity investment in Summit last month, giving it a roughly 12% stake while Summit kept full development and commercial rights to the drug. The investment came with a clinical collaboration to test AstraZeneca's sonesitatug vedotin alongside ivonescimab.

#5515. PRMG hires 100-person team from Gold Star in organic growth push

PRMG has recruited the Responsive Mortgage team from Gold Star Mortgage. The move fits PRMG’s strategy of organic, team-based growth instead of acquisitions and is the second large group to join in 90 days.   AI Summary

Paramount Residential Mortgage Group (PRMG) has hired a roughly 100-person team of loan officers, processors and underwriters from Gold Star Mortgage Financial Group, leaning on recruitment as its primary growth strategy.

Responsive Mortgage‘s move comes during what PRMG chief lending officer and partner Kevin Peranio described as a seasonal window for larger team transitions.

“I call this time of year the peak transition season,” Peranio said in an interview with HousingWire. “When the year slows down between August and February, larger teams typically make the moves.

“Everyone’s busy in the spring — it’s purchase season — so people don’t really make moves during that period. Then they have some time to reflect over the summer, and if they are going to make a transition, they typically do it when the leaves are changing.”

RETR data on loan officer migration patterns shows that LOs changed companies at a relatively steady pace throughout 2025, but “mega producers” that close more than 100 units per year have been more likely to move in October and May.

According to data from InGenius, 55 loan officers moved from Gold Star to PRMG. They’ve produced about $252 million since January, with most of that volume in Texas and Florida.

Peranio said the Responsive team, led by Mike Benton, had another proposal from a large retail lender that included a sizable signing bonus. But they chose PRMG based on what Peranio called a “cultural fit and a model match,” as well as alignment on technology.

“The Responsive team has proprietary technology in building relationships between Realtors and originators, and they wanted to continue to build that out and maximize the investment that they’ve made in their own technology,” Peranio said. “We plug into that technology to bring the loan into our fulfillment.”

PRMG has reached about $2.7 billion in total production year to date, per InGenius. Data from the Nationwide Multistate Licensing System shows the lender had 805 sponsored loan officers and 117 active branches as of Friday.

Gold Star, based in Ann Arbor, Michigan, has originated about $1.6 billion year to date, compared to $1.9 billion during the same period last year, per InGenius. NMLS shows Gold Star with 221 sponsored loan officers and 48 active branches. A spokesperson for Gold Star did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Peranio said PRMG is focused on organic growth and does not buy companies.

“We don’t acquire companies. We’re like a nice, slow, controlled grower. We’ve been around for 25 years,” he said. “Originators like to feel they control their destiny. And when a single owner — or whatever the ownership group is — just sells people to another group of people, it inherently doesn’t sit right. It’s like, what am I doing here if I can be sold to another company without my permission or being asked about it?”

Peranio added that when these transitions work, it is typically because there’s a leader within the group who’s transparent and communicates clearly with the team ahead of the move.

The Responsive team is the second large group — defined by PRMG as more than 20 people — to join the company in the past 90 days. Peranio said PRMG structures deals with upside on future revenue and offers some upfront funding to support transitions, rather than signing bonuses.

“If you write a check to trap someone for a certain amount of years, the reason that’s a trap is because the lenders that write those checks usually give them worse pricing,” Peranio said. “We think that doesn’t make any sense, especially when all pricing is getting more and more competitive in this new world of AI.”

#5514. Main Capital Partners Invests in TaskRay, Joining Cloud Coach and JustOn to Transform Customer Delivery on Salesforce

DENVER, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Main Capital Partners ("Main") has invested in TaskRay, an AI-native project management platform built on Salesforce, joining it with portfolio company  Cloud Coach and its German subsidiary JustOn. Together, the three companies aim to redefine customer delivery with an AI-powered platform connecting project management, resource management, professional services automation (PSA), and financial operations for enterprises.

The combined company will be led by Sam Swan as Chief Executive Officer and will serve over 800 customers across North America and Europe with approximately 80 employees across three offices.

One platform from closed deal to collected cash

The combination of TaskRay, Cloud Coach, and JustOn brings together complementary Salesforce-native solutions to address a significant market opportunity. TaskRay provides AI-powered customer onboarding and project management; Cloud Coach delivers professional services automation (PSA), portfolio and resource management; and JustOn connects billing, invoicing, and project financials.

Together, the companies will deliver greater value to existing customers through expanded capabilities and shared expertise, while building toward a unified, AI-powered customer delivery platform. The vision is to transform the entire post-sale lifecycle, from closed deal to collected cash, helping enterprises accelerate customer outcomes, improve operational efficiency, and unlock revenue faster.

TaskRay was among the first Salesforce ISVs to introduce autonomous AI workflows and MCP technology, including one of the first ten ISV MCP servers on AppExchange. Building on this momentum, the combined company will advance agentic AI to automate routine delivery and billing tasks, freeing teams to focus on strategy and customer relationships. Additional AI capabilities are planned for the first half of 2027.

For existing customers, nothing changes today. All three businesses will continue to offer the same products, support teams, and partner programs without disruption. Over time, customers will benefit from expanded capabilities as the companies bring their solutions together into a more unified platform.

"We see significant value in bringing the businesses together and believe the combination will create a compelling joint offering, extending the value of best-in-class solutions built on Salesforce," said Daan Visscher, Partner at Main & Chairman of Cloud Coach's Supervisory Board. "The collective businesses have built deep expertise in the Salesforce ecosystem, and customers will benefit from a unified best-of-breed solution spanning the entire post-sale cycle. We look forward to working closely with the combined team to support a successful integration and realize the full potential of the combined offering."

"Together, the three companies share a vision to fundamentally change how enterprises manage customer delivery on Salesforce," said Sam Swan, CEO. "From the moment a customer signs a contract to the final payment, we see an opportunity to connect the people, projects, and processes behind the scenes. By connecting every stage of customer delivery and putting AI to work in practical ways, we can help businesses operate more efficiently, accelerate growth, and deliver better experiences for their customers."

"Our highest priority remains delivering exceptional value to the customers who trust our people and products every day. What excites me most is the opportunity to build on that foundation, combining our expertise, expanding our capabilities, and accelerating investment in AI to help our customers achieve even greater success."

https://main.nl/Main Capital Partners is a software investor managing private equity funds across the Benelux, DACH, the Nordics, France, the United Kingdom, and the United States, with approximately EUR 12 billion in assets under management. With over 20 years of experience, Main works closely with management teams to achieve profitable growth and create larger international software groups. Main has approximately 105 employees across seven offices and maintains an active portfolio of over 55 software companies.

https://taskray.com/TaskRay is an AI-powered project management platform built natively on Salesforce. TaskRay helps enterprise teams accelerate customer onboarding and implementation with purpose-built templates, standardized workflows, and automation that reduces manual work and streamlines delivery. Enterprise organizations in technology, healthcare, financial services, and hospitality industries rely on TaskRay to manage customer delivery at scale, including FlashParking, Greystar, Basic-Fit International, Commerce Bank, AON, Charles Schwab Bank, ZRS Management, Rockwell Automation, and Truveris.

https://www.cloudcoach.com/Cloud Coach is a provider of professional services automation (PSA), project management, and customer success software built natively on Salesforce. With robust functionality for project portfolio management, resource planning, and time tracking, Cloud Coach helps organizations deliver projects on time and within budget.

https://www.juston.comFounded in 2010 and based in Jena, Germany, JustOn develops Salesforce-native software that automates financial processes from billing and invoicing to payment management and accounting. This helps organizations stay compliant and audit-ready. JustOn serves more than 300 organizations across software, media, real estate, logistics, and other industries.

#5513. Mirendil raises $1B in funding to speed up AI model development

Mirendil Inc., a provider of software that speeds up artificial intelligence development, has raised $1 billion in early-stage funding.

The startup stated on Thursday that Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital jointly led the Series A investment. They were joined by more than a half-dozen others including Google LLC.

Mirendil was launched last year by two former Google DeepMind and Anthropic PBC researchers. Chief Executive Officer Behnam Neyshabur is a co-inventor of SAM, a popular algorithm that makes AI models better at tasks they were not specifically trained to perform. Chief Technology Officer Harsh Mehta, in turn, spent his time at Google DeepMind and Anthropic working on pretraining projects. Pretraining is a term for the initial phase of the AI development workflow.

Mirendil’s first product, Lor, is a platform that automates many of the tasks involved in model training runs. The company says that the software does so by splitting work among hundreds of AI agents.

Large language model development involves a significant amount of trial and error. Researchers create multiple versions of an algorithm that differ from one another in small ways and compare them to find the most performant variant. According to Mirendil, Lor can automate that workflow. If an error crops up during the evaluation, the platform fixes it automatically.

Earlier this year, Mirendil asked one of its researchers to build a coding model that can compete with leading open-source LLMs. Usually, such projects are carried out by teams of specialists. Mirendil says that its automation technology enabled the researcher to build the model without any help from colleagues. The project cost $10 million and took about 3.5 months to complete.

The company’s agents wrote more than 99% of the code that powers the model, which is called Mirendil-Base. They set up infrastructure, found a suitable training algorithm and collected training data from the web. The agents then refined both the training dataset and Mirendil-Base’s architecture to boost output quality.

The LLM is the foundation of a specialized coding model called Fern that the company unveiled last month. According to Mirendil, it’s designed to automate programming challenges commonly encountered by AI labs. Fern can process 10 million input tokens per prompt, or 10 times more than Claude Opus 5.5. That’s the equivalent of about a half-million lines of code.

Fern is based on a version of Mirendil-Base with 100 billion to 500 billion parameters. Late last month, the company previewed two upgraded versions of the latter model with between 500 billion and 10 trillion parameters. Mirendil plans to use those algorithms to develop more capable LLMs.

#5512. Movement Mortgage seeks to recoup $1.2M from former LOs

Movement Mortgage is moving to enforce an arbitration ruling that says former loan officers Victor Shkolnikov and Igor Velyunskiy must repay $1.235 million in signing bonuses after leaving about a year into their three-year commitments.  AI Summary

Movement Mortgage wants two former loan officers to pay back a total of more than $1.2 million in signing bonuses after they left the company about a year into their three-year agreements.

According to court and arbitration documents, Movement paid a total of $1,235,000 in “start-up payments” to loan officers Victor Shkolnikov and Igor Velyunskiy when they joined the company in March 2022. Shkolnikov received $835,000 and Velyunskiy received $400,000.

The contracts said these payments were advances on future wages and had to be paid back in full if the loan officers left before working 36 consecutive months at the company. If they left early, the money was due within 30 days.

Both Shkolnikov and Velyunskiy left Movement around March 2023, roughly one year into their three-year commitment. Public records show Shkolnikov now works as a loan originator with United Lending Team in Illinois, while Velyunskiy is with Smart Rate Lending LLC.

Movement and the two former loan officers did not immediately respond to HousingWire’s requests for comment. National Mortgage News first reported the dispute.

Movement started arbitration in February 2024, and the cases were combined before arbitrator H. William Constangy. The LOs pushed back, filing counterclaims that accuse Movement of breach of contract, unjust enrichment, fraudulent inducement and violations of the Truth in Lending Act.

In July, the arbitrator ruled in favor of Movement. The decision said the employment agreements were valid contracts and that the two breached the contracts when they did not repay the start-up payments after leaving before the 36-month mark. All of their counterclaims were dismissed.

The award says the repayment amount will also accrue interest at North Carolina’s legal rate of 8% per year, starting in April 2023, which the arbitrator treated as the date of the breach. The arbitrator did not order either side to pay the other’s legal fees, so each party must cover its own attorneys’ costs.

In early November, Movement asked the U.S. District Court for the Western District of North Carolina, Charlotte Division, to confirm the arbitration award and turn it into a court judgment. That would make it easier for the lender to collect the money if it isn’t paid voluntarily.

#5511. Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

“Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

“I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

“A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”

#5510. Papa John's is using customer pizza photos to build an AI quality-control system

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The chain is giving a free pizza for photos of delivered orders; the promotion runs through Nov. 20 and has drawn thousands of photos

Papa John’s is handing out a complimentary pizza in exchange for a picture of a delivered order plus feedback, part of an effort to train an AI system that checks pizza quality, according to Reuters.

CEO Todd Penegor told Reuters the promotion aims to raise the standard of pizzas coming out of the chain's franchise-run locations. He said it targets inconsistencies that have become the "Achilles' heel" of the brand.

Penegor said the goal is software that can replicate the quality checks performed by the cameras installed inside the chain's stores. Those cameras rely on AI to verify that the cheese has not burned, the pepperoni is neatly sliced and the crust is properly shaped.

The in-store cameras exist at only a few hundred of the chain's 6,000 restaurants around the world, Penegor said. Customer photos might let the company bring photo-driven quality checks to many more restaurants at a lower price, according to Reuters. The customer images are less accurate than the in-store cameras.

A dashboard collects the incoming photos and customer feedback, Penegor said. The promotion began on Nov. 9 and generated thousands of photos in its first few days. It runs until Nov. 20.

Penegor said the technology was developed in-house and extends AI tools the chain previously built jointly with Google $GOOGL Cloud.

He said the responses will guide the chain in ranking which problems to tackle first and will show franchisees the areas where their stores may be lagging. The company disclosed on Nov. 5 that its global same-store sales fell 6.5% in the latest quarter.

#5508. Exclusive: Onyx Security brings AI agent governance to Glean’s enterprise AI platform

AI agent security startup Onyx Security Inc. today announced an integration with enterprise artificial intelligence platform company Glean Technologies Inc. to help enterprises govern the AI agents they build and run on Glean.

Onyx and Glean are pitching the integration at companies that are moving quickly to roll out autonomous, connected agents across their departments. Onyx claims, however, that most of them are not yet prepared to manage the risks that agents bring.

According to Onyx, security teams now need to keep continuous track of agent access, actions and policy compliance. Under the partnership, Glean provides the platform to build, deploy and operate the agents, while the Onyx secure AI control plane is used to extend governance and security across the AI environment.

At the core of the integration is discovery, with Onyx able to inventory every Glean agent and the access and capabilities it holds. Ownership, business purpose and a risk classification can then be assigned to each agent, according to the companies.

Enterprise AI governance and compliance policies can also be applied through the integration, after which Onyx continuously assesses changes to the permissions, tools and data access granted to each agent. Intent-aware runtime controls, which Onyx applies to prompts, responses and agent actions, provide protection while the agents are running.

Unsafe requests can be blocked outright under the controls. In other cases, the controls are said to steer unintended agent actions back in line with company policy. Centralized audit evidence is also maintained across AI environments. From deployment through ongoing operation and expansion, the companies say, agents fall under a single governance model.

“As agents gain greater access and autonomy, security teams need visibility and control over what they can do,” said Gil Elbaz, co-founder and chief AI officer at Onyx, who previously worked under Nvidia Corp.’s chief technology officer. “By combining Glean’s enterprise context with Onyx’s security control plane, customers can govern agent activity consistently and confidently across their AI environment.”

Glean regards context and governance as “foundational to making enterprise AI both useful and trustworthy,” according to Zubin Irani, the company’s vice president of partnerships. The Onyx integration is said to build on that foundation as organizations deploy agents across their business.

Coming into the partnership, Onyx has raised $153 million to date, including a $113 million Series B round led by Bessemer Venture Partners in July. The company launched in March with $40 million in seed and Series A funding.

Glean, for its part, last raised $150 million in a Series F round at a valuation of $7.2 billion in June 2025.

#5507. NHTSA is probing more than 1 million Hondas over stop-start engine failures

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The agency received 701 complaints about engines that failed to restart in 2024-2026 Odyssey, Passport, Ridgeline, Pilot and Acura MDX models

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration began a formal engineering analysis of 1,033,632 Honda $HMC vehicles in the U.S. on Monday, citing engines that would not start back up once the automatic stop-start system had cut them off, according to Reuters.

NHTSA has logged 701 complaints tied to the stop-start function on Honda's Odyssey, Passport, Ridgeline and Pilot from the 2024-2026 model years, along with the Acura MDX, according to Reuters.

The stop-start system aims to cut down on fuel consumption. It shuts the engine off once a vehicle has fully stopped, then is meant to fire it back up as soon as the driver eases a foot off the brake. Drivers have reported that their engines stayed dead once the system switched them off, according to Reuters.

NHTSA already has a separate inquiry open on comparable engine trouble tied to stop-start systems in certain Honda models, according to Reuters. That earlier probe encompasses all of the vehicles now under review apart from those from the 2026 model year.

The agency said the two groups exhibit comparable failures, yet the newly investigated vehicles seem to stem from distinct underlying problems and do not react to repairs in the same way, according to Reuters.

The probe follows a Honda recall of 635,808 vehicles in the U.S. to fix a software problem that can disable power steering assistance, leaving the vehicles harder to steer, according to Reuters.

Honda has issued a series of recalls this year. In June, the automaker recalled 1,049,883 U.S. vehicles over a flat tire repair kit defect that could cause a sealant bottle cap to detach and strike the user or bystanders. Honda also recalled more than 440,000 Honda Odyssey minivans in April over a software flaw that could cause side and curtain airbags to deploy without warning.

#5505. Apartment rents diverge: San Francisco rises, the Sun Belt falls

RealPage reported a 1.7% year-over-year rise in October rents nationally, with the Bay Area posting the strongest gains and many Sun Belt and Florida markets still declining. Deliveries and absorption are nearing balance, and occupancy was 95%.  AI Summary

America’s apartment landscape has become a tale of two opposing rent trends. Rents are climbing in the Bay Area and the Midwest, while much of the Sun Belt is still sliding.

National same-store asking rents edged up 1.7% from a year earlier in October, the biggest annual gain since May 2023, apartment industry data firm RealPage reported Nov. 11.

The national figure hides a wide gap. San Francisco rents jumped 14.7%, evidence of why city officials are pressing the supply button to drive housing construction. San Antonio rents dropped 2.6%.

The month-over-month picture illustrates less dramatic change. RealPage showed that rents fell 0.7% in October, the first monthly cut of 2026. The company said the annual gain came less from strong pricing than from weak months dropping out of the calculation, making for stronger year-over-year comparables.

Other trackers show the same upward drift, with different monthly readings. Yardi Matrix reported rents up 0.1% in October, with annual growth of 1.4%, the strongest in more than three years. Apartments.com put annual growth at 1.6%, even as rents slipped 0.15% for the month.

Supply and demand are edging toward balance. RealPage said renters absorbed nearly 304,800 conventional apartments in the year ending in Q3 2026. Developers completed nearly 318,000 units over the same period, almost half the late-2024 peak.

Occupancy eased to 95%, down 20 basis points from September. It is still up 40 basis points this year and 10 basis points above October 2025.

Improving rents haven’t translated into a property buying spree. Camden Property Trust, a large apartment landlord, walked away from two acquisitions and canceled two planned development projects. The Federal Reserve’s rate hike was a main reason, rental economist Jay Parsons wrote on LinkedIn.

Two deals under contract fell through after the hike, Camden CEO Alex Jessett said on the third-quarter earnings call. Camden asked for lower prices, and the sellers declined.

Buying also beat building on cost. Camden bought an asset at about $370,000 a door, while building it would have cost north of $600,000, Jessett said.

Camden’s earnings show an unevenly improving market. Funds from operations, a standard earnings measure for real estate investment trusts, were $1.70 per diluted share in the third quarter. Core funds from operations were $1.71, $0.02 above the company’s guidance midpoint.

“A higher-for-longer rate environment may equate to a lower-for-longer supply environment,” Parsons wrote.

Fewer projects penciling out means fewer new apartment options for renters.

Northern California took the top three spots for rent power among the 50 largest markets, RealPage said. San Francisco rose 14.7%, San Jose 9.5% and Oakland 8.5%. All three are running near 97% occupancy.

Midwest metros fill much of the rest of the top 10. Milwaukee led at 4.2%, followed by Chicago at 3.3%, and Kansas City and Cleveland at 3.1% each. Detroit and St. Louis each gained 2.7% and just missed the cut.

Most Sun Belt and Florida markets continued to decline. The South as a region returned to annual growth, but only by 0.5%.

San Antonio had the deepest decline in rents among big markets at 2.6%. Its occupancy of 92.5% was the lowest of the 50 largest markets. Houston fell 1.8%, followed by drops in Tampa of 1%, Charlotte of 0.9% and Denver of 0.8%.

Several Sun Belt markets have turned the corner, however. Jacksonville rose 2.6%, Raleigh 1.0%, Atlanta 0.8%, Austin and Miami 0.6% each, and Phoenix 0.4%.

#5503. Legislative risk continues to cloud BTR’s capital outlook; here’s why

Despite a carve-out in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, BTR and SFR operators say Treasury implementation and legislative risk is still suppressing capital. NAA Q3 2026 data shows units under construction down 18.5% YoY, completions down 40.2%, and sales volume down 51.5%.  AI Summary

Despite securing carve-outs from the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act‘s institutional investor ban, build-to-rent (BTR) and single-family rental (SFR) operators continue to grapple with lingering legislative uncertainty that weighs on capital availability and new construction, both of which dramatically lag 2025 levels.

According to the National Apartment Association’s Q3 2026 Market Pulse, released Nov. 5, BTR units under construction fell 18.5% year over year, newly completed units declined 40.2% and sales volume of communities dropped 51.5%. Even against a broader nationwide slowdown in residential construction, the declining BTR pipeline continues to stand out.

The industry’s legislative uncertainty initially stemmed from an earlier version of ROAD, first introduced in March, that would have required investors and developers to sell newly built rental homes to individual buyers after seven years. The provision, among others, threatened the viability of the BTR business model, prompting investors to pull back from committing capital to new projects.

Although the final version of ROAD exempted and protected BTR, uncertainty remains around how Treasury will implement the institutional investor ban, along with the potential for new federal and state legislation that could impose further institutional ownership restrictions. That lingering uncertainty continues to weigh on capital flowing into the industry.

“I would say it hasn’t normalized. In other words, it wasn’t where it was a year ago, where capital was really flowing into the business,” Richard Ross, CEO at QuinnResidences, said when discussing the BTR market, in an interview with HousingWire TBD.

“I almost don’t care what the rules are, as long as you tell me what the rules are,” Ross added. “With uncertainty, people just aren’t going to invest.”

Ross cited the Strait of Hormuz as a timely and illustrative comparison. While oil is still moving through the Strait, traffic remains more restricted than it was a year ago. BTR, he suggested, finds itself in a comparable position.

“Capital’s coming in, but it’s not like it was pre-ROAD. The hope was that the regulatory process would give some clarity. And I think once it gets done, it will provide clarity, but you might remember this was only part one of the regulatory process,” he said, pointing to the prospects of a “ROAD 2.0” housing bill. “Until capital knows what the rules are, it’s really hard for them to write checks.

According to Sean Dobson, chairman, CEO and CIO at The Amherst Group, a builder, buyer and manager of single-family rentals, the capital environment for BTR had been flashing signs of softening even before the federal government introduced the idea of an institutional investor ban. New projects often came with modest returns, and rent growth was moderating or even falling across many high-growth Sun Belt markets.

Add a steady drumbeat of policy risk from Washington, and many investors have simply taken their money elsewhere.

“When you add policy uncertainty to the asset, it just doesn’t have the return to pay for that,” Dobson said in an interview.

Invitation Homes CEO Dallas Tanner also acknowledged that the capital environment hasn’t bounced back from an uncertain 2026 during the company’s Q3 2026 earnings call on October 29.

“Capital’s just starting to poke its eyes up after the ROAD Act piece of it. The market’s still trying to find itself,” Tanner said.

In a Q3 2026 Form 10-Q document filed with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on November 5, 2026, AMH also called out ongoing legislative uncertainty as a concern.

“Further, the ROAD Act and the prospect of other such laws or regulations have adversely impacted and may in the future continue to adversely impact our access to capital markets and the attractiveness of our securities to certain investors,” the document warned.

The U.S. Department of the Treasury, which implements the institutional investor ban included in ROAD, released a notice of proposed rulemaking in October that would grant BTR communities a range of notable exemptions from the ban. However, concerns remain about some of Treasury’s proposed interpretations.

“If you read the law as a layman, you’d say, ‘all right, built-to-rent is carved out.’ But then you get this rulemaking, and it’s like you have to pat your belly and tap your head and hop on one foot for the built-to-rent to not be banned,” Dobson said.

Quinn Residences, in an open letter to Treasury, outlined several concerns about Treasury’s proposed rulemaking. Chief among them is a proposal to exempt purpose-built BTR communities from the institutional investor ban provided they haven’t been owner-occupied and are purchased within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy.

Ross argued that this timeline isn’t sufficient, as the 18-month certificate-of-occupancy requirement could prevent institutional investors from acquiring purpose-built rental homes that have been operating as rentals for more than 18 months, even if they have never been owner-occupied. And building and stabilizing a community typically takes about 30 months, longer than the rule allows, Ross argued.

The rule, therefore, could prevent subsequent sales of newly built BTR homes among institutional investors, effectively limiting the pool of potential buyers and potentially discouraging investment into new projects.

Ross also signaled his opposition to another one of Treasury’s proposed rulemakings that would fail to exempt single-plat BTR communities zoned for multifamily use, despite congressional record statements indicating lawmakers intended those properties to be excluded from the ban.

For The Amherst Group, uncertainty continues to obscure how Treasury will define the exception for homes requiring substantial repairs under the ROAD institutional investor ban. Many of Amherst’s acquisitions are older homes, typically 25 to 40 years old, that require substantial renovations. While the renovate-to-rent exception could allow Amherst to continue acquiring and renovating these properties for rent, the lack of finalized parameters has left investors uncertain.

“There’s no money to be raised right now,” Dobson said, of capital for financing renovate-to-rent acquisitions.

What’s more, the possibility of a “ROAD 2.0” housing bill raises even more concerns among many BTR operators and developers. They fear they face continued uncertainty and risk over whether future federal or state legislation could restrict the BTR business model.

However, it’s not yet clear whether any such legislation will gain traction in the next Congress. While many successful candidates for the U.S. Senate and the U.S. House of Representatives ran on a platform of opposing institutional ownership of single-family homes, campaign rhetoric and slogans don’t necessarily translate full-stop into policy.

“I worked campaigns for a number of years throughout the country, and the first thing they kind of teach you in campaigning out there is everyone needs a boogeyman. I think you campaign in slogans, and you govern in prose,” Owen Caine, Assistant Vice President of Federal Legislative Affairs at the National Apartment Association (NAA), said in an interview.

Despite the expectation that some members of Congress may push for more aggressive institutional ownership restrictions, Cain was encouraged by the widespread bipartisan pushback against previous provisions that would have undermined BTR. Caine hopes this bipartisan support will keep Congress from passing such far-reaching legislation in the future.

“The fact that we got to where we were with such bipartisan support, and with basically complete industry and nonprofit support, [means] messing around with that at this point, before it’s been fully implemented and before we’ve seen any benefits of the bill whatsoever, doesn’t make a lot of sense from a policy perspective,” he explained.

However, the new Congress comes with another challenge — the sheer size of the incoming freshman class. In the House of Representatives, for example, about 110 new representatives are expected, along with new staff members.

“Those are each offices we have to hit individually to educate about build-to-rent because the odds that the average person has any idea what a build-to-rent development is, is pretty low,” Caine explained.

Ross noted that lawmakers are usually receptive once they learn more about BTR and the legislative challenges facing the industry. A recent meeting with Senator-elect Roy Cooper (D-N.C.) was one example, with Cooper responding positively to those concerns.

“I spent 30 minutes with him personally, explaining what build-to-rent was. He said, ‘Oh, I understand. That makes sense.’ So that’s just something that everyone in this business will have to do again,” Ross explained.

While much of the attention has focused on federal legislation, state-level policy, particularly proposals to restrict institutional investors, may be just as critical an area to watch.

While it’s not clear what the newly elected state legislatures and governors may prioritize, several states have already considered bills limiting the influence of institutional ownership of housing.

In Virginia, for example, state lawmakers from both parties introduced legislation to restrict institutional home purchases. SB 693 and SB 1424 would have prohibited entities with more than $50 million in assets under management from buying single-family homes, but neither bill passed.

In Michigan, however, a similar measure, HB 6074, was signed into law on July 21, 2026. The bill prohibits corporations with a net worth of $375 million or more from owning more than 100 single-family homes in the state, while explicitly exempting build-to-rent (BTR) properties.

As more states consider restrictions on institutional ownership of single-family homes, will BTR secure the exemptions achieved in Michigan, or could operators face a tougher legislative environment in Congress and in other state legislatures?

That’s a key question to watch in 2027 and beyond.

#5502. Main Capital Partners Invests in TaskRay, Joining Cloud Coach and JustOn to Transform Customer Delivery on Salesforce

DENVER, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Main Capital Partners ("Main") has invested in TaskRay, an AI-native project management platform built on Salesforce, joining it with portfolio company  Cloud Coach and its German subsidiary JustOn. Together, the three companies aim to redefine customer delivery with an AI-powered platform connecting project management, resource management, professional services automation (PSA), and financial operations for enterprises.

The combined company will be led by Sam Swan as Chief Executive Officer and will serve over 800 customers across North America and Europe with approximately 80 employees across three offices.

One platform from closed deal to collected cash

The combination of TaskRay, Cloud Coach, and JustOn brings together complementary Salesforce-native solutions to address a significant market opportunity. TaskRay provides AI-powered customer onboarding and project management; Cloud Coach delivers professional services automation (PSA), portfolio and resource management; and JustOn connects billing, invoicing, and project financials.

Together, the companies will deliver greater value to existing customers through expanded capabilities and shared expertise, while building toward a unified, AI-powered customer delivery platform. The vision is to transform the entire post-sale lifecycle, from closed deal to collected cash, helping enterprises accelerate customer outcomes, improve operational efficiency, and unlock revenue faster.

TaskRay was among the first Salesforce ISVs to introduce autonomous AI workflows and MCP technology, including one of the first ten ISV MCP servers on AppExchange. Building on this momentum, the combined company will advance agentic AI to automate routine delivery and billing tasks, freeing teams to focus on strategy and customer relationships. Additional AI capabilities are planned for the first half of 2027.

For existing customers, nothing changes today. All three businesses will continue to offer the same products, support teams, and partner programs without disruption. Over time, customers will benefit from expanded capabilities as the companies bring their solutions together into a more unified platform.

"We see significant value in bringing the businesses together and believe the combination will create a compelling joint offering, extending the value of best-in-class solutions built on Salesforce," said Daan Visscher, Partner at Main & Chairman of Cloud Coach's Supervisory Board. "The collective businesses have built deep expertise in the Salesforce ecosystem, and customers will benefit from a unified best-of-breed solution spanning the entire post-sale cycle. We look forward to working closely with the combined team to support a successful integration and realize the full potential of the combined offering."

"Together, the three companies share a vision to fundamentally change how enterprises manage customer delivery on Salesforce," said Sam Swan, CEO. "From the moment a customer signs a contract to the final payment, we see an opportunity to connect the people, projects, and processes behind the scenes. By connecting every stage of customer delivery and putting AI to work in practical ways, we can help businesses operate more efficiently, accelerate growth, and deliver better experiences for their customers."

"Our highest priority remains delivering exceptional value to the customers who trust our people and products every day. What excites me most is the opportunity to build on that foundation, combining our expertise, expanding our capabilities, and accelerating investment in AI to help our customers achieve even greater success."

https://main.nl/Main Capital Partners is a software investor managing private equity funds across the Benelux, DACH, the Nordics, France, the United Kingdom, and the United States, with approximately EUR 12 billion in assets under management. With over 20 years of experience, Main works closely with management teams to achieve profitable growth and create larger international software groups. Main has approximately 105 employees across seven offices and maintains an active portfolio of over 55 software companies.

https://taskray.com/TaskRay is an AI-powered project management platform built natively on Salesforce. TaskRay helps enterprise teams accelerate customer onboarding and implementation with purpose-built templates, standardized workflows, and automation that reduces manual work and streamlines delivery. Enterprise organizations in technology, healthcare, financial services, and hospitality industries rely on TaskRay to manage customer delivery at scale, including FlashParking, Greystar, Basic-Fit International, Commerce Bank, AON, Charles Schwab Bank, ZRS Management, Rockwell Automation, and Truveris.

https://www.cloudcoach.com/Cloud Coach is a provider of professional services automation (PSA), project management, and customer success software built natively on Salesforce. With robust functionality for project portfolio management, resource planning, and time tracking, Cloud Coach helps organizations deliver projects on time and within budget.

https://www.juston.comFounded in 2010 and based in Jena, Germany, JustOn develops Salesforce-native software that automates financial processes from billing and invoicing to payment management and accounting. This helps organizations stay compliant and audit-ready. JustOn serves more than 300 organizations across software, media, real estate, logistics, and other industries.

#5501. Massive Microsoft outage disrupts businesses, government agencies worldwide

A glitch in Microsoft Corp.’s network has disrupted the work of businesses and government agencies in more than 70 countries.

The bug, which reared its head on Thursday about 12:35 p.m. EST, knocked the company’s popular Exchange Online platform offline. Organizations use the cloud service to store employees’ inboxes and calendars. Microsoft has still not fully restored its infrastructure.

Deployments of Exchange Server, a version of the platform that users run on-premises, are not affected. However, the outage did disrupt a number of Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Copilot 365 features that rely on data from users’ Exchange inboxes. Intune, a tool that administrators use to manage employee devices, is also experiencing technical issues.

The outage has hit numerous companies worldwide. Workhorse Group Inc., an electric vehicle maker, pushed back its earnings call from today to Monday. Shipping giant Maersk and stock exchange operator Euronext notified customers that they’re experiencing communications issues.

The public sector is also impacted. Several U.S. municipalities reported technical problems, while a number of court cases had to be delayed. In the U.K., the National Pharmacy Association warned that the Exchange Online outage may slow prescription processing. Hospitals, public transportation agencies and schools are affected as well.

The operator of Downdetector, an outage tracking service, received downtime reports from hundreds of thousands of users.

Parts of Microsoft’s infrastructure started recovering early this morning. In an update published at 2:30 a.m., the company stated that it was seeing “positive results” after patching an “upstream authentication/routing configuration” module. About three hours later, Microsoft’s systems in the Asia Pacific region began regaining service access. North America and Europe followed suit shortly there.

Microsoft shared its first explanation of what went wrong around noon today. “The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the company explained. “We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.”

Microsoft added that the outage wasn’t caused by a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.

The company’s status page indicates that infrastructure restoration work is still ongoing. As a result, some users may have trouble accessing Exchange Online and certain Microsoft products that interact with it. The company is monitoring the backlog of emails that piled up while the service was offline to ensure no data loss occurs.

Microsoft plans to release a detailed technical report about the outage once all its services are fully restored.

#5500. Eli Lilly is buying a rare blood cancer biotech for up to $1.5 billion

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The deal covers Calytrix's preclinical antibody for essential thrombocythemia and myelofibrosis, with milestone payments included

Eli Lilly $LLY agreed to acquire Calytrix Bio, a privately held developer of therapies for myeloproliferative neoplasms, for up to $1.5 billion in cash, the company said on Monday.

Under the definitive agreement, Calytrix shareholders could receive up to $1.5 billion, made up of an upfront payment and further payments that depend on clinical and regulatory milestones being met, the company said. Calytrix did not say how large the upfront payment will be or when it expects the transaction to close, according to Reuters.

Calytrix's lead asset is an investigational antibody for essential thrombocythemia (ET) and myelofibrosis (MF) driven by mutant calreticulin. The antibody is preclinical and targets both Type 1 and Type 2 mutant calreticulin, the company said. Current drug therapies for the two myeloproliferative neoplasms, or MPNs, primarily manage symptoms and complications, according to the company.

The acquisition broadens Lilly’s presence in the MPN field, the company said. Lilly’s hematology business already counts Jaypirca, a blood cancer drug cleared by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, among its products, according to Reuters.

"Calytrix was founded on the belief that patients with MPNs deserve therapies that do more than manage symptoms," said Brad Prosek, Calytrix's president and chief executive officer, in a statement. Prosek said the company looks forward to Lilly advancing the program through the clinic.

Lilly agreed in August to acquire Merida Biosciences for up to $2.875 billion, adding a developer of therapies that target disease-causing antibodies. The Calytrix transaction adds to a run of Lilly acquisitions as the Indianapolis-based drugmaker seeks to lessen its reliance on diabetes and weight-loss products, according to Reuters.

J.P. Morgan Life Sciences Private Capital founded Calytrix in 2025. The company launched with a Series A financing co-led by J.P. Morgan Life Sciences Private Capital and Westlake BioPartners, followed by a Series B financing led by Avoro Ventures.

Centerview Partners is exclusive financial adviser to Calytrix, and Goodwin Procter is its legal counsel. Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison is legal counsel to Lilly.

#5499. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He said he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be said for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

“I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan said. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”

Jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

“Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she said, but it showed cold.

“By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova said. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”

For mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

“If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova said. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

She leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

He also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

“In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer said. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”

Marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

His Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

“Every week, I share new songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”

On setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she said.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova said she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

So the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova said, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”

#5498. The seasonal decline in housing inventory is in full force

Inventory declined to 895,988 as mortgage rates reversed higher to 7.50%. New listings remained fell slightly year over year to 53,162, while weekly pending sales showed 4 weeks of stabilization.  AI Summary

Even with volatility in mortgage rates last week, the seasonal decline in inventory is in full force. Weekly housing demand has continued to stabilize over the last four weeks and the new listing data is not showing any stress in the housing market. We had a lot of crazy things happen last week — in fact I’m writing this article still stuck in Dallas because of the FAA’s nationwide ground stop — but housing data never sleeps, so let’s take a look.

Housing inventory has picked up recently, after mortgage rates went above 6.64% and then shot up toward 7.60%. Inventory growth had been very tame this year, with some weeks negative year over year. As housing inventory returns to normal levels, it takes weaker demand to get stronger growth and rates moving toward 7.60% did that. Still, it’s more about sales taking longer to happen and demand being hit, because new listings data didn’t budge much recently. Now, we are in the full-blown seasonal decline as we get ready to prep for spring 2027.

Inventory growth is running at 7.11% over last year even with easier comps, as last year demand was running toward a 9-month high in December of 2025.

New listings have been in their seasonal decline since June and nothing abnormal with this data line has happened in 2026; in fact, it’s been the best year of new listings since 2022. One concern I had about higher rates is that more people might simply not list their homes — as they did in the second half of 2022 due to higher rates. However, that hasn’t happened; we did see a more noticeable year-over-year decline this last week, but for the most part it’s been a healthy year.

In a normal environment, new listings range from 80,000 to 100,000 per week during peak periods. For context, during the housing bubble years, new listings ranged from 250,000 to 400,000 per week for several years.Here is last week’s new listings data for the past two years:

Typically, about one-third of homes see price reductions before they sell, reflecting the housing market’s dynamic nature. Overall, price-cut percentages this year have been lower than last year. This held true until rates moved above 6.64% and then above 7%. At that point demand fell and the year-over-year price-cut percentage rose 1%.In my 2026 home-price forecast, I called for a national decline of -0.62% for the year. Home-price growth really isn’t going anywhere this year and my -0.62% forecast may be hard to achieve, since most home-price indices show growth between 1% and 2%.However, with higher rates and a rising price-cut percentage, we will be closer to the forecast. Clearly, if rates hadn’t risen above 6.75%, pricing data wouldn’t have shown the recent slowdown.

In the 2026 HousingWire forecast, I anticipated the following ranges:

Last week wasn’t good for mortgage rates or the bond market: we had hawkish Fed statements and hot inflation data. We were getting closer to mortgage rates below 7% for the holidays, but they made a big reversal from 7.17% to 7.50%. In addition, President Trump talked about raising tariffs against Mexico and we still have no deal with Iran. Pretty much everything you needed for rates to go lower went the other way — something I talked about in this episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor in Chief  Sarah Wheeler.

Mortgage spreads have worsened recently, but they did improve last week. Traditionally, when mortgage rates escalate with the 10-year yield and then make a big reversal — like we just had from a 5.35% 10-year yield top that dropped down toward 4.82% — spreads do get worse to try to compress mortgage rate volatility. However, we had a big reversal higher, and spreads improved some as the 10-year yield rose toward 5.14%.

Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads fell to 2.13% from 2.27% a week earlier.

Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been at the best spread levels this year and the worst levels of this cycle.

Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data.

The key for the last four weeks: housing demand has stabilized, as our weekly pending sales have shown. Now, higher rates most likely will impact this week’s data more than last week, but the last four weeks have shown if we can get rates back below 7% and just have them stick, we can work with this.

Housing demand typically grows when rates get below 6.64% and fades when rates are above 7%, especially if the move in rates is fast, like we saw recently. Still, it was encouraging to see stabilization in the data when rates were trying to get below 7% again. Of course, we are seeing big year-over-year declines in this data line as rates were heading toward 6% last year.

Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years:

Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. We did have 8% week-to-week growth last week as rates tried to get below 7% the week before. I expect the next purchase application data to get hit as rates picked up. This data was very positive year over year when rates were under 6.64%, but not so much when it headed toward 7% and got to 7.60%.

Here are the stats on purchase apps so far in 2026:

It’s going to be an interesting week because we have a ton of Fed members speaking and they really left their mark last week! We’ll get some housing data: the builder survey won’t be great, nor will housing starts. Pending home sales might lag our stabilization by one month, but if we do see some stabilization, remember it’s working from record-low levels. We have retail sales as well, and some of the economy has been beating to the upside. Also, we have to be mindful of Trump headlines with the Iran conflict and the trade war.

#5496. NiCE’s next-generation Cognigy bets the hard part of AI agents is running them, not building them

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

The contact center has been the low-hanging fruit for the artificial intelligence industry. Ask any information technology or business leader what they want to use agentic AI for, and they will say it’s to improve the customer experience, which starts with the contact center.

However, to date, the industry has spent the past two years arguing over which AI agent is the smartest. That’s the wrong debate. Model capabilities are improving so quickly and are getting so much cheaper that raw intelligence and reasoning are becoming the least differentiated part of the stack.

The real challenge for enterprises is operating a fleet of AI agents reliably across complete customer journeys, with the visibility and control a large business requires. Without that, the human, or worse, the customer, is left connecting the dots among the outputs of the growing number of agents they are communicating with.

That’s the thesis behind the next generation of NiCE Cognigy, which NiCE Ltd. launched this week. The release includes a redesigned Agentic Experience Studio, an AI Assist companion spanning the building, testing and improvement of agents, reusable “skills” that package instructions and tools, turn-by-turn tracing and native voice-to-voice model support.

Default speech-to-text, text-to-speech and large language models are now included in the per-conversation price, with premium models from Deepgram, ElevenLabs and Anthropic available with a few clicks and billed by usage.

Ahead of the launch, I attended an analyst briefing with Nhu Ho, senior product marketing manager at NiCE Cognigy, and with Clement Boutier, director of product management, who leads the team that built the release and owns the platform roadmap.

Here are the important points from this release:

Ho opened with a chart showing how long AI can work on its own before a human has to step in. In 2020, it was seconds; in 2024, it was minutes; and this year it’s roughly 16 hours. The footnote was interesting, as it calculated that figure at a 50% success rate. “Capable and dependable do not always mean the same thing,” Ho said. “That is exactly where the platform matters.”

For CX leaders, that’s a solid benchmark to consider. A 50% success rate is a research milestone. In a contact center, it’s a churn event or a compliance violation. As models commoditize, value shifts to the system around them: testing, tracing, guardrails and deterministic fallbacks. NiCE doesn’t build frontier models, and frontier model builders don’t run contact centers. Positioning Cognigy as the layer that makes AI dependable is a smart place to plant a flag.

Cognigy earned its pre-acquisition leadership position by handling complex production deployments for large brands such as Lufthansa, Mercedes and DHL. But that flexibility and customizability added complexity. Boutier put it this way: “The large number of options when configuring an agent creates friction to get started, which slows things down.” The new studio lets a builder stand up an agent in a few clicks, with models already provisioned, while power-user tools, including full access to the agent’s system prompt, are available in advanced sections.

This is important because NiCE aims to create a “1+1=3” value proposition for its current customers. NiCE needs Cognigy to expand broadly across the CXone installed base, not just among expert teams at the largest enterprises. Boutier described three builder personas: smaller businesses building simple agents, contact center administrators and team leads, and engineers at technically sophisticated companies. AI Assist is aimed squarely at the first two.

In the demo, it built an agent, tested it, fixed the problems it found, and deployed it to WhatsApp. The flip side is that lowering the barrier means more agents built by less experienced people, which makes the governance features the real story of this release.

Despite all the agentic hype, most enterprises aren’t ready to hand over entire journeys to an autonomous agent. Boutier outlined three modes: traditional natural language understanding, hybrid and fully agentic. Hybrid “is actually where most of our customers are,” he said, while fully agentic deployments are at the “beginning of the adoption curve.” This approach lets customers ease into agentic, build confidence and move to fully autonomous at their own pace.

NiCE designed the product for that approach. An agent can serve as the orchestration layer, calling existing flows as tools. Flows can also be placed in front of agents, for example, to scrub credit card numbers or other personal data before any data reaches a model. Ho described the release as “an evolution, not a replacement,” with production deployments, application programming interfaces and integrations continuing to run unchanged.

That’s a meaningful advantage over AI-native challengers whose pitch effectively requires a rebuild. Contact centers are the fastest-moving environments, and deterministic workflows aren’t legacy baggage. They’re how a business enforces what a large language model shouldn’t be deciding.

“You can have the best builder experience, but if you don’t have any feedback loop on what you’re building, you’re never going to build a great agent,” Boutier said. The new tracing shows each turn: which skill loaded, which tool was called and with what arguments, and when the agent handed off to a flow.

The Simulator now supports multivariate testing of up to 10 variants, using an LLM-as-judge to run synthetic customers against an agent. Boutier ran the same agent on two models and found that one was faster and consumed fewer tokens. This shifts model selection from a preference to a data-backed economic decision.

Voice-to-voice support may be the first feature customers deploy. Boutier noted that buyers are open to using a speech-to-text and text-to-speech cascade, “but what they realize is that voice-to-voice models sound just better.” In the demo, the agent delegated tool calls to a separate model while continuing to talk, making the conversation sound far more natural.

Cognigy now serves as both a Model Context Protocol client and server and supports agent-to-agent connections, including one customer linking Cognigy to agents built with Microsoft’s tooling. NiCE is also co-developing the Personal Agent Protocol with Meta and Sierra, which isn’t live yet. Boutier described Cognigy as “the front door” of the contact center, where a consumer’s personal agent must authenticate before it can proceed. It’s great to see NiCE collaborating with Sierra, a direct competitor, on this, as it makes things easier for a customer.

The industry views agent identity as a shared responsibility. But as Sierra outlines, companies can also let personal agents work through their websites and APIs, so the front-door position depends on enterprises routing that traffic through Cognigy. This lets brands interact with personal agents safely.

There has been a wave of companies banning personal agents, which I think is a mistake. If something is good for a consumer, it will happen, so it’s better to be on the leading edge of enabling it rather than fighting it.

This release is less about new capabilities and more about NiCE betting on where value will accrue as AI agents mature. Intelligence is getting cheaper. Dependability, governance and the ability to blend autonomous reasoning with deterministic control are not.

NiCE is the market leader in contact center as a service, as Cognigy was in conversational AI. Now the challenge is to get an easier-to-work-with Cognigy into the hands of thousands of CXone customers without creating a sprawl of individually governed agents. This will allow NiCE to maintain its industry leadership as personal agents arrive. As it does that, the Cognigy acquisition will move from an add-on to a core component of the NiCE platform.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.
