#5495. SK Hynix will spend $1 billion to build up its South Korean chip supplier base

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The chipmaker plans an 874.6 billion won shared testing facility at its Yongin complex, scheduled to open in May 2027

SK Hynix announced Monday that it plans to commit 1.4 trillion won ($1.05 billion) across the coming five years to back South Korean suppliers of semiconductor materials, parts and equipment, according to Reuters. The spending is meant to shore up the chipmaker's supply chain amid sharpening rivalry in the market for AI chips.

The support program spans four phases, starting with research and development and moving through testing and mass production to sales. It is meant to ease the financial and technological obstacles that smaller firms face.

Through its research support program, SK Hynix will pay suppliers in advance for as much as half of their early-stage development expenses. It will also pay suppliers for effort already spent if a project falls short of its goals. Together with financial institutions, SK Hynix will supply 2 trillion won of financing, with backing from the Korea Trade Insurance Corporation. Other programs extend technical consulting and loans at low interest rates, and smaller subcontractors are among those eligible.

SK Hynix also plans an 874.6 billion won testing facility named Trinity Fab, funded by the company, the central government and local governments. SK Hynix will put up 443.2 billion won, while the central government will provide 373.6 billion won and local governments will add 57.7 billion won. The facility is due to begin operating in May 2027.

Trinity Fab will be built within the first plant of SK Hynix’s Yongin chip complex, roughly 40 km (25 miles) south of Seoul. It will house a 3,305-square-meter (35,600-square-foot) cleanroom plus tools for lithography and etching as well as deposition and inspection. Suppliers can assess their materials and equipment on 12-inch wafers before the items go onto production lines.

An independent non-profit foundation will operate the facility, a setup meant to safeguard intellectual property and confidential business data. SK Hynix said the shared site would let small suppliers spend less on testing and get their products to market faster. The company intends to put 600 trillion won into four chip fabrication plants at the Yongin cluster.

SK Hynix reported record third-quarter operating profit of 83.33 trillion won last month and said it expects demand for memory chips to exceed supply through 2030. The company said it expects investment to increase significantly next year as the first phase of Yongin enters full-scale operation.

In August, the company's board approved 54 trillion won in investments to build two new fabs, one for DRAM in Yongin and one for NAND flash in Cheongju.

SK Hynix stock fell 4.4% in Seoul on Monday.

#5494. Your technology wish list is only half the story

Lender feature requests are often symptoms, not the real problem. Share the business goal behind requests and evaluate vendors by what they build next, including unprompted releases that reduce steps and measurable cost per loan.   AI Summary

Every mortgage technology company keeps a list of lender feature requests. Most treat it as a roadmap. That habit is one reason lenders keep buying technology, even as the cost to originate a loan remains stubbornly high.

I have sat on both sides of that list. Early in my career, I was the lender buying and running point-of-sale systems, loan origination systems and CRMs. Later, I built customer success teams for lenders like the one I used to be. A feature request is a lender’s best guess at a solution. The real problem lies beneath it, and a technology partner that only builds to the request leaves that problem in place.

Here is my advice to lenders, from someone who now runs a technology company: Don’t stop at the wish list. Send the why along with it. Tell your technology partners what you’re trying to accomplish, and judge them by what they do next.Not every list is the same. Some items are requirements, such as a compliance rule, an investor guideline or a business process the technology must support. Any provider worth hiring should be flexible enough to handle those. Others are feature requests, usually tweaks to something that already exists. Then there’s the wish list: new ideas about what the technology could do. Wish lists are among the most valuable inputs a technology partner can receive. They just aren’t the whole story without the reason behind them.

Say your team asks its technology partner for a new field on the application. One provider adds the field and checks the box. Another asks why and learns you’re launching a new loan product. That provider adds the questions, then builds in logic so borrowers are prompted to upload the right documents based on their answers. Same request, very different result. The difference is context.Not every lender wants that conversation every time, and that’s fair. If you’re hungry and order a salad, you may not want the server asking why. Sometimes you just need the field. But when a request is tied to something bigger, such as a new product, a new market or a change in how loans move through your shop, a few extra minutes on the why can save a lot of rework later.

The best technology partners ask bigger questions than “What do you want from your point of sale?”

What do you expect from the industry over the next few years? Which loan products matter most to your growth? What should borrowers experience at each step? How are your loans performing after they close?

A partner that asks those questions is building for your business. One that only collects feature lists is building for its backlog.

The same dynamic shows up when lenders buy technology. For many banks, credit unions and larger lenders, a formal request for proposal (RFP) is required, and for good reason: Single-source procurement is bad practice. The RFP isn’t the issue. The format often is. A spreadsheet passed around without context and scored with checkmarks rewards the provider willing to say yes to every line. It reveals little about whether that provider understands how a loan moves from application to servicing, or whether it will still ship useful work two years after the contract is signed.

Lenders can maintain rigor and add context. Pair the spreadsheet with live working sessions, share the business goals behind the requirements and ask finalists how they would solve the problem behind a line item, not just whether they can check it.

A point-of-sale decision touches processing, underwriting, closing, secondary marketing and servicing. Choices made in the first minutes of an application ripple through the loan’s entire life. A provider that only sees its own screen will optimize that screen.

Shipping on a regular schedule is the bare minimum. What I look for in a partner, and what lenders should expect from us, is a release that solves a problem in a way the lender didn’t picture or never thought to request. You know you’ve seen one when the lender’s first reaction is some version of, “Wait, why didn’t we have this already?”

Getting there means a technology company has to say no to some requests. If you build whatever gets the most votes, you end up with a product designed for the average lender. I’ve never met a lender who thinks of themselves as average.

Cost is the pressure every lender feels most. In the second quarter of 2026, independent mortgage banks and bank-owned mortgage companies spent $10,936 to produce each loan, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. The average, dating back to the second quarter of 2008, is $7,945.

Automation should take repetitive work off the desks of loan officers, processors and underwriters, not replace them, so those people can spend their time on judgment, problem-solving and the borrower relationships that build a business. Every technology company claims to deliver that. Few can prove it.

Make them show you. Before you sign anything, have the provider take a real loan file from application to closing and point to the specific steps its technology took off someone’s plate. If they can’t walk you through those steps, I’d be skeptical of any savings they’re promising.

Around 2016, one of the first things I did in that IT role was map the lender’s borrower journey. Many of our borrowers came through real estate agents. Imagine a couple finding their dream home online, with professionally shot photos that make everything feel possible. Then they go to apply for a mortgage and are sent back decades in time to a confusing PDF. Should they print it? Can they type into it? Do they check the box or circle it? Didn’t they already provide this information?

A decade later, point-of-sale technology is standard, and no one is going back to that PDF. But the industry has a new version of it: borrowers who upload a pay stub and then type the same numbers into a form. Borrowers notice. They can’t tell you what’s wrong. That is why lenders need partners who can.

Feature lists still matter. Every lender compares them, and they should. But a feature list only tells you what a partner has already built. The question I’d ask every technology partner, including us, is simpler: What did you build last year that no customer asked for?

If the answer is nothing, you’re buying a list. If the answer surprises you, you’ve found a partner.

Bryan Traeger is general manager of Floify, a leading point-of-sale platform. This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

Congratulations, you’ve made it to Friday again this week. But before you head out for the weekend, we’re bringing you a quick catch-up on the biggest headlines and the most helpful how-tos for your business. So, Take 5 and peruse our top editor picks for this week and why they matter to your business.

P.S. Don’t miss The Download, our weekly column that breaks down one of the week’s top stories and equips you with what you’ll need to meet next Monday head-on.

Homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

Why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

EXTRA: The buyer who can’t close for a year is your best asset in 2026

AI has been the topic of conversation for the past couple of years. And there’s a lot of talk. So how do you suss through the noise and find what works for your business? Jimmy Burgess has created a no-nonsense list of seven AI tools that are actually worth your time.

Why it matters: Burgess shares not only his top tools but also how to use them. These tools will help you turn prompts into better questions, find the questions your future clients are asking, remember the details that matter, evaluate your AI search visibility, turn one video into multiple pieces of content, make video editing easier and use AI as a strategist rather than a writing assistant. Don’t feel overwhelmed. You don’t have to use all of them at once.

Krystopher Benyamein recently sold a property in San Pedro where his team hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. They found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and they had to start again.

They eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when they shared the case study on Instagram, they didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing they’d done. They opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

That opening puts the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, they explained how they responded, got the property back in front of buyers and ultimately closed.

Why it matters: In today’s market, there are many stories of buyers backing out of deals. This approach allows you to create content that keeps you top of mind, show sellers exactly how you work and reach a wider audience. Benyamein shows you how to do it and shares a FREE Canva template to help get the job done.

VA loans often get passed over for conventional loans. Inman’s Nick Pipitone spoke with Fathom Realty’s Lindsey Schmidt, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, about why VA financing still carries a stigma among sellers and listing agents, how she gets around it and why VA assumptions remain one of the most misunderstood tools in the market.

Why it matters: Military members often have to move. Understanding and busting myths about VA loans can help you get ahead of objections before making an offer, which will help you get more deals across the finish line and get more service members into homes.

Compass has been busy, creating and formalizing policy around employees in association leadership positions and how Compass brokerage agents cooperate on private listings.

The company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

Why it matters: Compass International Holdings is currently in litigation with 16 total MLSs across 18 federal lawsuits. Not only is this big news that’s making waves throughout the industry, but its ripple effects could impact your MLS’s rules, if they haven’t already.

#5491. Nationwide Equities’ Philip Parziale on getting ReverseReach in the hands of more LOs

Nationwide Equities President Philip Parziale discusses his move from general counsel to president and the launch of ReverseReach. He says the platform is meant to help forward loan officers identify reverse mortgage fits and support wholesale expansion.  AI Summary

Philip Parziale, president of Nationwide Equities Corp., is looking to expand the reverse mortgage lender’s wholesale business and bring more forward mortgage loan officers into the reverse market through the company’s newly launched ReverseReach platform.

In an interview with HousingWire‘s Reverse Mortgage Daily, Parziale discussed his transition from general counsel to president while retaining his legal responsibilities, the early industry response to ReverseReach and plans to expand the platform.

Editor’s Note: This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Sarah Wolak: You recently became president of Nationwide Equities following Glenn Wallace’s retirement. Can you tell us how that decision transpired, what the transition means for Nationwide Equities going forward and how you’re balancing two roles?

Philip Parziale: I’ve known Glenn and [CEO] Paul Lamparillo for probably 30 years. They were the owners of Nationwide Equities, and I started at the company probably 15 years ago as an attorney. From there, I worked my way up to general counsel, and they basically saw in me that there was more than just an attorney there. I paid attention to sales and every part of the business, and I actually got promoted to chief operating officer.

From COO, I think they really started grooming me for a leadership role back then. If anything ever happened to either one of them, if anybody wanted to retire, I would be there waiting in the wings. So when Glenn was ready to retire, it was just a natural progression. By then, working under them for 15 years, I got to know almost everything about the company. I was exposed to every part of the company, and it really made for more of a seamless transition.

I know there’s been some articles I’ve seen online about holding the president and general counsel positions and how sometimes they could be at odds. Actually, I think it helps. In the old days, it used to be if management came up with an idea, they’d have to go to legal, and legal would say, “Well, what about this? And what about compliance?”

Now, if we have an idea in a meeting, a lot of times, I’ll know the answer right off the bat. And then if we need to, we can go to the other attorneys in the legal department and say, “Can you give an opinion on this and see if you agree with where we stand?”

Wolak: Going back to your law school days, did you anticipate you would ever have anything to do with the reverse mortgage space? How did you end up learning the business?

Parziale: I had no intention of having anything to do with real estate law at all. I thought I was going to be a litigator. All the classes I took at Fordham School of Law were corporate litigation, criminal litigation, and then when I got out of law school, the job market was kind of tight, and I got offered a job at a real estate firm.

They told me basically, “Listen, we’re mostly real estate. We get some litigation, and you could have all the litigation you want, but we’re mostly real estate.” I said, “Fine,” and it turned out there was no litigation. But the owner of the firm, his uncle owned a mortgage company. It was Parkway Mortgage. They were a big subprime business back in the late ’90s, and so I started doing real estate closings, learning about the mortgage business there.

To make my closings go easier, I would actually learn some of the underwriting, how to process loans and stuff like that. So when a borrower had a question, I knew what the answer was.

From there, I just got invested in the mortgage companies. All my clients, when I put out my own shingle, were mortgage companies, and I basically did compliance work for probably 10 different companies. The first company that actually ever hired me to do title review work was Glenn and Paul’s company.

Wolak: Did you ever think about stepping outside of real estate? What has kept you passionate all these years?

Parziale: I actually like the space. It’s different every day. There’s new challenges every day. It’s not like in the legal field, where you’re really doing the same thing a lot of the times, especially contract reviews and stuff like that. You see different clients every day. You have different problems every day, and it makes the day go a lot faster.

It’s one of those businesses where, especially as an attorney, you’re balancing a lot of different hats. I feel like we have a responsibility to the borrower. We have to make sure this loan is truly a benefit to them. Then you have the responsibility to the investor. Safety and soundness are absolutely paramount when doing a loan. We wouldn’t do any loan that we wouldn’t hold ourselves.

But you also want to help out people that need help. Is there a way to help out that person who may be staring at a foreclosure because a spouse died or somebody got COVID and was out of work for three years? It’s just a series of unfortunate incidents. They’re not bad borrowers, but they just had some bad luck.

That’s literally what led to the idea of ReverseReach. There are so many borrowers seeking conventional and FHA loans that didn’t qualify because they had lost income or they had bad credit, but they were actually good borrowers who just came across hard times. With the reverse mortgage, you could actually help them out, make sure their taxes and insurance get paid, and bail them out of a bad situation.

Wolak: Can you explain the ReverseReach product and who it’s geared for?

Parziale: It’s really geared to mortgage loan officers and companies that do primarily forward loans. What we came across was a lot of these forward LOs would just be having a conversation, and they would have a borrower they couldn’t help. They just didn’t qualify. They didn’t have the income because they couldn’t meet the DTI requirements. And we’re like, “Well, how old are they?”

They’d have a 50% LTV and they’d be 75 years old, and we’d say, “Listen, what about a reverse mortgage?” They hadn’t even considered it because it wasn’t on their plate. It wasn’t something their company offered and they didn’t understand it.

So we’ve learned just by talking to them, these guys had tons of leads, and it was a simple sell for them because they’re just reengaging their old borrowers and all their contacts. They were able to go back to borrowers who may not have qualified because they had to make a mortgage payment. But now, without that mortgage payment, they qualify.

It’s funny in this industry, though. I’ve talked to financial planners who are really respected, but because their company didn’t offer reverse mortgages, it wasn’t even on their plate of financial planning.

Wolak: I’ve heard that experience from others in the space, that it’s a little-known tool or was even taboo at one point.

Parziale: Yes, it absolutely was. There was a negative stigma with the loan, especially back in the day when I first started. It was considered a loan of last resort. It was what people did when they were desperate.

In the old days, the underwriting was really lax. It was, what’s the LTV and how old is somebody? We didn’t have financial assessment. We didn’t have any of that stuff. But now it’s very different, especially with the proprietary product.

When we first got into the proprietary product, our average loan size was hovering around $1 million, and borrowers were using the money for home improvements or buying second homes. It wasn’t, “I’m in trouble. I’m desperate.” It was, “Yeah, I want to. I’ve saved my entire life and I want to enjoy my money.”

Wolak: ReverseReach is new, but what kinds of results and feedback have you gotten so far from users?

Parziale: I was actually very pleasantly surprised. We got a contact maybe eight hours after our first emails went out, and we signed up a broker immediately who had a loan that was ready to go. Whenever you roll out a new product, you expect it to take a while to get some traction, and we were trying to roll it out in waves. But we’ve gotten a good enough reaction just from the first week that we’re already looking at scaling.

We’ve had the conversation of hiring new account executives already because the response has been that good. I was really pleasantly surprised. I always think a new product takes time to get some traction.

I think the thing that helps right now is, rates are so high that forward loan officers are having a hard time. I heard some companies were doing furloughs, so these guys are really looking for new leads, and I don’t think there’s as many leads out there as there once was. So us going out there and saying, “Listen, you may already have your next loan in your pipeline already. Go through your LOS and see what you have,” it’s an easy sell. It makes people really say, “Oh, I could do this,” and we’re happy to look at the scenarios.

We’re actually rolling out a ReverseReach University that’s going to have commonly asked questions. We have an FAQ, but we really want to do it with a whole list of classes that these loan officers can access anytime they want. They can go online and say, “I don’t understand what a LESA is,” and they can see a quick two-minute video explaining what it is.

I think we really have to educate. And I want to take everybody from a forward loan officer who may never have heard of a reverse mortgage to somebody who’s experienced and done them before but doesn’t do them regularly. I want to really appeal to all those people. We’re hoping to roll out an AI chatbot and that university in a couple of weeks.

Wolak: Can you talk about some of the other things you plan to do as company president?

Parziale: Honestly, the one thing I’m looking forward to is scaling. With ReverseReach, we try — and I believe that even a small improvement helps. If I can get 10 small improvements, it’s just as good as coming up with one major improvement.

I look at ReverseReach as a large step forward. But if I can find even one little thing that helps the industry or the borrower in a day, I want to try and do it.

In terms of my next goal as president, it’s definitely scaling. With some of the furloughs going on and layoffs, I think there’s a lot of good people out there who are going to be available, and I’d like to hire some of them. I’d like to increase our wholesale presence and grow that way.

#5490. FAA grounds all domestic flights after reported network outage

The Federal Aviation Administration today grounded all domestic flights in the U.S.

The rare order was issued by the Air Traffic Control System Command Center, or ATCSCC. It’s an FAA facility in Northern Virginia that is responsible for monitoring air traffic and mitigating potential risks. When ATCSCC identifies issues such as airport congestion, it provides local officials with guidance on how to address them.

The ATCSCC sent today’s ground stop order to all 22 regional air traffic control centers in the U.S. The memo explained that the move was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy elaborated in a post on X that the FAA “issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.”

The post didn’t provide any details about the communication issue. According to CBS News, the problem affects a “private communications network” that connects components of the U.S. air traffic control system. The outlet cited sources as saying that an update caused the network to reboot, which in turn led it to crash.

On Tuesday, the FAA announced that it was expanding its use of an artificial intelligence system called SMART. The software analyzes weather patterns, flight paths and related data points to generate air traffic scheduling recommendations. The FAA says that the software is designed to reduce delays and fuel consumption.

The agency last issued a national ground stop in January 2023. It was a response to an issue in the FAA’s NOTAM system, which it uses to notify pilots about hazards such as closed runways. The shutdown lasted about two hours and grounded 9,500 flights.

The current shutdown is already much longer, having started at 3:54 p.m. EST. More than 13,000 flights have reportedly been delayed or canceled. Eurocontrol, an organization that helps European Union member states coordinate air traffic, suspended flights to the U.S. at the request of the FAA.

FAA officials said that inbound international flights will be “handled on a case by case basis.” American Airlines, meanwhile, stated that flights already airborne will proceed to their destinations. The airline reportedly expects the disruption to last all day.

#5489. China's economy stumbles as retail sales, factory output, and investment all miss

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Retail sales rose 0.4% in October and industrial output 4.8%, while fixed-asset investment fell 8.1% in the first 10 months

China's National Bureau of Statistics released October data on Monday showing retail sales up 0.4% year on year, industrial output up 4.8%, and fixed-asset investment down 8.1% over the January-to-October stretch.

Each reading missed analyst forecasts, according to CNBC, which put expectations at 0.8% growth for retail sales, 5.3% growth for industrial output and a 7% decline for investment.

The bureau said investment in real estate development fell 21.6% in the first 10 months. Infrastructure investment declined 5.1%, manufacturing investment fell 2.9% and private investment dropped 11.4%. The value of newly built commercial building sales fell 14.3%. Looking at October by itself, investment was down 17% against the same month a year earlier, according to Bloomberg.

Retail sales of consumer goods in urban areas rose 0.2% in October, while rural sales rose 1.5%. Exports of goods rose 28.7% in yuan terms. The urban surveyed unemployment rate was 5.1%, down 0.1 percentage point from September. Consumer prices rose 0.7% from a year earlier, and producer prices rose 5.7%.

The bureau described the economy as "generally stable." It also said the domestic imbalance between strong supply and weak demand is acute and that some enterprises face operating difficulties.

“We’re still in the waiting period for the stimulus impact to kick in,” Helen Qiao, chief economist for greater China at BofA Global Research, told Bloomberg Television.

Beijing announced mortgage subsidies and targeted rate cuts in late September. The economy grew 4.5% in the third quarter from a year earlier. September retail sales rose 1.1% and industrial output grew 5.5%. Fixed-asset investment had contracted 7.2% through September, with real estate development investment down 20.6%.

#5487. NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO says

License under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license.

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents said.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint said he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”

White also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton said it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”

Pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also said the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

“NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears said the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”

“Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”

#5486. Longbridge survey: Senior independence, aging in place are top retirement priorities

A Longbridge Financial survey of 2,021 homeowners ages 55 and older finds 90% prioritize maintaining independence and 88% prioritize aging in place, outpacing debt, leisure and long-term care. Women rated independence and aging in place 5 points higher than men, while helping family ranked lowest at 32%.  AI Summary

For older homeowners, retirement is defined less by leisure or legacy and more by a desire to stay independent and remain in their own homes, according to new research from Longbridge Financial released during National Family Caregivers Month.

The company’s 2026 Home Equity Confidence Index, drawn from a nationwide survey of 2,021 U.S. homeowners ages 55 and older, found that 90% rate maintaining independence as extremely or very important to their ideal retirement — the highest-rated priority in the study. Aging in place ranked a close second at 88%.

Both priorities significantly outpaced traditional financial concerns. Paying for healthcare was cited by 77% of respondents, followed by paying off debt (64%), leisure and travel (55%), and long-term care (55%). Helping family members financially ranked last, at just 32%, suggesting that older Americans place far greater value on their own self-sufficiency than on intergenerational financial support.

“Much of the retirement conversation focuses on whether Americans have saved enough, but our research adds another dimension — where people want to live and what it costs to stay there,” Chris Mayer, CEO of Longbridge Financial, said in a statement. “The economic challenge is aligning financial resources with the costs of maintaining a home, paying for health care, and getting additional support when needed, all while preserving the independence that homeowners clearly value.”

The research found that the pull of home grows stronger as people get older. While 85% of homeowners ages 55 to 64 consider aging in place extremely or very important, that figure rises to 88% among those 65 to 74 and 93% among those 75 and older.

Independence follows the same pattern, climbing from 87% among the youngest group to 96% among those 75 and older — the highest rating for any priority in the entire survey. Healthcare concerns also intensify with age, jumping from 73% among 55-to-64-year-olds to 85% among those 75 and older, reflecting the mounting weight of medical costs in later life.

The study also revealed consistent differences between men and women. Among women 55 and older, 93% rated independence as extremely or very important, compared with 88% of men — a five-point gap that repeated for aging in place (90% of women versus 85% of men) and healthcare (80% versus 75%).

The gap narrowed on purely financial concerns such as debt and long-term care, suggesting the divergence is rooted more in autonomy and stability than in money alone. The one area where men led was helping family financially, prioritized by 34% of men versus 30% of women.

The findings, part of a broader series of Longbridge reports, were based on a Morning Consult survey conducted between March 26 and April 5, 2026. It was designed to reflect a broad cross-section of older homeowners and was conducted without reference to Longbridge to ensure unbiased responses.

#5485. JALEN ROSE LAUNCHES POP THE TRUNK, A GENRE-DEFYING NEW SHOW THAT BREAKS THE MOLD OF TRADITIONAL SPORTS AND CULTURE PROGRAMMING

A trailblazer in athlete-driven media, Rose brings his hometown of Detroit to the forefront with a first-of-its-kind show featuring twice-weekly episodes and ongoing content

DETROIT, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Same Page Entertainment, the Detroit-based multi-media production company founded by NBA legend, media personality, and entrepreneur Jalen Rose and Platinum Equity Founder, Chairman and CEO, and Detroit Pistons owner Tom Gores, today announced the launch of Pop the Trunk. Hosted by Rose, Pop the Trunk premieres in January with twice-weekly episodes on YouTube and audio streaming platforms, while exclusive content, behind-the-scenes moments, and real-time social media commentary keep the conversation going between episodes.

Produced by Same Page Entertainment, Pop the Trunk draws inspiration from the golden era of appointment-viewing television while exploring the people, ideas, and moments shaping today's sports, culture, and entertainment landscape. The show will feature marquee interviews, skits, thoughtful analysis, animated content, live performances, and recurring segments like "Story Time with Jalen Rose," creating a dynamic entertainment experience designed to engage audiences wherever they watch, listen, and connect. Confirmed recurring guests include Detroit icons and hip-hop artists Sada Baby and Detroit Diamond, who bring distinct perspectives and cultural insight to the show. Filmed out of Same Page Entertainment's new content studio in downtown Detroit, Pop the Trunk will maintain a year-round presence across digital platforms while laying the groundwork for future live activations at major events nationwide.

"At its core, Pop the Trunk is about creating the kind of conversations that happen when great stories, different viewpoints, and authentic personalities come together," said Jalen Rose, Co-Founder and CEO of Same Page Entertainment. "We're opening the door to something entirely new at Same Page and building something entertaining, unpredictable, and rooted in community. Filming in Detroit is especially meaningful because this city shaped who I am, and we're excited to showcase its talent and resilience on a global stage."

For Rose, Pop the Trunk represents the latest evolution in a career spent redefining what athlete-driven media can be. Long before today's wave of athlete-hosted programming, he helped lay the blueprint for how athletes could extend their voices beyond the game, becoming one of the first active NBA players to build a career as a media personality while still playing. His acclaimed run as co-host of Jalen & Jacoby, nearly two decades as a lead analyst at ESPN, his original co-hosting of Get Up, and his current role as a college basketball analyst for TNT Sports helped pave the way for a generation of athletes who have leveraged their platforms into influential media enterprises. Now, Rose is betting on himself again, channeling his talents as a true Renaissance Man to push the boundaries of sports and entertainment with a format unlike anything else in the space.

The launch marks another major milestone for Same Page Entertainment, following its February 2026 debut and the premiere of its first original television series, South West High, on Tubi. The company also recently wrapped production on The Streak, its first feature film, which it co-produced and co-financed. Inspired by the remarkable true story of a college basketball team determined to break the longest losing streak in NCAA history, the uplifting sports comedy stars Ed Helms, Nina Dobrev, and Natasha Rothwell and is written and directed by Steve Byrne. Together, the projects reflect the company's mission to champion Detroit, invest in homegrown creative voices, and elevate resonant stories and perspectives for audiences worldwide.

Jalen Rose burst onto the scene as a member of the University of Michigan "Fab Five," followed by a successful 13-year NBA career. He is the Co-Founder and CEO of Same Page Entertainment, a Detroit-based multimedia production company founded alongside Tom Gores, rooted in building stories that celebrate culture, champion new voices, and spark meaningful conversations that bring communities closer together. He is currently a college basketball analyst for TNT Sports and spent 18 years as a lead analyst for ABC/ESPN. Despite all of his accolades, Rose has made his biggest contributions off the court by founding the Jalen Rose Leadership Academy in 2011. The open-enrollment, tuition-free public charter high school located in Detroit now serves more than 400 students annually and over 1,000 alumni. A college graduate, Rose recently earned his Honorary Doctor of Humane Letters degree from the University of Michigan. Currently a Board Member of the National Basketball Players Association Foundation, Rose's contributions to society through sports, philanthropy, and business have earned him numerous honors. He currently resides in Detroit.

At Same Page, we believe everyone should be seen, be heard, and be understood. For more information, visit samepageentertainment.com or follow us at @samepageent.

#5484. A Fed governor warned AI agents could speed up bank runs that unfold in minutes

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Michael Barr said AI agents could move deposits at high speed during stress periods, overwhelming liquidity management

Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr warned in a speech for a conference in Milan on Monday that AI agents could accelerate bank runs that unfold in minutes by moving customer deposits at high speed.

"Where customers once needed to execute transfers, AI agents could instantaneously detect yield differentials or stability signals and autonomously move funds at high speed, potentially accelerating runs that unfold in minutes, overwhelming traditional liquidity management and regulatory intervention timelines," Barr said, according to Bloomberg.

Barr said major banks report finding AI agents that attempt to take actions in retail customer accounts, with the bank unable to verify authenticity, consent or alignment with customer instructions. He called for safeguards such as tight authentication, verification of explicit consent for particular actions, technical limits on what agents are able to do, and restrictions grounded in both rules and values.

Barr described himself as an optimist about the long-term promise of AI. He said AI can strengthen the financial system only if it also supports financial stability.

The speech also covered the AI investment boom. Barr cited the Fed's latest Financial Stability Report, issued Nov. 13, which estimates that the potential maximum nominal value of off-balance-sheet liabilities tied to the AI buildout now exceeds $3 trillion. He said on-balance-sheet debt of the seven largest AI firms is expected to exceed $800 billion before year's end.

Barr also pointed to more than $100 billion in cumulative equity investments by large cloud-computing firms and chipmakers in AI labs and cloud start-ups. He described these as a form of “circular financing,” in which the smaller firms use the money to rent or buy chips and computing power from the investor.

On trading, Barr said traders who rely on a small set of similar AI models face the risk of herding behavior, in which strategies become similar and react to news in sync. He said a market with many similar models that share the same flaw risks failures with systemic consequences.

The International Monetary Fund warned in October that a crash in AI-related stocks could threaten global financial stability. The IMF cited rising debt levels, concentrated market exposures and circular financing arrangements across the sector.

#5483. AT&T uses agentic AI to reinvent business processes from the ground up

CASE STUDY by Paul Gillin

AT&T Corp. is moving beyond using artificial intelligence to improve employee productivity, increasingly applying autonomous agents to redesign how its business operates. Nearly 500 agentic workflows are already in production, and the telecom giant plans to triple that number next year.

AT&T now processes about 45 billion AI tokens daily across the company, according to Luke Corbin (pictured, below), assistant vice president of digital transformation and AI at AT&T Business. Its agentic AI platform handles more than 1 million transactions monthly. Many of those workflows now operate autonomously, handling tasks ranging from customer provisioning to sales prospecting.

Speaking at an Amazon Web Services Inc. event in Boston earlier this month, Corbin said the company’s approach emphasizes rethinking entire processes rather than simply automating individual tasks. AT&T has moved quickly from experimenting with generative AI to systematically identifying business processes that can be redesigned around agentic capabilities.

At the heart of the transformation is Business Agent Foundry, a group established in early 2025 to work with individual business units. Rather than soliciting isolated automation ideas from employees, the foundry maps business processes using industry frameworks and identifies opportunities to eliminate unnecessary steps, organizational handoffs and legacy application dependencies, Corbin said.

One early initiative involved automating interactions with AT&T’s mainframe computers. Changes to customer fiber installation orders previously required employees to retrieve tickets from queues, manually update records and return them to the workflow.

Agentic automation eliminated portions of that manual process, reducing delays and accelerating service delivery.

“It was kind of cool having some of the most advanced technology talking to some of the oldest that we have,” Corbin said.

In another example, AT&T halved the time required to provision dedicated internet connections in buildings where fiber infrastructure was already installed.

AT&T’s architecture breaks from conventional approaches that build large numbers of independent, specialized agents. Instead, the company maintains a relatively small set of agents that execute business workflows using centrally managed business logic.

“We store the business logic in context or in memory,” Corbin said.

Retrieval agents identify applicable knowledge, while planning agents determine the actions, tools and data needed to complete a task.

“We’ve democratized agents to the point where people can use them for personal productivity, but not to where you would drive business workflows that could touch your customers or materially have an impact on your business,” Corbin said.

Every production workflow initially includes human oversight. Only after accuracy reaches the mid- to high 90% range within a permissible risk profile can agents operate autonomously. Continuous monitoring evaluates performance and detects drift.

Success metrics include labor savings, revenue generation, operating costs and customer satisfaction. Corbin said production AI investments are achieving fivefold returns within a year.

A 151-year-old company that has been using computers since they were invented “is built on a lot of legacy processes and applications,” Corbin said. “The cost of maintaining those applications, training employees to use them and ongoing maintenance is very high. When you can offset some of that with simpler generative workflows, you’ve got a business case that’s built for itself.”

Sales prospecting is one beneficiary. Agents identify promising customers by validating their locations and checking fiber availability before representatives invest time pursuing sales opportunities.

Scaling up those capabilities requires more than AI models. AT&T has had to consolidate fragmented data and provide reliable connectivity across data centers, cloud infrastructure and mobile workers.

“We’ve been through a lot of mergers and acquisitions,” Corbin said. “You can imagine what our data infrastructure looks like.”

Encouraging employees to come forward with ideas for using agents has helped limit resistance from those who worry AI could replace them. So has the opportunity to replace inefficient processes.

“There are a tremendous number of people in the organization who have knowledge and passion about the business process that they used to use but that they didn’t like,” he said.

Corbin said AT&T is now shifting its focus from improving existing processes toward using agents to launch services, enter markets and support new sales channels.

Ultimately, Corbin said responsibility for AI-driven business transformation should be distributed throughout the organization, rather than concentrated in a specialized team like Business Agent Foundry.

“I feel privileged to have the team that I do, but in the long run, my team shouldn’t exist,” he said. “What we do should be completely distributed.”

#5482. When new homes look the same, price wins, here is the alternative

Land development and capital expert Scott Finfer argues that differentiation creates demand, while scale only lowers delivery cost. Using Ford Eddie Bauer trim pricing, King Ranch premiums, and Apple iPod growth, he shows how credible design and brand stories can support pricing power.  AI Summary

America does not have a shortage of homebuilders. It has a shortage of reasons to choose one over another.

Drive through a new-home community. The floor plans look familiar. So do the elevations, finishes and incentives. When the houses become interchangeable, the conversation quickly turns to price. The builder with the biggest discount wins the buyer – and sacrifices the margin.

The industry’s answer is often to build more. Buy land. Consolidate purchasing. Standardize everything. Get bigger. But efficiency is the cost of delivering a product; differentiation is why someone wants it in the first place. A company can become highly efficient at producing something nobody particularly wants.

Consider three American stories: Eddie Bauer, King Ranch, and Apple. They begin with people who saw what competitors missed. The numbers show how far a genuine difference can go.

In 1935, Eddie Bauer nearly died after getting soaked and dangerously cold on a winter fishing trip in Washington. Wool was heavy and inadequate for his needs. His solution was a quilted, down-insulated jacket – warm without the bulk. The Skyliner arrived in 1936, with a U.S. patent following in 1940.

Bauer did not invent winter or the jacket. He solved a familiar problem in a way customers could feel. That distinction became the foundation of a brand known for credible outdoor performance. By 1999, the Eddie Bauer retail business generated approximately $1.8 billion in annual sales, according to filings by its then-parent, Spiegel.

Ford recognized the value of that reputation and put the Eddie Bauer name on SUVs. The partnership was formed in 1983, and Eddie Bauer editions reached Ford showrooms in the 1984 model year. In June 1999, Ford celebrated its millionth Eddie Bauer-edition vehicle. Clothing had become an automotive selling proposition. Customers were not buying a jacket. They were buying what the name made them believe about the vehicle.

By 1998, Ford listed the two-wheel-drive Explorer XLT at $24,740 and the Eddie Bauer at $28,910, an additional $4,170, or 16.9%. That year’s Expedition XLT started at $28,225, and the Eddie Bauer at $32,055, $3,830 more, or 13.6%. A different interior, better equipment, and an outdoor brand with a story gave customers a reason to pay more.

Now, the volumes. Ford reported that customers bought 48,680 Eddie Bauer Explorers and 98,823 Eddie Bauer Expeditions in 1998, for a total of 147,503 premium-trim SUVs in a single year. According to Ford’s model sales figures, Eddie Bauer editions accounted for about 44% of all Expeditions sold.

Apply the published starting prices to those units. The Explorer mix generates $1.204 billion at XLT sticker prices versus $1.407 billion at Eddie Bauer prices – a $203.0 million difference. The Expedition mix generates $2.789 billion versus $3.168 billion – another $378.5 million. Together, the same 147,503 vehicles generate $3.994 billion at base XLT list prices versus $4.575 billion at Eddie Bauer list prices.

This is an illustration at the manufacturer’s suggested retail price, not Ford’s booked revenue, profit, or royalty income. Ford did not disclose the drivetrain and option mix behind every sale, so the calculation consistently uses the two-wheel-drive starting MSRPs. Higher trims included additional equipment, including leather and distinctive finishes. The $581.5 million cannot be attributed to the badge alone. Still, buyers selected those more expensive configurations in enormous numbers. The name helped give Ford a product people wanted to move up to.

Now extend the calculation with appropriate caution. My reconstruction of Ford’s 1984–2010 partnership estimates 1,960,602 Eddie Bauer vehicles and $8.37 billion in additional list-price value compared with the lower XLT-equivalent trims; in 2025 purchasing power, about $16.10 billion. The Explorer accounts for 804,231 modeled editions and a $3.08 billion premium; Expedition, 889,457 and $4.53 billion; earlier Bronco, Bronco II, Aerostar, and F-150 editions, another 266,914 and $0.76 billion. The two SUVs alone represent approximately $47.38 billion in XLT-equivalent list value and $54.98 billion in Eddie Bauer-equivalent value, based on rounded component figures.

These lifetime numbers are my model, not Ford-reported sales or audited revenue.

Ford confirmed a million Eddie Bauer vehicles by June 1999 and disclosed the 1998 unit counts. It did not publish a complete later trim-by-trim series. For 1999–2010, my base case holds the 1998 Eddie Bauer take rates – 11.3% of Explorers and 43.8% of Expeditions – and uses model-year list prices. The remaining 266,914 units are an estimate allocated to earlier models, not a Ford-reported tally. Wide assumptions for the unreported years produce a lifetime premium range of $6.4 billion to $9.4billion, before inflation adjustment. A chart reconstructs the annual path; it should not be mistaken for a Ford financial report.

FIGURE 1  •  Annual model allocation, Explorer and Expedition, 1990–2010. Only the 1998 Eddie Bauer volumes and starting prices are directly sourced.

MODEL TABLE  •  1984–2010 partnership; nominal dollars. 2025-dollar estimated premium: $16.10B. Ford did not publish the underlying annual trim-level series.

The distinction has limits: Eddie Bauer’s North American store operator entered bankruptcy protection in 2026. A brand that once commanded a premium can outlast the economics of the company running it. Differentiation earns the right to compete for a higher price. It does not eliminate the need to make money.

In 1853, Richard King began what would become one of America’s most recognizable ranching enterprises in South Texas. The literal brand, burned into the ranch’s livestock and stamped on its goods, was known as the Running W. Its value was not simply the acreage. It was the knowledge developed by those who worked it: heat, grasses, drought, animals, disease, water and what could survive where.

That expertise was practical, not ornamental. King Ranch developed the Santa Gertrudis, which was recognized in 1940 as the first beef cattle breed developed in the United States. The brand’s power and value emerged from decades of decisions by people who knew their ground. They improved the product before asking the world to recognize the name.

Ford later carried the Running W into another business. The F-150 King Ranch debuted for the 2001 model year. For buyers who knew the name, a truck could now signal a specific blend of capability, craftsmanship and Texas identity. It was not a generic luxury package with a random Western label.

Ford lists the 2026 F-150 Lariat at $59,560 and the King Ranch at $65,825. The difference is $6,265, or 10.5%. The higher trim includes additional equipment, materials, and appearance treatments, so this is not a pure estimate of trademark value. It is an observable premium for a differentiated offering.

That difference matters in the same way the Eddie Bauer spread did: it gives the customer a specific reason to trade up. Multiply a premium by meaningful sales volumes, and it can change the economics of a product line. But Ford does not publish a clean, current unit count for King Ranch-only units that would support a responsible annual revenue calculation here. A beautiful spreadsheet does not make missing data real.

A more important connection matters for homebuilders. Every competent Texas land developer knows that two parcels 10 miles apart can be entirely different businesses. School districts, commute patterns, soils, lot widths, trade availability, municipal requirements, neighborhood identity, and the ability to pay all influence the right product.

A centralized buyer might negotiate a better window price. That is useful. But a national plan library cannot, by itself, determine which windows, home designs or neighborhood experiences are worth buying for that land. Local judgment is an asset. Remove it, and you may reduce the cost of a component while destroying the reason the family wanted the home.

King Ranch did not become King Ranch by treating its land as interchangeable. Homebuilders should understand that lesson better than anyone else.

I learned the design lesson long before I had a financial statement to back it up.

When I was in ninth grade, the Fadell family moved into the house behind ours. Greg Fadell became my friend. His older brother, Tony, was the cool older kid – into design, technology, girls, and Apple computers. I was a PC guy. We saw the world differently.

I remember being at their house when Tony talked about their Curtis Mathes television. Curtis Mathes used the advertising line, “The most expensive television sets in America – and darn well worth it.” Tony thought the set was beautiful. He insisted that its design made it worth more – not because it displayed different television programs, but because it was a better object to live with.

I saw a television. Tony saw the choices someone had made to create it: how it looked in a room, how it felt to own it and why a customer might willingly pay more than for another television that displayed the same programs. That was the lesson I took from him: design matters – and customers will pay for it when the difference is real. He also believed Apple Computer would change the world. I had my doubts.

That older kid was Tony Fadell. Years later, he helped lead the development of Apple’s iPod and was a central figure in the iPhone’s early development. He did not invent the concept of portable recorded music. He helped turn existing technology into an experience that consumers actually wanted.

The pitch was not “a better storage device.” It was a thousand songs in your pocket. Hardware, software, industrial design, interface, and music management were designed to work together. Apple made the hard choices so customers didn’t have to.

In 2000, U.S. portable MP3-player sales were estimated at about 587,000 units and $107 million. The market existed, but its products were often clumsy. The original iPod launched in 2001 for $399, even though some competing hard-drive devices were available near or below $200. Apple’s answer was not to be cheaper.

Apple reported $143 million in iPod revenue in fiscal 2002, from 381,000 units. By fiscal 2008, it sold 54.828 million iPods, generating $9.153 billion in annual iPod revenue. That’s 64 times the 2002 revenue and roughly 144 times the unit volume. The implied revenue per device was about $375 in 2002 and $167 in 2008; as the lineup broadened, Apple’s scale also enabled lower price points.

Global Apple iPod sales of $9.153 billion were roughly 85 times the entire $107 million U.S. portable MP3-player market reported in 2000. These are different geographies and dates; this is a scale illustration, not a market-share calculation. The defensible comparison is Apple’s own growth: $143 million to $9.153 billion in six fiscal years.

Tony’s Curtis Mathes argument was not that good looks alone guarantee a good business. It was that design can make the same basic category worth more to the customer. Apple provided the operational sequel: make the better experience repeatable, then scale it. Curation came before volume.

I worked at KB Home twice. I respect its brand and its commitment to giving buyers choice. Built to Order lets customers personalize floor plans, elevations and finishes through defined selections. It is not literally unlimited. But each additional cabinet, structural option, fixture or finish can create another purchasing combination, another schedule exception and another chance for a mistake.

The answer is not to eliminate personal choice. It is to curate it: compatible collections, engineered options, known prices, and reliable purchasing and trading that know the details. The buyer experiences a personal home.

The company delivers through a repeatable system. That’s the distinction Tony understood. Apple did not invite people to design their own iPod.

Economies of scale have a specific meaning: average cost per unit declines as volume increases. Imagine a builder delivering 1,000 comparable homes at an average cost of $300,000 each. With disciplined purchasing and process improvements, 2,000 homes might cost $285,000 each. That’s a real $15,000 per-home improvement. But if a 3,000-home business adds bureaucracy, construction mistakes, and poor product decisions, driving costs up to $310,000 per home, it is bigger but less efficient. Those numbers are hypothetical; the economic distinction is not.

A purchasing department can celebrate a $2,000 materials saving while the field absorbs $5,000 in delays and rework. Corporate headquarters can claim synergy while divisions lose experienced operators and customer relationships. Costs do not disappear; they migrate between accounting categories.

Consider the different business models at scale. Toll Brothers delivered 11,292 homes in fiscal 2025 at an average price of approximately $960,000, reporting $10.84 billion in home-sales revenue and a 25.6% home-sales gross margin. Lennar reported a 17.0% home-sales gross margin in its fourth quarter of 2025. Different reporting periods, price points, and product mixes mean this is not an apples-to-apples comparison or proof that design explains the spread. It shows that unit volume by itself tells us very little about the economic value created.

The sequence is simple. Differentiation creates demand. Curation identifies what customers value. Standardization makes the offering repeatable. Scale lowers the cost of delivery. Reverse the order, and a company risks standardizing away the very thing that made it worth choosing.

Eddie Bauer solved the problem of cold and brought credibility into a Ford showroom. King Ranch turned generations of local judgment into a name buyers recognized. Tony Fadell saw value in a television’s design when I saw only a television – and later helped make digital music a product consumers wanted at extraordinary scale.

The lesson for builders is not to make every house expensive. It is to make the right house unmistakably valuable to the right family, then build it efficiently. When your only lever is a bigger incentive, you are not earning a premium. You are buying the sale.

Better is the objective. Scale is the result.

The article is written for general readers. This appendix is for the editor and fact-checker; its assumptions should not be collapsed into reported facts.

Reported by Ford: one million Eddie Bauer editions by June 1999; 1998 Explorer 48,680 and Expedition 98,823 Eddie Bauer editions; 1998 Explorer total 431,488, Expedition total 225,703.

Author-supplied lifetime model: 804,231 Explorers; 889,457 Expeditions; 266,914 older models; total 1,960,602 editions. Premium: $8.37B in nominal dollars / $16.10B in 2025 dollars. Low–high case $6.4B–$9.4B.

Reconstructed chart (not original Perplexity workbook): annual all-trim U.S. Explorer and Expedition model sales, with modeled EB mixes. 1998 unit counts and MSRPs are fixed at reported values; 1999–2010 modeled shares are 11.3% Explorer and 43.8% Expedition. Early-year rates are calibrated to the user-supplied lifetime unit totals. Other-year MSRP-equivalent annual amounts are distributed from lifetime values using an illustrative 2.5% annual price-growth curve calibrated to each lifetime total. Ford never disclosed all annual EB-unit sales. The 1991 Explorer MSRP spread is disputed across secondary references ($767 versus $2,661) and is not used in the published calculation.

#5481. Johnson & Johnson agreed to buy eye disease biotech Ollin for $2.2 billion upfront

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Blackstone Life Sciences will pay $750 million to fully fund Phase 3 development of Ollin's lead drug candidate, OLN324

Johnson & Johnson $JNJ agreed to acquire Ollin Biosciences, a clinical-stage drugmaker focused on treatments for serious eye diseases, in a deal worth $2.2 billion upfront, the company said on Monday.

The agreement also provides for as much as $1.125 billion in additional payments if certain regulatory and commercial targets are met. J&J expects the transaction to close before the end of 2026, subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions.

The acquisition would add OLN324 to J&J's pipeline. The investigational bispecific antibody targets two pathways in retinal disease: vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and angiopoietin-2 (Ang2). It is being developed for conditions including wet age-related macular degeneration and diabetic macular edema, which J&J said affect more than 40 million people worldwide and are leading causes of vision loss.

Kip Connor, vice president and ophthalmology disease area stronghold leader at J&J, said in a statement that OLN324 could reduce retinal fluid more effectively and allow more time between treatments. He said the data generated to date point to that potential.

J&J will enter a separate development funding agreement with Blackstone Life Sciences, contingent on the acquisition closing. Blackstone will provide J&J a total of $750 million, spread across several years, to cover the entire cost of Phase 3 development of OLN324. In return, Blackstone could receive royalties in the single digits, plus certain payments tied to regulatory and sales goals.

J&J said it will communicate the accounting treatment on or before the close of the transaction.

The Ollin deal follows J&J's June agreement to acquire Firefly Bio for $1 billion in cash. That transaction is also expected to close before the end of 2026, pending regulatory approvals and standard closing conditions.

#5479. Detectify’s Agentic Tooling lets AI agents test suspected flaws in running applications

Swedish application security company Detectify AB today launched Agentic Tooling, a set of tools aimed at letting an organization’s own artificial intelligence agents test whether suspected vulnerabilities can be exploited in running applications.

A new Security Ledger, also part of the launch, is designed to record the evidence behind each test. Detectify is pitching the release at DevSecOps teams that are unsure whether they can trust what their AI agents report.

Detectify customers report that roughly 80% of the findings from their AI-driven static application security testing tools are noise. Under pressure to deliver an answer, an agent can also produce a convincing report about a test it never ran, the company warned.

Even before AI agents enter the picture, many security teams are falling behind. Nine in 10 open critical and high-severity vulnerabilities had stayed exposed for more than 90 days, according to Detectify’s H2 2026 Cyber Hygiene Index. In a study by researchers at Fudan University and Tencent Holdings Ltd., 76% of the static-analysis alerts examined were found to be false positives. Each one took developers 10 to 20 minutes to review.

Through Agentic Tooling, agents can tap the testing engines Detectify has built over more than a decade. Included are payload assessments sourced from its ethical hacker community, attack surface data from its Surface Monitoring product and Alfred, an AI system the company launched in March 2025 to automate tests for known vulnerabilities.

Running in a customer’s own environment, the tools connect to agents through either the Model Context Protocol or a command-line interface. They operate only on the data a customer provides and are said to work with whichever agent the customer already uses.

At the center of the design is loop engineering, an emerging practice of running AI agents in automated, repeating workflows rather than prompting them by hand. Kicking off each loop is a trigger such as a continuous integration run. Whether it comes from a code scan, a bug bounty report, a red team or Detectify’s own attack surface data, each finding is turned into a ticket.

Once an agent picks up a ticket, it reads the relevant code before testing the live application from the outside, as an attacker would. Run continuously, the loop becomes what Detectify calls a verification factory.

The requests sent, the payloads used and the results returned are all logged in the Security Ledger each time an agent uses Detectify’s tools. Written by Detectify rather than the agent, the append-only ledger lets teams separate findings backed by actual tests from unsupported AI conclusions. Any ticket that could cause harm, such as a denial-of-service test, is marked unsafe for a person to decide on.

“Ask an agent to write your code, then ask the same agent whether it’s secure. If it says yes, you don’t actually know,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Rickard Carlsson. There are plenty of examples of agents fabricating proof to please the person asking, according to Carlsson, who described Detectify’s aim as “building proof that an agent can’t fabricate.”

Available on request starting today, Agentic Tooling builds on the Detectify MCP Server that the company announced in May to give AI agents access to its security findings. Investors include Insight Partners, which took a majority stake in October 2024, along with Balderton Capital (UK) LLP, Inventure, First Fellow Partners Oy and SquareOne App Ltd.

Nvidia $NVDA stock fell close to 3% in premarket trading on Monday, weighing on U.S. stock futures ahead of the chipmaker’s fiscal third-quarter earnings report and Anthropic’s initial public offering this week.

Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were down 90 points, a drop of 0.2%. S&P 500 futures fell 0.6%, and Nasdaq $NDAQ-100 futures declined 1.4%.

Across that work, the challenge is clear: teams understand why accessibility matters, but struggle to prioritize it against everything else they have to deliver. #5476. Amazon captured records of AI agents trying to steal AI provider keys

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The agents' own records describe stolen keys paying for the AI models that searched for more keys; Amazon cannot verify outcomes

Amazon $AMZN captured records from AI agents describing a campaign to steal AI provider keys, with the stolen keys covering the cost of the models behind the hunt for additional keys, the company said on Friday.

Amazon's MadPot network of decoy sensors collected the records from Oct. 3 to Nov. 5. The sensors were set up to look like widely used large language model inference APIs, and the agents transmitted their own campaign histories to them. Amazon said it did not watch the activity unfold and has no way to confirm the results the agents claimed.

Amazon assessed with moderate confidence that the agents ran on ARTEX, an open-source AI penetration testing framework, and that the operators were separate China-nexus groups. It cited Simplified Chinese prompts, China time-zone settings and targeting consistent with Chinese interests.

In the records, agents scanned for AI applications reachable from the open internet, pulled out the upstream provider keys inside, checked that they worked and kept them in a managed pool. They concentrated on applications that keep credentials from numerous providers in one place. Those included LLM gateways such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API and LiteLLM, as well as tools for building apps, among them Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat and Ollama.

A playbook in the records matched each product to known entry points. These included factory-set admin logins such as the LiteLLM default master key, CVE-2025-3248 in Langflow, CVE-2026-28797 in RAGFlow and a way around authentication in One API family systems by sending the isCliRequest header. To find keys, the agents drew on GitHub repositories, npm and PyPI packages, container image layers, paste sites and Telegram channels.

A second campaign used deepfakes in an attempt to get past know-your-customer checks at a pair of cryptocurrency exchanges. One verification vendor's server refused the deepfake each time the agents logged an attempt.

Amazon said it notified AWS customers it assessed as potentially affected. It could not confirm activity against other organizations and published indicators of compromise so others can check their environments.

"None of the techniques in these campaigns were new. What AI agents change is the speed and persistence of the attacker," the company said. Amazon recommended applying standard production security controls to AI applications, gateways for models and endpoints that serve inference, and keeping an eye out for surprise charges or odd usage patterns.

The FBI issued a FLASH alert dated Nov. 13 saying ARTEX has been employed by assorted threat groups dating back to at least August. The agency said the developer removed the GitHub repository in October, but the tool is still obtainable through forks made by the community, archived copies and a commercial variant named ARTEX PRO.

Cloudflare tracked more than 50 framework families attempting to scan its customers in the three days before its Nov. 13 post. Cisco $CSCO Talos analyzed ARTEX activity and said a developer using the pseudonym Autumn-27 published the framework on GitHub in July. Talos said it is used largely by financially motivated cybercriminals and China-nexus actors.

#5474. Exaforce’s ExaU lets security staff spin up a personal team of AI agents

Agentic security operations startup Exaforce Inc. today announced the launch of ExaU, a service that lets any security staff member spin up a personal team of artificial intelligence agents.

The new service seeks to move past the first wave of AI agents in security, which Exaforce says were built to offload a single task such as alert triage, risk assessment or penetration testing.

Exaforce argues that as AI absorbs more of the routine work, security staff are now responsible for outcomes that cannot be handed off one task at a time. Added to the mix is that staff are also facing a backlog of tasks, such as checks they mean to run, questions they plan to chase down and briefings owed to senior management.

Leading the list of ExaU features is the ability to create an agent by describing the job in plain language, down to the way a practitioner wants it done. Templates are also available. Each agent is designed to retain decisions, exceptions and past instructions.

To use, a security staff member begins by telling an agent what they are responsible for. The agent then works out what needs doing next and when. The response includes discoveries, questions and recommendations.

The new service also supports sharing agents across a security organization. A chief information security officer’s briefing agent can gather status from the agents used by every team. Exaforce’s own example has a finding setting off a threat hunt, an activity audit and outreach to an employee at the same time. A single assessment then pulls the results of all three together.

Everything runs inside Exaforce on the customer’s own data. With connections to identity providers, cloud services and security telemetry already part of the platform, there are no tokens to mint for ExaU agents. The company’s real-time security knowledge graph is claimed to give each agent an understanding of how systems relate from its first task.

Investigations are carried out by the agents on their own. Under the controls built into ExaU, any action affecting employees, systems or communications requires approval first. Recorded in the Exaforce audit log, every step an agent takes can be reviewed later.

Exabots, the agents Exaforce manages itself, already handle threat detection, alert triage and investigation for every customer on the platform. ExaU is pitched as a complement to that standing workforce. Available now as part of the Exaforce platform, the release follows the September launch of Exaforce AI Security, a kill switch for AI agents that go rogue.

HarbourVest Partners, Peak XV Partners, Mayfield Fund, Khosla Ventures and Seligman Ventures were among the investors in Exaforce’s $125 million Series B round in May. Including that round, total funding since the company’s 2023 founding comes to $200 million.
