#5473. Remedy Robotics Raises $62 Million Series B to Bring Life-Saving Cardiovascular Intervention to Patients Everywhere

Funding will support clinical trials, advancement toward FDA approval, and planned commercial deployment of the company's AI-enabled endovascular robotic platform and software suite

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Remedy Robotics, Inc. ("Remedy"), a leading healthcare and physical AI company developing robotic systems for cardiovascular care and endovascular intervention, today announced it has raised $62 million in Series B funding to accelerate its mission of delivering flawless, immediate robotic care to all patients, regardless of location.

The funding will support several major milestones, including a planned pivotal clinical trial in partnership with the University of California and advancement toward FDA approval for neurovascular intervention. Remedy will also deploy prototype N1 Systems across its network of clinical partners, including through its strategic partnerships with SVIN Mission Thrombectomy and the Australian Stroke Alliance, while continuing to advance the system's industry-leading AI capabilities and autonomous functions.

"Endovascular intervention is the gold standard treatment for stroke and many cardiovascular emergencies, yet access remains limited to a small number of hospitals. For these time-critical conditions, that's devastating. Even when specialist intervention is available, treatment is often delayed, and complications are frustratingly common," said Dr. David Bell, CEO and Co-founder of Remedy Robotics. "This funding will allow us to accelerate toward deployment of our N1 System so we can bring quality intervention to patients everywhere, regardless of geography."

DCVC led the Series B, with participation from new investors including UC Investments (the University of California's investment office), Skip Capital, and Hostplus (one of Australia's largest pension funds). Existing investors Build Collective by Tony Fadell, Blackbird, Divergent Capital and KdT Ventures doubled down.

"Remedy Robotics represents a new generation of medical robotics and physical AI companies, focused not only on technical innovation, but on solving real-world challenges," said James Hardiman, General Partner at DCVC. "We believe the company is uniquely positioned to redefine how life-saving intervention is delivered and are thrilled to support them as they advance toward broader clinical and commercial adoption."

Remedy is finalizing development of the N1 System, an AI-enabled robotic platform and software suite that uses machine learning to analyze preoperative imaging, simulate cases in advance, provide real-time 3D-2D image registration and complete entire endovascular procedures robotically. Designed for on-site, remote, or autonomous operation, the system has the potential to dramatically expand access to and improve the quality of specialized neurovascular, coronary, and peripheral vascular care. Remedy now works with more than 100 hospitals worldwide and is among a small group of physical AI companies bringing robotics into real-world clinical use. In October 2025, Remedy announced that it had successfully completed the world's first remote neurointerventional procedures using the N1 System.

"This funding will allow our world-leading hardware, software, and machine learning teams to progress the N1 system towards clinical trials and potential FDA approval, while also developing additional features including full autonomy," said Jake Sganga, CTO and Co-founder of Remedy Robotics. "We are particularly excited to deepen our partnership with the University of California, having worked closely with their clinical experts since 2021, and as we prepare for our planned pivotal clinical trials to be held across the UC network."

"Remedy is building the kind of company we look for at Blackbird: one with world-class technical talent, a massive global problem to solve, and the potential to create an entirely new category," said Michael Tolo, Partner at Blackbird. "We believe Remedy is uniquely positioned to transform how endovascular care is delivered, and we are excited to support the company through its next phase of growth."

Cardiovascular disease, including stroke and heart attack, is the leading cause of death globallyâclaiming nearly 20 million lives each yearâabout twice the toll of all cancers. Beyond the human cost, stroke alone carries an annual economic burden of approximately $891 billion worldwide through healthcare costs and lost productivity. Access to endovascular intervention, the most effective treatment for many cardiovascular conditions, remains severely limited because only highly specialized physicians at a small number of hospitals can perform it. Today, just 2.8 percent of eligible stroke patients worldwide have access to endovascular treatment, leaving millions each year with otherwise preventable disability. Because cardiovascular emergencies are so time-critical, patient outcomes vary sharply based on proximity to specialized care, even in countries with well-developed specialist networks, such as the United States. Remedy's technology directly addresses this access gap, delivering expert care for stroke, severe heart attacks, hemorrhagic conditions, and other time-critical cardiovascular emergencies to patients wherever they are.

Remedy aims to elevate the standard of care across the cardiovascular continuum, from diagnosis to discharge and surveillance, with the goal of making flawless, immediate cardiovascular care available to patients everywhere, from San Francisco to rural areas of Arkansas where timely care is out of reach, or to Lagos, Nigeria, where intervention is almost entirely unavailable.

The N1 System is under development and is not currently available for sale or clinical use in any jurisdiction.

Its proprietary N1 System combines robotics, AI, and advanced computer vision to raise the standard of care across the cardiovascular continuumâfrom diagnosis and intervention to discharge and surveillanceâbringing expert-level treatment within reach of patients wherever they are. Remedy's clinical and research work has been published in leading peer-reviewed journals, including Interventional Neuroradiology and the American Journal of Neuroradiology, and the company holds 48 patents covering its platform, including foundational patents in machine learning applied to surgical robotics. Headquartered in San Francisco, Remedy is backed by DCVC, Blackbird, UC Investments (the University of California's investment office), and Tony Fadell's Build Collective, among others, and partners with clinicians at leading medical institutions across the U.S. and worldwide. #5472. Denmark's Leo Pharma is pushing its IPO plans past 2026 on market volatility

Free daily briefing on global business news.

CEO Christophe Bourdon said Leo Pharma's owners see market conditions as unsuitable and declined to give a new timeline

Leo Pharma is pushing its planned initial public offering beyond 2026 because of market volatility, CEO Christophe Bourdon said in an interview, according to Bloomberg. The Danish skin-treatment drugmaker had targeted a listing this year.

Bourdon said the company is ready for an IPO but that conditions will keep it from happening in 2026, according to Bloomberg. "The timing of the IPO lies in the hands of the shareholders and both shareholders have assessed that current market conditions do not support a listing," he told Bloomberg.

The LEO Foundation holds 80% of the company, and private equity firm Nordic Capital owns the rest, according to Reuters. Bourdon told Reuters that when a listing happens hinges on how the business performs and how willing investors are to back fresh market debuts.

An IPO is still what the company intends, Bourdon said, but he would not say when it might now happen, according to Bloomberg. He told Reuters an IPO is a "natural and viable option" for the company. He said Leo Pharma is concentrating on steady expansion and on reinforcing its operations so that it can move ahead with a listing once conditions are right.

Other companies have also delayed or scaled back planned listings as equity market volatility grows, according to Reuters.

Leo Pharma on Monday reported nine-month results. Revenue rose 9% to 10.96 billion kroner ($1.65 billion), or 11% at constant exchange rates, the company said. It kept its 2026 outlook for revenue growth of 9% to 11% at constant exchange rates.

Nordic Capital put €450 million ($496 million) into Leo Pharma in 2021 for a minority stake, when the company outlined its intention to get ready for a possible listing over the following four to five years, according to Reuters. Leo Pharma enlisted seven investment banks to assist in running an IPO earlier this year, according to Bloomberg.

Reuters reported that press coverage earlier in November suggested turbulent markets might delay the IPO until 2027, and that Leo Pharma chose not to respond to that speculation when it surfaced.

#5471. Activist investor is pushing Invitation Homes to keep selling off its houses

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Land & Buildings wants at least $2 billion a year returned to shareholders and says talks with the board have gone nowhere

Jonathan Litt's Land & Buildings Investment Management is pushing Invitation Homes to keep selling houses and to return more cash to shareholders, according to The Wall Street Journal. The activist hedge fund intends to mail a letter to Invitation's investors spelling out what it wants.

Land & Buildings says its discussions with Invitation's executives and directors failed to produce any progress on its worries, according to The Wall Street Journal, which reviewed the letter. The firm owned less than 1% of Invitation as of June 30.

The letter says Invitation should continue disposing of homes "one at a time" while its stock sits at a discount to net asset value, a figure Land & Buildings pegs at roughly $45 per share, according to The Wall Street Journal. Invitation Homes stock was at $26.85 at its latest close.

The firm also wants Invitation to hand shareholders $2 billion or more each year, in the form of buybacks or dividends. Among its additional demands are a 6% rebate on the down payment for renters who purchase the homes they lease, along with scaled-back acquisitions and development.

“The Board should say plainly that it will keep selling homes and returning capital for as long as the discount persists, even if that ultimately means liquidating the Company,” Litt wrote in the letter, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Land & Buildings argues that a new law will cap Invitation's room to expand, and that the company's cash is best spent repurchasing its own stock. Invitation Chief Executive Dallas Tanner has said the company can work within most of the regulations proposed to carry out the law.

Dallas-based Invitation is valued by the market at roughly $15.5 billion and held close to 86,000 houses in September. Its stock has lost over 30% across the last five years, according to The Wall Street Journal, which pointed to higher interest rates and the new law as factors.

In the third quarter, Invitation sold more than 600 homes, spent $245 million on stock buybacks and bought more than 200 homes, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The measure, H.R. 6644, became law on July 11 and will bar institutional investors from buying additional single-family homes without requiring them to sell existing holdings. It defines an institutional investor as one owning 350 or more single-family homes. Exceptions include build-to-rent developments and a program that lets investors buy homes to renovate and offer tenants a path to ownership.

Invitation was marketing 549 homes as of July, and it bought the homebuilder ResiBuilt earlier this year.

Land & Buildings, based in Stamford, Connecticut, concentrates on investing in listed real-estate firms. It has pressed for changes at firms such as Equity Commonwealth and First Industrial Realty Trust, according to The Wall Street Journal.

#5469. Palo Alto Networks report finds organizations struggle to track and secure AI agents in the cloud

A new report out today from cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks Inc. finds that artificial intelligence agents have quickly become a fixture in software development, but many organizations can’t properly track or secure what those agents are doing in the cloud.

Now in its sixth year, the State of Cloud Security Report 2026 is based on a survey of 2,800 security executives and practitioners in 10 countries. Along with how AI is being used to build and deploy software, the report looks at how quickly organizations are able to respond when something goes wrong.

The use of AI agents was found to be close to universal, with 99% of respondents saying they use agents for autonomous or semiautonomous actions in their development pipelines. Some 73% said the agents are allowed to modify code, pipeline configurations or production environments, and agents are even doing security testing at 44% of organizations.

The amount of change is going up as a result. Some 82% said AI-driven development has increased the volume of infrastructure updates reaching their cloud, yet organizations on average enforce fewer than three of the eight predeployment security checks measured in the survey. AI is also being used to generate infrastructure-as-code templates at 42% of organizations, but only 34% scan that code before production.

Not surprisingly, problems are getting through. Respondents said that on average, 19% of high and critical application security issues reached production over a 90-day period. It takes an average of 18.4 days to get a fix for a security issue found in code into production.

When respondents were asked what was stopping them from fixing issues before deployment, the most common answer was business pressure to release quickly at 39%. Unclear risk acceptance policies came second at 30%.

Accountability is also an issue when it comes to agents. Two in five organizations said they are unable to reconstruct what an AI agent did, a share that rises to 46% in financial services, while 53% said agent activity is logged under a developer’s identity or personal access token. That means when something goes wrong, investigators first have to figure out which actions were taken by a person and which were taken by an agent before they can work out what was affected.

Removing access once something does go wrong is also slow. Some 60% of organizations still need manual intervention to revoke access for nonhuman identities, and it takes an average of 2.5 days to revoke or rotate compromised developer credentials, API keys or pipeline secrets.

Data governance has its own issues. Nearly all organizations, 99%, said they had found ungoverned AI in their environment in the past year, yet only 9% are able to automatically discover and classify it. Some 40% said governed data had been copied into ungoverned AI tools, and 39% had seen sensitive or regulated data used to train or fine-tune models without authorization.

Despite the gaps, confidence is high. Almost every respondent, 97%, said they are at least somewhat confident they can secure their AI supply chain and applications, though only 36% can monitor AI behavior in production and just 30% can detect prompt injection.

The final section of the report looks at the threat from frontier AI models that can find and exploit software vulnerabilities on their own. Nearly all respondents, 98%, said they are concerned about it, and 65% said it poses a significant or severe threat to global critical infrastructure and financial systems over the next 12 to 18 months. Utilities were the most likely of any sector to rate the threat as significant or severe at 79%, compared with 48% in telecommunications.

Interestingly, though the report refers to “frontier AI-powered capabilities,” the survey questions at the back of it call them “Mythos-grade” threats, a reference to Anthropic PBC’s Claude Mythos models. Palo Alto Networks was one of the launch partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, which gave defenders early access to Claude Mythos Preview in April.

The report argues that against attackers working at machine speed, an 18.4-day fix cycle leaves organizations exposed for more than 17 days after a vulnerability can be discovered. Part of the problem, according to the report, is fragmented tooling, with only 19% of organizations saying they operate with unified telemetry and workflows across code, cloud, identity and runtime. Nearly half of organizations, 47%, still do the work of correlating application vulnerabilities with runtime threats by hand, a number that’s even higher in the U.S. at 55%.

The report ends with a series of recommendations for organizations to secure their cloud environments as AI agents take on more work. Agents should be given their own identities with a clear owner and only the permissions they need to do their job. Security teams are also advised to automate the fixing of recurring issues, though only after rollback procedures have been put in place.

Led by Blue Cloud Ventures, the round brings total funding to $96 million, with more than 1,500 dealerships across the U.S. and Canada already running on Numa's AI Operating System

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Numa, the AI Operating System for dealerships, today announced a $45 million Series C led by Blue Cloud Ventures, with participation from Threshold Ventures, Costanoa, Touring Capital, Gradient Ventures and Tokio Marine Future Fund. The round brings Numa's total funding to $96 million. It caps a year in which Numa tripled in size, tripled its annual recurring revenue and became the AI system GM, FordDirect, BMW and Stellantis each put in front of their dealerships.

Numa has already won the hardest part of the dealership: the customer conversation. The system has handled more than 1 billion calls, texts and chats and booked more than 4 million appointments. Dealerships that run on Numa stay and grow with it. Net revenue retention has risen over the past year, and more dealerships are moving to longer agreements.

For decades, dealership software was built one task at a time. Each system kept its own record of what happened, and none of them acted on what the customer just said. The first wave of AI did not change that. It answered faster, then handed the work back to people to chase by hand.

Numa does not hand the work back. It knows not just who the customer is but what they need, and it acts on it: booking the visit, finding the right car, routing the call or flagging the customer about to leave.

"In two years, every general manager will have an AI COO," said Tasso Roumeliotis, founder and CEO of Numa. "At more than 1,500 dealerships, they already do, and it is Numa. It knows every conversation in the store, sees what needs attention and runs the work that follows. That is not another dashboard or another point tool. It is an operating system. The DMS was built to record the dealership. It was never built to run it. Numa was, and this round puts more engineers to accelerate it."

"What is unique about Numa is that the company understands the DNA and culture of a dealership and seamlessly AI-enables the workflow while empowering all constituents including the dealerships customers", added Mir Arif, Managing Partner of Blue Cloud Ventures.  "Numa is not prescriptive but rather deeply understands the objectives of the BDC representative, the salesperson, the service technician, the parts specialist and the sales manager and significantly enhances their productivity."

"As an insurer, we view dealerships as a critical part of the ecosystem that supports customers throughout their vehicle ownership journey," said Mitsutoshi Shizuru, Managing Executive Officer of Tokio Marine & Nichido Fire Insurance Co., Ltd, "Numa is using AI to make this important customer touchpoint faster, more efficient, and more seamless. We believe Numa's technology has the potential to revolutionize the relationship between dealerships and their customers and help shape the next generation of mobility customer experiences in the U.S. and beyond."

This year, Numa took its system across the whole store.

In the service lane, Numa already knows every conversation. In August, Numa acquired SocketTime to put the work behind those conversations into the same system, so what a customer tells the store and what the store does about it run in one place.

In sales, Numa for Sales, launched this month, as the first agent with Inventory Fluency. It knows every new and used vehicle on the lot down to the trim, features and miles, learns each buyer's situation and gets them in the car that fits best, even when the one they called about has sold. Every qualified lead lands in the dealership's CRM with the full conversation, so the salesperson who picks it up already knows the buyer.

On every line into the store, Operator, launched in September, is the first Precision Routing system for dealerships. It answers first, understands why each customer is calling and puts them in the right hands with that reason carried through. When the phone rings, everyone at the dealership knows the call is for them. Operator continues to climb above 95% with calls going to the right destination.

LiveCSIâ¢ reads customer interactions as they happen and flags the ones putting satisfaction at risk while there is still time to fix them, instead of waiting for a survey to report what went wrong. In 90 days, it analyzed 50 million interactions.

Every dealership on Numa now has over 25+ natural voices to choose from, with regional accents, a new Spanish voice, sharper recognition of vehicle makes, models and VINs, and adjustable speaking speed. The voice on the line sounds like someone who works at the dealership. It comes at no added cost, with nothing for the store to set up.

Three of the largest automakers in North America have each chosen Numa. GM named Numa an iMR Approved Turnkey Vendor, and more than 240 GM dealerships run on Numa today. Numa is also approved on Stellantis' MarketCenter, opening access to more than 2,600 dealerships in the U.S. and 440 in Canada.

The operating system for the dealership is not on its way. It is already running.

Numa is the AI Operating System used by leading dealerships to modernize customer operations across voice, text, service, sales, fixed operations, and customer intelligence. #5467. Krybit to Settra: how 6 ransomware groups of 2026 operate

Free daily briefing on global business news.

New ransomware groups of 2026, from Krybit to Settra, profiled by how they operate, what sets each apart and the defenses one security vendor recommends

Not every ransomware group that surfaced in 2026 locks files. Some of the year's new operators steal data instead of encrypting it. One tries to pass itself off as a legitimate business. Another, Deadlock, is a returning name that came back in June 2026.

These new ransomware groups of 2026 come from an analysis by Smarttech247, a security vendor, titled "Six Ransomware Groups That Emerged in 2026." Tadhg De Barra wrote the post, which the company published on its blog on September 4, 2026. It covers six emerging ransomware gangs: Krybit, Payload, Insomnia, AiLock, Deadlock and Settra. The source describes them as groups that emerged or re-emerged during the year.

The profiles are not a ranking. Smarttech247 does not rank the groups by the size or impact of their breaches. This list follows the same approach and treats each group on its own terms.

Victim figures in the source cover different reporting periods. Krybit's count runs through the end of its first full quarter. Payload's and Insomnia's counts are as of late April 2026. AiLock's figure reflects early June 2026. Deadlock named 75 victims in a month. These windows do not line up. The numbers cannot be compared directly or combined into a single total.

The groups also differ in how they operate. Insomnia is described as having no encryptor at all and relies on data theft. The post describes Settra's legitimate-business front, and no Settra encryptor has been publicly analyzed. Deadlock uses a driver exploit. The source ties no single intrusion vector to Krybit. For its two data-theft groups, Smarttech247 offers defenders this advice: "Your backups won't save you."

The post also includes case studies from Smarttech247's client work. Those cases reflect the vendor's own reported work, not independent findings. Each slide that follows covers one ransomware threat actor and what the source establishes about how it operates.

Krybit is one of six ransomware groups that emerged in 2026, according to an analysis by Smarttech247. The security vendor tracked the group's activity through the end of its first full quarter of operation.

Smarttech247 profiles Krybit in a blog post by Tadhg De Barra, published September 4, 2026. The post is a security vendor's assessment, not an independent study.

Krybit's figure applies only to that first-quarter window. It should be read within that period rather than set against counts the post gives for other groups.

No single intrusion vector has been tied to Krybit. Smarttech247's section on the group does not link it to any one method of getting into a victim's network.

Payload is one of six ransomware operations that security firm Smarttech247 profiled as having emerged or resurfaced in 2026. The vendor reports Payload's activity as of late April 2026.

That late-April cutoff applies to Payload's figures alone. Other groups in the same analysis are measured over different windows. Payload's numbers are not comparable with theirs and cannot be added to them.

Insomnia is a data-extortion group that Smarttech247 describes as having no encryptor at all. Its leverage over a victim comes from the data it steals, not from locking files.

This sets Insomnia apart from a conventional ransomware operator. A group with an encryptor makes a victim's files unreadable and disrupts its systems. Insomnia, as Smarttech247 describes it, skips that step. The pressure it applies rests entirely on what it has taken.

Smarttech247's key takeaways tie Insomnia to stolen credentials as a route into victims' networks. In that summary, the vendor places the group among those it says lean on identity to gain access. The claim appears in the takeaways rather than in a detailed account of a specific intrusion.

The vendor pairs Insomnia with one other data-theft operator on its list. For both, its advice to defenders is "Your backups won't save you." That line is Smarttech247's recommendation, not the result of a measured test.

The advice follows from the group's method. Backups help an organization restore files an attacker has encrypted. They cannot recall data an attacker has already copied out of the network.

AiLock is a ransomware group that Smarttech247, a cybersecurity vendor, counts among the threat actors that emerged in 2026. The vendor's figure for AiLock reflects the group's activity as of early June 2026.

That early-June date is the only reporting period the source attaches to AiLock. Activity after that point falls outside what the profile covers.

Deadlock is a ransomware group that resurfaced in June 2026 after an earlier period of activity, rather than appearing for the first time. Smarttech247 counts 75 victims named by the group in a single month.

That return puts Deadlock among the threat actors the vendor describes as re-emerging during the year. It is an existing name back in circulation, not a new label.

The Smarttech247 profile also lists a driver exploit among the methods Deadlock uses.

Settra is a ransomware group that tries to pass itself off as a legitimate business, according to Smarttech247. The cybersecurity vendor lists it among six ransomware threat actors that emerged or re-emerged in 2026.

That effort to look legitimate is the main trait the vendor attaches to Settra.

Little has been published about the group's technical tooling. No Settra encryptor has been publicly analyzed, according to Smarttech247.

An encryptor is the program a ransomware group uses to lock a victim's files. With no public analysis available, there is no published technical breakdown of how Settra encrypts data.

The lack of an analysis does not mean Settra has no encryptor. It means only that no Settra encryption tool has been examined in public.

#5466. From Under Armour to Telegram: 10 familiar names in 2026 breach data

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Data breaches in 2026 have touched 10 brands most people know, from Under Armour and AT&T to Telegram, and show how attackers reach customer records

A phone call, not malicious code, opened the door in two of the 2026 breaches on this list. The hacking group ShinyHunters used a phishing call to get into Charter Communications' Salesforce $CRM environment in April 2026. It used the same approach against Madison Square $SQ Garden Sports Corp. There, a call to a low-level employee led into the company's Microsoft $MSFT Entra identity system.

The second recurring pattern is pressure. Groups on this list posted victims on leak sites, set deadlines and published stolen files when no payment arrived. The Russian ransomware group Everest listed Under Armour $UAA on its leak site in November 2025 and gave the company seven days. Under Armour did not respond publicly. After the ransom went unpaid, Everest released the customer dataset in January 2026. ShinyHunters published MSG Sports data the day after the company missed its ransom deadline.

The third pattern is that stolen data keeps coming back. A dataset of 176 million records, built from AT&T $T's 2019 and 2024 breaches, resurfaced in February 2026. Social Security numbers in it that were previously encrypted now appear decrypted. That is why this list describes what happened in 2026 — a posting, a release or a resurfacing — rather than claiming every company was first hacked this year.

The 10 slides that follow draw on SpyCloud's log of data breaches in 2026 and focus on names most readers already know. They are a selection, not a ranking. The list covers Canvas maker Instructure, Under Armour, AT&T, Charter Communications and its Spectrum brand, MSG Sports, Exact Sciences, DentaQuest, WhatsApp and Telegram. It also covers a breach at Klue that reached LastPass, Huntress, Recorded Future, Tanium, Jamf and 8x8.

Breach sizes are reported in different units, and the numbers can disagree. In the MSG Sports case, ShinyHunters claimed about 26 million records. The published data held nearly 10 million unique email addresses. SpyCloud's own log shows 55.4 million. Where an attacker's claim, a confirmed count and SpyCloud's figure differ, the slides label each one separately. That way readers can see who is counting what. For anyone with an account at one of these companies, the exposed data ranges from email addresses to Social Security numbers.

Instructure, the Salt Lake City company that makes the Canvas learning management system, appears in the 2026 data breach list compiled by SpyCloud. SpyCloud is a security firm that tracks stolen credentials and leaked datasets.

Canvas is software that schools, colleges and universities use to run their courses online. Instructors post syllabi, readings and assignments on the platform. Students use it to submit work, take quizzes and check grades.

That daily use is why the name is familiar to many households. Students, parents and teachers sign in to Canvas throughout the school year.

Under Armour $UAA customer data went public in January 2026, when the Everest ransomware group released a dataset holding 72 million email addresses. The release came after Under Armour left a ransom demand unpaid.

Everest, a Russian ransomware group, first named the sportswear company on its leak site in November 2025. That timing shapes how the incident should be described. The listing belongs to late 2025, while the publication of the customer data is the 2026 event.

A leak site is a public page where an extortion group names the companies it says it has hit. A listing there tells the victim, its customers and other criminals that the group claims to hold stolen files and intends to publish them.

Everest set a seven-day deadline on the Under Armour listing. A short countdown is a pressure tactic. It gives a company a fixed window to pay before the data goes out, and it makes the threat visible to anyone watching the site.

Under Armour made no public response while the clock ran. No payment followed, and Everest went ahead and released the dataset.

The scale of that release does not depend on Everest's own claim. The 72 million figure is a confirmed count, and SpyCloud's findings back it up. That sets this case apart from incidents where the only available number comes from the attackers.

The unit matters as well. The figure counts email addresses, not customers, accounts or total records. One person can have more than one address, and an address can appear in a dataset without a matching active account.

An email address is not a password or a payment card. It is still the login name for many shopping, fitness and banking accounts. A leaked address gives criminals a ready target list for phishing emails that pose as a trusted brand. It can also be paired with passwords exposed in other breaches and tried against other services, a technique known as credential stuffing.

A dataset of 176 million AT&T $T records resurfaced in February 2026, according to SpyCloud. Social Security numbers in the set that had once been encrypted now appear in decrypted form.

AT&T is the Dallas-based telecommunications company behind one of the largest wireless and home internet businesses in the U.S. The records in this dataset were not taken in a new 2026 intrusion. They were assembled from earlier AT&T breaches in 2019 and 2024.

What changed in 2026 was the condition of the data. The dataset brought the material from both earlier incidents together in one place.

Encryption scrambles a piece of data so it cannot be read without the matching key. An encrypted Social Security number in a stolen file is far harder to use for fraud than the same number in readable form. Once the encryption is stripped away, the number can be read and copied directly.

A Social Security number is a nine-digit identifier issued by the Social Security Administration. Banks, lenders, employers and insurers use it to confirm who a person is. That is why it is a central target for identity thieves.

Unlike a password, a Social Security number does not expire. The Social Security Administration assigns a new number only in limited cases, such as when a person can show ongoing harm from misuse of the old one. For most people whose numbers leak, the original number stays in use.

One protection available in the U.S. is a credit freeze. A freeze blocks new lenders from pulling a person's credit file at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Federal law has made placing and lifting a freeze free since 2018.

For AT&T customers whose details appeared in the 2019 or 2024 breaches, the February 2026 resurfacing puts that old information back in circulation in a more usable form.

Charter Communications, the cable and internet provider that sells service under the Spectrum brand, was breached in April 2026. The ShinyHunters group got into Charter's Salesforce $CRM environment through a phishing phone call. Confirmed counts start at 4.9 million, and a claimed count reaches 42 million, according to SpyCloud.

A phishing call, often called vishing, works by persuading an employee to hand over login details or approve access. In a typical attack, the caller poses as someone the employee has reason to trust, such as a colleague or a member of an IT help desk. The request is framed as routine.

The weak point in this kind of attack is a person rather than a software flaw. When an employee hands over access willingly, there is no malicious file or code for security tools to flag.

Salesforce is a customer relationship management platform. Companies use it to store customer accounts, contact details and records of service interactions. A system like this is designed to gather customer information in one place. Access to a company's Salesforce environment is therefore a route to its customer data.

The two figures tied to this incident measure different things. The 4.9 million figure is the low end of the confirmed counts. The 42 million figure is a claimed count, not a verified total. The confirmed number marks the lower bound of what has been checked. The claimed number marks the upper bound of what has been alleged.

Madison Square $SQ Garden Sports Corp. was breached after the ShinyHunters group placed a phishing call to a low-level employee. The group used that call to get into the company's Microsoft $MSFT Entra identity system. ShinyHunters posted the breach on its leak site in June 2026.

MSG Sports owns two of New York's major-league franchises: the Knicks of the NBA and the Rangers of the NHL. Both teams play their home games at Madison Square Garden in Manhattan. MSG Sports is a separate public company from the business that operates the arena itself. Its shares trade on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker MSGS.

Microsoft Entra is Microsoft's identity and access platform. Until a 2023 rebrand, Microsoft called it Azure Active Directory. Organizations use it to decide which employees can sign in to which cloud apps and services. Administrators can also use it to require multifactor authentication and to set conditional access rules that limit sign-ins by device or location. A working login there can reach whatever systems that account is permitted to use.

The intrusion started with a phone call. That method is often called vishing, short for voice phishing. The target was a low-level employee, not a senior executive.

After the leak site posting, ShinyHunters gave MSG Sports a deadline to pay a ransom. MSG Sports did not meet that deadline. The group published the data the following day.

Three different figures describe the size of the breach. ShinyHunters said it held about 26 million records. The data it published contained nearly 10 million unique email addresses. SpyCloud's own log shows 55.4 million for the incident. SpyCloud's number is more than twice the size of the attacker's claim.

The figures come from different counters and use different units. A record is typically one row in a database. The same person can appear in many rows. A count of unique email addresses removes those duplicates.

Exact Sciences, the Madison, Wisconsin, cancer diagnostics company best known for the Cologuard at-home colorectal cancer screening test, appears in SpyCloud's reporting on 2026 data breaches.

DentaQuest, a U.S. dental benefits company, appears on SpyCloud's list of data breaches reported in 2026.

WhatsApp, the messaging app owned by Meta $META Platforms, is one of the well-known brands that appear in SpyCloud's roundup of 2026 data breaches.

The Klue breach appears in SpyCloud's 2026 data breach tracking as a single incident that touched six other technology companies: LastPass, Huntress, Recorded Future, Tanium, Jamf and 8x8.

The incident carries Klue's name. The six companies linked to it are the more familiar brands, and SpyCloud groups all of them under the Klue entry.

The listing shows that a single breach record can reach several companies beyond the one named in its title.

Two separate scraped Telegram datasets appear in SpyCloud's tracking of 2026 data breaches. One, labeled Part 2, contains 328.9 million records. The other contains 54.2 million records.

Both datasets show up as rows in SpyCloud's breach table. Each row lists a dataset name and a record count. The listing gives no date for either file. It does not describe how the data was gathered, and it includes no response from Telegram.

The absence of a date limits what the entries reveal. An entry in 2026 tracking places a dataset in this year's log. It does not by itself show when the information inside was collected. Without a date, the listing cannot indicate whether these files were assembled this year or circulated earlier.

The word "scraped" sets these entries apart from most of this list. Scraping generally refers to automated collection of information that a service displays or returns, such as public profile details. That is a different act from breaking into a company's internal systems. SpyCloud's table does not say which method produced these two files or which fields the records hold.

The two figures count records, not people. One person can appear more than once in a single dataset. Separate datasets can also share entries. SpyCloud does not report how many unique Telegram accounts the files cover or whether the two files overlap. The listing also does not explain what the Part 2 label refers to.

Each file also comes with a single count. The listing names no attacker group, so there is no claimed figure to set beside SpyCloud's number. No confirmed count from Telegram appears either. That leaves SpyCloud's table as the only source for both totals.

For Telegram users, the entries confirm that two large data collections tied to the messaging app appear in 2026 breach-tracking data. They do not establish what information about any individual user is included.

#5465. EXALTA Establishes Global Headquarters in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania

Bethlehem to serve as the central hub of EXALTA's integrated global network, supporting MedTech programs from development through launch and into production

BETHLEHEM, Pa., Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- EXALTA, an integrated MedTech solutions provider, today announced the establishment of its global headquarters in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania. The designation begins a new chapter for the company's long-standing presence in the Lehigh Valley. It also puts Bethlehem at the center of EXALTA's work supporting fast-growing MedTech programs notably in Trauma, Extremities and Spine.

Bethlehem will serve as a key scale and coordination hub within EXALTA's integrated global network. The site brings together the critical capabilities needed to move programs efficiently from development through launch and into production. These capabilities support 510(k) clearance and EU MDR readiness through testing, prototyping, in-house regulatory expertise and a microbiology laboratory. Together they reinforce a track record of supporting regulatory submissions, product launches, and post-market surveillance.

"Getting to launch in MedTech already requires tight coordination across development, regulatory, and manufacturing," said Olivier Wolber, Chief Executive Officer of EXALTA. "Where many programs struggle is maintaining that alignment as they scale. By bringing these capabilities together in one place, we reduce handoffs, shorten feedback loops, and give customers a more controlled and predictable path from concept to launch and into sustained production."

The headquarters designation reflects EXALTA's model of aligning development, regulatory, and manufacturing within a single, accountable structure. This approach reduces fragmentation, supports faster decision-making, and enables more predictable timelines as programs move toward launch and scale.

Centrally located in the Northeast, the Lehigh Valley gives EXALTA's headquarters convenient access to customers, partners and talent across the region, along with strong connections to EXALTA's sites around the world.

"Bethlehem has been part of our story for a long time, and this next chapter reflects where EXALTA is going," said Jeff Tyber, Group President and Board Member. "We're proud to be building the future of EXALTA right here in Bethlehem, alongside the talent and partners that make the Lehigh Valley such a strong home for MedTech."

Since its formation in 2025, EXALTA has grown to more than 1,700 employees. From Bethlehem, EXALTA will lead a global network of 10 sites across 3 continents, enabling flexible and scalable support for MedTech programs worldwide.

About EXALTA GroupEXALTA Group is an integrated MedTech solutions provider bringing together development, regulatory, and manufacturing capabilities to accelerate the path from concept to launch. With more than 1,700 employees across 10 sites on 3 continents and a focus on orthopedics and adjacent markets, EXALTA supports OEM partners through connected, scalable solutions designed to reduce complexity and accelerate time-to-market.

#5464. Goodbye, manual work: AI-native CRM platform Dreamteam raises $53M to automate enterprise sales

Intelligent sales software startup Dreamteam AI Inc. said today it has raised $53 million in early-stage funding to try to flip the narrative around customer relationship management platforms, which often seem like more of a hindrance than a help, by actually getting work done for sales teams.

The funds come by way of a seed and Series A round led by Accel Partners with participation from Together Fund and Premji Invest.

CRM platforms such as Salesforce and Hubspot have served as vital cogs in the wheel sales-focused enterprises for more than a quarter of a century. But these days they often create just as much work as they save, says Dreamteam co-founder and Chief Executive Anand Venkatraman (pictured, center, alongside co-founders Ramesh Parthasarathy and Senthil Kanthaswamy). While organizations are striving to use artificial intelligence to automate more of their business processes, CRMs are holding them back, he believes.

The problem with legacy CRM platforms is that they’re totally reliant on manual data entry, Venkatraman explained. Because their architectures are built around structured data fields and rigid, hand-coded workflows, they create a tight bottleneck that makes it almost impossible for autonomous AI agents that feed primarily on semantic data to get anything done.

“When a sales prospect expresses price hesitation or mentions a competitor, a salesperson registers it immediately,” he said. “But a legacy CRM, starving for unstructured nuance, misses it entirely, leaving AI agents without the vital context needed to reason effectively.”

To provide this context, Dreamteam has rebuilt the CRM from the ground up around the idea of a “company brain,” or a living memory of the business that constantly updates itself by ingesting new information from meetings with clients, prospects and team members, emails and other connected tools. As with all AI-native platforms, there’s also a generous dose of automation in the shape of four AI agents, or teammates, which specialize in different tasks.

The agents include Rachel, which handles account research; Sally for meeting preparations and follow-ups; Raj, which monitors for pipeline risks; and Alex, which serves as the CRM administrator, keeping the platform ticking over without any human intervention.

Venkatraman said he and his co-founders designed Dreamteam’s architecture specifically to address the historic shortcomings of legacy CRM platforms, which struggle to dig up the most vital business intelligence, leaving teams flying blind. “When a CEO asks why the quarter’s three biggest deals were lost, RevOps spends two weeks building a partial answer from whatever the reps happened to type,” he said. “The richest signals from meetings, emails, and calls were never captured, so the answer is always incomplete and always late.”

Legacy CRMs also fail to capture institutional knowledge, which means that everything a senior sales representative knows about the clients they work with leaves when they depart the company. There’s also a heavy administrative tax, with users forced to waste valuable time entering data to keep the platform up to date.

“CRMs don’t have a shortage of features,” Venkatraman said. “But they have a shortage of context and trust, and they lack the ability to get actual work done.”

Dreamteam does things differently. By capturing the unspoken context around each deal an organization does, it says, its platform can help to prevent new leads from going stale. Monitoring everything that’s said and agreed to in meetings, via chats and emails and other tools, the platform can pick out the most important signals, such as pricing sensitivities, objections and stakeholder dynamics.

It remembers all of the fine details of each specific deal. That way, even if the main sales rep involved suddenly leaves, it will retain all of the context so whoever takes over the account knows what needs to be done next.

The platform also employs humanlike reasoning. “When a prospect says, ‘The board is pushing hard on costs,’ it knows the proposal should lead with ROI, not features,” Venkatraman explained. “The CRM was supposed to give companies a complete picture of their customers, yet the richest parts of that picture have always lived outside the CRM.”

The startup has already witnessed significant traction with its agentic, contextual approach: It’s used by hundreds of organizations across the AI, healthcare, manufacturing, consulting and online media sectors. Dreamteam has enabled those early adopters to transform the way they handle sales.

Because the CRM continuously self-updates its records following daily customer interactions, it means sales people have much more time to focus on actually selling rather than data entry. Senior leaders have more visibility into deal pipelines, and can immediately find out why deals are stalling or how their customer’s sentiments are shifting.

Scott Olechowski, chief product officer at the video streaming service Plex Inc., said he was especially taken with the tight level of integration with Dreamteam and the company’s existing information technology stack. “The combination of simplicity and power hits the sweet spot for us,” he said. “The ability to integrate with the AI tools we are using across our organization is a game-changer.”

Venkatraman believes Dreamteam can have an even greater impact in future by expanding its shared intelligence layer beyond sales operations. His ambition is to build a platform that spans the entire customer lifecycle, from onboarding to customer success, renewals and upselling, to ensure that organizations can squeeze the most value out of the deal context it captures.

“Much of what’s learned during sales is lost or fragmented when a customer moves into implementation or customer success,” he pointed out. “But the same company brain that knows why a customer bought should also help teams onboard them, spot risks and find ways to grow the relationship.”

One way Dreamteam intends to pursue this vision is through what it calls “Magic Apps,” which is a capability that lets users build custom dashboards and tailored CRM workflows using natural language prompts. “The apps live inside Dreamteam, inherit its data permissions and action-level authorizations, and stay connected to customer records, workflows and the Company Brain, so you can customize without rebuilding the foundation,” Venkatraman said.

Premji Invest’s Saravanan Nattanmai has already bought into this vision, stressing the need for CRM systems to become more than just a system of record. He characterizes what Dreamteam is building as a “system of intelligence.”

“Dreamteam sets out to intuitively understand user intent, build deep contextual intelligence and execute workflows seamlessly through autonomous AI teammates,” he said. “We believe the future of enterprise software lies in AI-native systems that don’t just augment existing workflows but fundamentally reimagine how work gets done.”

#5463. From DNS to undersea fiber: 10 organizations the web depends on

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A selection of companies that run the internet, plus two nonprofits, behind the domain names, cables, data centers and security certificates few people ever see

Typing a web address and watching a page load feels instant. Inside that brief gap, the request passes through a chain of organizations that most people never see and rarely hear named. Their work goes unnoticed when it functions and becomes visible only when it fails.

The first step is translation. A browser has to turn a name such as qz.com into a numeric IP address that computers use to find each other. That lookup runs through the domain name system, a layered hierarchy of registries and servers coordinated worldwide. Next comes delivery. The page often arrives from a copy stored on a content delivery network server near the reader, not from one distant machine. The site itself may run on computing power rented from a cloud provider rather than hardware its owner bought. The data moves over fiber backbone networks and, between continents, through cables laid on the seabed. An encrypted HTTPS connection depends on a digital certificate issued by a certificate authority.

This list profiles internet infrastructure organizations across 10 entries. It is a selection, not a ranking or a complete roster. Most entries are companies that run the internet's core services as commercial businesses. Two are nonprofits. ICANN coordinates domain names and IP address allocation. Let's Encrypt, a free certificate authority, is run by the Internet Security Research Group.

The reason to know these names is concentration. Many websites rely on the same small group of providers for naming, delivery, hosting and security. When one provider handles a function for many sites, a fault there can reach all of them at once. A configuration error, an outage or a policy decision at a single organization can disrupt services that look unrelated to the people using them.

The slides that follow take each organization in turn. They explain what it does, where it sits on the path between a reader and a website, and what the technical terms around it mean. Some took on their role in the late 1990s, while others arrived more recently.

Cloudflare sits between a website and its visitors, handling traffic before it reaches the site's own servers. In that position, the company combines three services: a content delivery network, a domain name system (DNS) provider and protection against distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks.

Sitting in front of a website has a specific technical meaning. When a site uses Cloudflare as a reverse proxy, visitors connect to Cloudflare's servers rather than directly to the site's origin server. Cloudflare then decides which requests to answer itself and which to pass along. The origin server's real address can stay out of public view.

That position at the network edge is what lets one provider do several jobs at once. Every request to a protected site already flows through its machines. The same servers that deliver content can also inspect incoming requests and filter out unwanted ones.

The content delivery side works through caching. Cloudflare stores copies of files that rarely change, such as images, scripts and style sheets. It serves those stored copies to visitors without asking the origin server for them each time. That cuts the load on the site's own hardware.

DNS is the second layer. Cloudflare can act as the authoritative DNS provider for a domain. That means its servers hold the official records saying which IP address a domain name points to. Lookups for the domain end at Cloudflare's servers, which return the address. A slow or failed DNS answer means a page never starts loading, however healthy the server behind it.

DDoS protection is the third. A DDoS attack floods a target with traffic from many machines at once, often hijacked devices, until it cannot respond to real users. Cloudflare already receives a protected site's traffic. That lets it absorb or drop attack traffic before it reaches the origin.

Combining these roles carries a trade-off. A site that routes its traffic, its DNS and its defenses through Cloudflare depends on Cloudflare staying online. A fault inside the edge network can make the sites behind it unreachable together. Their own origin servers may keep running normally the whole time.

Akamai $AKAM Technologies is one of the earliest content delivery networks, a company founded in 1998 out of research at MIT. It runs a distributed network of servers that delivers web content to users from nearby locations.

A content delivery network, or CDN, addresses two problems: distance and demand. Without one, every visitor requests files from the website's own origin server. That server may sit far from many of the people using it.

Distance adds delay. Data crossing continents passes through more networks and more handoffs before it arrives. Each handoff is another point where traffic can slow down or get congested.

Demand creates the second problem. A single origin server has limited capacity. When a large number of people request the same page at once, that server can become overloaded and stop responding.

A CDN spreads the work out. It stores copies of a site's content on servers in many locations. It then directs each user to a nearby server rather than to the origin. The origin handles fewer requests, and the user's data travels a shorter path.

The steering often happens through the domain name system. When a browser looks up a site's name, the CDN can answer with the address of a server close to that user. The user never chooses a server and usually never notices the redirection.

Spreading content across many servers also adds resilience. If one server or location fails, requests can be sent to another that holds the same files. The site stays reachable even when part of the network is down.

The arrangement changes what a website owner has to build. The owner does not need servers on every continent. The owner pays a CDN operator to provide that reach instead.

Akamai came out of university research rather than out of a telephone or cable company. Its business is the servers and software that deliver content, not the cables that carry it.

Most people who use the internet never interact with Akamai by name. Its servers work behind the brands whose pages and files they deliver. A user sees the website's address, not the CDN carrying its content.

Amazon $AMZN Web Services, known as AWS, is Amazon's cloud computing unit. It rents storage and computing power over the internet to businesses that would otherwise have to buy and run their own servers.

AWS launched publicly in 2006 with two services. S3, short for Simple Storage Service, lets customers keep files and data on Amazon's machines. EC2, short for Elastic Compute Cloud, lets customers run software on virtual servers that Amazon operates.

Those two products split the job of a traditional server room into separate pieces. Storage holds the data. Compute does the processing. A customer can add more of one without paying for more of the other.

The model behind both is renting instead of owning. A company that runs its own servers has to buy the hardware, house it, power it, cool it and replace it when it fails. It also has to guess in advance how much capacity it will need. A cloud customer skips most of that work. It requests capacity when demand rises and releases it when demand falls. The word elastic in the EC2 name refers to that ability to scale up or down.

Renting changes the economics of starting a software business. A new app no longer needs a large upfront hardware purchase before it can serve its first user. Costs track usage, such as the amount of data stored or the server time consumed, instead of arriving in one lump sum.

The arrangement is mostly invisible to the people using those apps. A shopping site, streaming service or mobile game can run on rented AWS computing with no Amazon branding on the screen. The user sees the app's name, not the infrastructure underneath it.

AWS works in that background role. Amazon's retail site carries the company's name on every page. Its cloud unit operates out of sight, supplying the storage and processing that other companies' products rely on whenever someone uses them.

Verisign operates the registries for .com and .net, the master databases behind every domain name ending in those two extensions. There are 13 root name server identities run by 12 organizations, and Verisign runs two of them, A and J.

A registry and a registrar do different jobs. A registrar is the retailer that a person or business pays to claim a domain name. The registry sits behind it. It acts as the wholesaler and official record keeper for an entire top-level domain.

When someone buys a .com address through a registrar, the registration is passed along to Verisign. Verisign adds the name to the authoritative .com database. It also publishes the records that tell the rest of the internet which name servers answer for that domain.

That second job ties the registry to everyday browsing. A resolver looking up a .com site on a browser's behalf needs to know where that site's own name servers live. The .com registry's servers supply that pointer. If they stopped answering, names ending in .com would become hard to reach, even with the websites themselves still running.

Root servers sit one level higher in the domain name system. They do not hold the address of any individual website. Their job is to point queries toward the servers responsible for each top-level domain, such as .com, .net or a country code like .uk.

Each root identity is labeled with a letter from A to M. With 13 identities split among 12 operators, Verisign is the only organization that runs more than one.

No identity is a single machine. Operators usually serve one root letter from many servers in different locations. A routing method called anycast sends each query to a nearby copy. That spreads the load and limits the damage if one site fails.

Most lookups never reach a root server. Resolvers run by internet providers and other services store recent answers and reuse them until they expire. When those stored answers run out, the resolver can return to the root and work down the hierarchy again.

ICANN, the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, is a nonprofit formed in 1998. It coordinates the domain name system and the allocation of IP addresses. It is not a company in the commercial sense, but much of the internet's addressing depends on its coordination.

Two kinds of identifiers fall under that role. Domain names are the readable labels people type, such as a site ending in .org or .com. IP addresses are the numeric labels that computers and routers use to locate one another.

Both systems work only if every identifier is unique. If two networks claimed the same address, traffic could not reach either one reliably. If two operators tried to run the same domain ending, lookups would return conflicting answers. ICANN coordinates at that level to prevent such collisions.

Coordination is different from operation. ICANN does not run the servers that answer most domain lookups, and it does not host websites. Separate organizations, including commercial firms, operate individual domain registries and the servers behind them. ICANN's job sits a level above. It sets the shared rules and keeps the overall map of names consistent.

The numbers side follows a similar pattern. Large blocks of IP addresses are handed down to regional internet registries, each serving a part of the world. Those registries pass smaller blocks to internet service providers and other network operators. The operators then assign addresses to customers and devices.

Address supply is part of why that coordination matters. The original IPv4 format has a fixed, limited pool of addresses. Demand has outgrown it. The newer IPv6 format offers a far larger pool. Both formats now run side by side across the internet.

ICANN has no shareholders. Its decisions about which domain endings exist and how address blocks are distributed form the base layer that registries, network operators and other providers build on.

Equinix is a data center and colocation operator, and many internet exchange points sit inside its facilities. That makes its buildings physical meeting places where separate networks connect and hand traffic to one another.

Colocation means a customer rents space inside a data center rather than building its own. The customer typically installs its own servers and networking gear in racks or cages. The operator supplies the building, electrical power, backup power, cooling and physical security.

That arrangement suits companies that need reliable infrastructure but do not want to construct and staff a facility. It also lets many different organizations share one building while keeping control of their own equipment.

An internet exchange point, often shortened to IXP, is a place where networks connect directly to swap traffic. The participants can include internet service providers, content companies, cloud platforms and enterprise networks. Each one plugs into shared switching equipment and exchanges data with the others there.

This direct exchange is called peering. Without it, two networks might have to route traffic through a third-party carrier. That paid service is known as IP transit. Peering at an exchange can shorten the route data travels between networks. A shorter route can lower delay for the end user.

Peering arrangements differ in cost. Many are settlement-free, meaning neither network pays the other to carry the exchanged traffic. Others involve payment, which can happen when the traffic flowing between the two networks is unbalanced.

Networks tend to gather where other networks already are. Once several carriers and platforms have equipment in the same building, connecting to them there is simpler than running separate links across a city or region. Inside a single facility, two customers can be linked with a physical cable known as a cross-connect.

This explains why a colocation operator's role extends beyond renting floor space. Its buildings become junctions in the internet's map, where traffic moves from one company's network to another's.

Lumen Technologies is a fiber network operator that owns the backbone once run by Level 3. The company, then named CenturyLink, acquired Level 3 in 2017. It later took the Lumen name.

A backbone is the long-distance, high-capacity layer of the internet. It links cities, regions and the networks inside them. Local broadband and mobile carriers handle the last stretch to a user's device. Backbone operators carry traffic across the much longer distances in between.

The physical medium is optical fiber. Each strand is a thread of glass that carries data as pulses of light. Fiber moves far more data over long distances than copper wire, with less signal loss. Long-haul cables often follow existing rights of way, such as rail lines and highways.

Capacity can grow without laying new cable. A technique called wavelength division multiplexing sends many signals through a single strand at once, each on a different wavelength of light. Upgrading the equipment at each end can add capacity to fiber already in the ground.

Backbone operators sell capacity to other businesses. Buyers can include internet service providers, content companies and large enterprises. One common product is IP transit. In it, a smaller network pays a larger one to carry its traffic to the rest of the internet.

Routing ties these networks together. Networks use the Border Gateway Protocol to announce which blocks of IP addresses they can reach. Other networks read those announcements to pick paths for traffic. A mistaken announcement can send traffic down the wrong path or leave blocks of addresses unreachable until it is corrected.

Most internet users never deal with Lumen directly. Their data can still cross its fiber on the way to a website, a video stream or a cloud service. Lumen's network sits between the local access networks people pay for and the content companies they connect to.

Let's Encrypt is a certificate authority that gives website operators TLS certificates at no charge. The nonprofit Internet Security Research Group runs it, and the service opened to the public in 2015.

A certificate authority vouches for a website's identity. When a browser connects to an address that begins with https, the server presents a digital certificate. That certificate ties the site's domain name to a cryptographic public key.

The browser then checks who signed the certificate. Browsers and operating systems ship with a list of authorities they already trust. If the signature traces back to one of them, the connection goes ahead. If it does not, the browser shows a warning page instead of the site.

After that check passes, the browser and the server use TLS, short for Transport Layer Security, to encrypt the traffic between them. Encryption keeps passwords, card numbers and messages unreadable to anyone else on the network path. That includes another person on a shared café Wi-Fi network. It also makes it harder for a third party to alter a page while it is in transit.

The padlock icon in a browser's address bar is the visible sign of this process. Browsers let users click through to see which organization signed the certificate behind it.

Let's Encrypt took the price out of this step. A site owner does not pay it anything to obtain a certificate. That removes cost as a barrier for small blogs, community groups, personal projects and hobby sites that want HTTPS.

Its nonprofit structure separates it from certificate authorities that sell certificates as a business. The Internet Security Research Group operates the service, not a shareholder-owned company.

Certificates do not last forever. Each one carries an expiration date. An expired certificate triggers the same kind of browser warning as an untrusted one. Site operators have to renew certificates on a schedule, whether the certificates are free or paid.

An outage or error at a certificate authority can affect every site that depends on its certificates. Most people who visit a site secured through Let's Encrypt never see the issuer's name.

DigiCert is a commercial certificate authority. It sells the digital certificates that let a browser confirm a website is the site it claims to be.

A certificate authority sits inside a chain of trust. Browsers and operating systems ship with a root store, a built-in list of authorities whose certificates they accept. Mozilla, Apple $AAPL, Microsoft $MSFT and Google $GOOGL each run their own root program to decide which authorities qualify. A certificate from an authority outside that list triggers a warning instead of a secure connection.

Commercial authorities sell certificates at different validation levels. Domain validation is the most basic and confirms only that the applicant controls the domain. Organization validation adds a check that the applicant is a real, registered legal entity. Extended validation applies the strictest vetting of the three.

The rules for publicly trusted authorities come from the CA/Browser Forum, an industry body of certificate issuers and browser makers. Its baseline requirements govern how identities are checked and how certificates are issued. A browser maker can drop an authority from its root store for breaking those rules.

Browsers such as Chrome and Safari require publicly trusted TLS certificates to appear in Certificate Transparency logs. These are public, append-only records that anyone can search. Domain owners use them to spot certificates issued for their names without permission.

The commercial certificate business extends beyond web pages. Authorities in this market also issue code signing certificates. These let software publishers show that a program has not been altered since it was signed. Some authorities also issue certificates for signing email and documents.

Each certificate carries an expiration date. After that date, browsers reject it and the site owner must replace it. An authority can also revoke a certificate before it expires. That step matters when a private key is stolen or a certificate was issued in error. Software checks revocation status through certificate revocation lists or the Online Certificate Status Protocol, known as OCSP.

SubCom and Alcatel Submarine Networks build and lay the undersea cables that carry international internet traffic between continents. Alcatel Submarine Networks is now part of Nokia, the Finnish telecom equipment group.

A submarine cable is a line of optical fiber laid along the seabed. Data travels through the glass as pulses of light. A single cable bundles several fiber pairs inside layers of protective material.

Light weakens as it travels long distances. Repeaters spaced along the cable boost the signal so it can cross an ocean. Those repeaters need electricity. It is fed through a conductor inside the cable from power equipment on shore.

Cable suppliers such as SubCom and Alcatel Submarine Networks handle more than manufacturing. Their work can span surveys of the seafloor route, production of the cable and repeaters, and installation from specialized cable-laying ships.

The supplier is usually not the owner. Many cables belong to consortiums of telecom carriers, and some are financed by large technology companies. The owners hire a supplier to deliver the finished system.

Cable design changes with water depth. In shallow coastal areas, cables carry heavier armor and are often buried in the seabed. That protects them from ship anchors and fishing gear, two common causes of damage. In the deep ocean, where those risks are lower, a lighter cable rests directly on the bottom.

Each cable comes ashore at a landing station. There it connects to land-based fiber networks, which carry traffic onward to data centers and internet exchange points.

When a cable breaks, a repair ship sails to the fault and lifts the damaged section to the surface. Crews splice in a new length of cable and lower it back to the seabed. Traffic can often be rerouted over other cables while the repair is underway.

Satellites also carry internet traffic, but most data moving between continents travels over undersea fiber. That reliance places cable builders such as SubCom and Alcatel Submarine Networks at the physical base of global connectivity.

#5462. TeacherLists Data Show 2026 Back-to-School Shopping Started Earlier and Lasted Longer

Families spread purchases across the summer, followed retailers' earlier promotions, and relied on school supply lists to stay on track.

WRENTHAM, Mass., Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- TeacherLists, the leading digital platform for school supply lists, reports that back-to-school shopping continued to shift earlier in 2026, with families spreading purchases across several months, responding to earlier retail promotions, and navigating tight budgets. Independent research from ICSC (International Council of Shopping Centers) shows the same pattern nationally.

Major retailers helped pull the season forward. Amazon, Walmart, and Target each scheduled their summer deal events earlier in 2026, giving families more reasons to buy before the traditional late-July and August rush. ICSC found that among shoppers who started in June, 57% finished all or most of their back-to-school shopping during the late-June promotional week.

The TeacherLists Preseason Parent Survey confirmed the shift:

TeacherLists data reinforced the pattern. Family engagement on TeacherLists.com began in June and continued into early September, with traffic peaking on August 3, 2026. Families returned to the site multiple times throughout the season, consistent with shopping and list completion occurring over time.

ICSC's national survey points the same way. 84% of back-to-school shoppers planned to start earlier than usual, and 54% had already started or finished by early July. Yet August still accounted for the largest share of spending, at 44% on average, meaning the season got longer rather than simply moving earlier.

Budgets were a constant concern. In the ICSC survey, 54% of shoppers worried about affording everything they needed, and 93% said higher prices had affected or would affect their purchases. Many responded with a plan: 29% made a list and tried to stick to it, and 21% spread purchases across pay periods.

According to the TeacherLists Preseason Parent Survey, 89% of families said they "would" or "probably would" shop from a back-to-school supply list if their school or teacher provided one. That intent shows up in actual spending: ICSC found that school lists and teacher requirements were the top influence on Kâ12 back-to-school purchases, cited by 47% of shoppers.

With 1.9 million school supply lists available online, TeacherLists gave families a way to access the exact items teachers requested and shop them directly through trusted retailers like Walmart, Target, Amazon, Staples, Office Depot, H-E-B, Meijer, Dollar General, Kroger, and CVS, all in just a few clicks.

By making supply lists shoppable online and available anytime, TeacherLists enabled families to spread purchases over weeks instead of days, take advantage of earlier retail promotions, compare prices across retailers, and keep track of what was still needed.

For a deeper look at TeacherLists' 2026 impact and key highlights from the year, read our full blog post here.
