#5461. Google says an AI framework turned security patches into exploits with no human in the loop

A new report out today from Google LLC’s Google Threat Intelligence Group finds that for the first time, attackers have used an artificial intelligence framework running with no human in the loop to turn security patches into exploits.

Called exploit_agent, the framework turned up on an exposed staging server, where it was wired into several frontier and locally hosted large language models. Its job, according to GTIG, is continuous comparison of popular web application code before and after each patch announcement. Once a likely flaw is identified, the exploit it drafts is executed automatically.

Data taken from victims was sitting on the same server, alongside scripts for brute-forcing, installing webshells and even removing webshells left by rival attackers. Victim telemetry suggests the operator was most interested in French websites tied to media, entertainment and education. Written in Russian, one comment in the framework’s configuration file tells whoever set it up to enter the keys “right here, not in the chat.”

In the previous edition of the quarterly tracker two months ago, GTIG said it had not observed fully autonomous attack pipelines deployed against targets in the wild. That changed over the past quarter, according to the new report, titled “Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold.” Because the source material for a patched flaw is finite, GTIG believes attackers may find it more efficient to point LLMs at n-day vulnerabilities than to hunt for zero-days.

How quickly the gap between disclosure and a working exploit can close shows in the case of two flaws in print management servers from PaperCut Software Pty Ltd., chained together and exploited as zero-days in late August. Security researchers and Huntress Labs Inc. used large language models to generate working exploits within a day of disclosure.

A campaign tracked by GreyNoise Intelligence Inc. four days after disclosure is believed to have relied on LLMs to build its exploits before it hit hundreds of organizations. One foothold in that campaign reached domain administrator within minutes, GreyNoise found.

Elsewhere, open-source agentic penetration testing frameworks are being used to automate discrete steps of live intrusions. During one intrusion against the U.S. aerospace sector, a threat actor was observed using the multi-agent framework CAIRN.

Another actor ran a customized platform built on PentAGI between late August and early October to scan a wide range of organizations in Asia for vulnerabilities. For now, the noisy forensic trail left by unrestricted autonomous execution is said to make the frameworks easier to detect.

According to GTIG, influence operations now use models for far more than writing posts. Using cloud phone farms, a turnkey platform that one commercial contractor was building with help from the Gemini API is designed to run more than 100,000 social media accounts. To make generated photos pass as smartphone shots, prompts behind a separate platform, which targeted political sentiment across Europe and the Middle East, are said to have called for deliberate camera flaws.

Among government-backed actors, photos on the fake recruiter profiles that a suspected North Korean group tracked as UNC6836 used to approach cryptocurrency organizations in North America and Europe were found to carry Google’s SynthID watermarks. By way of altered .claude/settings.json files in internal code repositories, the group later rigged each launch of Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code to download its SOMBERMEME backdoor.

Google said it disabled the accounts and assets tied to the Gemini misuse it found. Google DeepMind has also used the findings to strengthen its classifiers.

#5460. A 10-step response plan for when a website you use is hacked

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Knowing what to do after a data breach limits the damage, from changing reused passwords to freezing your credit, plus how AO3 users can protect a pen name

A breach notice usually arrives after the damage on the company's side is already done. The data has been copied, and nothing a customer does can pull it back. What a person controls is the window that follows. The hours and days after a leak decide whether a stolen email address and password stay a single problem or become a key to many other accounts.

That is the core of knowing what to do after a data breach. The main danger to other accounts does not come from the hacked website itself. It comes from credential stuffing. This is the practice of taking leaked email and password pairs and trying them automatically on other sites. Banks, email providers, shopping accounts and streaming services all become targets if the same password protected them. A breach at a small hobby forum can end with someone inside a person's main inbox.

The right response also depends on what was exposed. A leaked email address alone calls for caution about scam messages. A leaked password calls for changes across every account that shared it. A leaked Social Security number, card number or date of birth raises the stakes to fraud and identity theft. The tools for those problems are different.

Some exposures are personal rather than financial. Archive of Our Own, the fan fiction archive known as AO3, is run by the nonprofit Organization for Transformative Works. Its accounts are tied to a username and an email address. Many writers there publish under pen names. On any site built around pseudonyms, the most sensitive piece of data may be the email address. That address can connect a pen name to a real person. The same risk applies to other fan archives, gaming communities and anonymous forums, whether or not a given site has ever been breached.

The 10 steps that follow move in a deliberate order. They start with confirming that a breach actually happened and finding out what it covered. They then turn to securing accounts with new passwords and two-factor authentication. Next come monitoring tools, including breach-lookup services, credit freezes and credit reports. The list closes with reporting identity theft if it occurs and reducing how much any single site knows about you. Each step works on its own. Readers can start with the one that matches what leaked.

Before changing anything, confirm the breach on the company's own website, its official social media accounts or in a notice it sent you directly. A verified announcement tells you what was exposed, and that detail decides which later steps you actually need.

News of a breach often arrives secondhand. A screenshot circulates on social media, a forum thread claims a database is for sale, or an email warns that your account is at risk. Some of these reports turn out to be accurate. Others are exaggerated, recycled from an older incident or written by scammers hoping to catch people in a panic.

The safest route is to type the site's address into your browser yourself rather than following a link. Companies typically post breach information in a press release, a blog post, a help center article or a status page. Many also email affected users. If the only evidence is a message you cannot match to anything on the company's own channels, treat it with suspicion.

A site going offline is not proof of a breach either. Archive of Our Own, the fan fiction archive known as AO3, has had outages caused by distributed denial-of-service attacks. Those attacks flood a site with traffic to knock it offline. That is a different problem from attackers stealing account records.

A useful notice explains what happened and roughly when it was discovered. It lists the categories of data involved, such as email addresses, usernames, passwords, payment card numbers or Social Security numbers. It should say whether stored passwords were hashed. Hashing makes passwords harder to recover, but it does not make them safe to keep using. The notice should also describe what the company is doing and what it wants users to do.

That list of exposed data shapes your response. A leak limited to email addresses mainly raises the risk of targeted scam messages. Exposed passwords mean resetting credentials. Leaked financial or government ID numbers call for stronger protections against fraud.

Legal rules push many companies toward disclosure. Every U.S. state has a breach notification law. In the European Union, the General Data Protection Regulation requires organizations to report qualifying breaches to regulators within 72 hours of becoming aware of them, where feasible. The U.K. applies the same deadline under its own version of the regulation. Timing and detail still vary from company to company. Check back for updated notices as an investigation continues. Early announcements are sometimes revised as more is learned.

Reset the password on the affected account as soon as the company confirms the breach. Make the change by typing the site's address into your browser or opening its official app, not by following a link in an email or text.

A new password matters even if the company says stored passwords were hashed or encrypted. Hashing makes stolen passwords harder to read. Weak or common passwords can still be cracked, though. Changing yours closes that gap regardless of how the site stored it.

The replacement should be long, random and used nowhere else. Length does more work than a scattering of symbols. The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology takes that position in its digital identity guidelines, published as Special Publication 800-63B. Those guidelines favor longer passwords over complicated composition rules. A passphrase built from several unrelated words is one way to get length that is still practical to type.

Avoid small edits to the old password. Adding a digit at the end or capitalizing a different letter produces something an attacker holding the leaked version can guess. The new password should share nothing with the one that was exposed.

After the reset, look for a setting that signs you out of other devices or ends active sessions. Many services place it near the password option in their security settings. Ending old sessions cuts off anyone who logged in with the stolen password before you changed it. If the site keeps a log of recent sign-ins, check it for locations or devices you do not recognize.

Review the account's recovery details next. Confirm that the recovery email address and phone number are still yours. Someone who briefly controlled the account could have swapped them to regain access later. If the site uses security questions and their answers may have been exposed, change those answers as well.

On the fan fiction archive Archive of Our Own (AO3), users change their password from the account's Preferences. The same approach carries over to any site. Find the account or security settings, make the change there and confirm you can sign in with the new password.

Update the password anywhere it is saved, such as a phone app or a browser's built-in password store. A stored copy of the old password will no longer work. Leaving it in place can produce repeated failed sign-in attempts. Some sites treat those as suspicious and respond with a temporary lockout.

If the leaked password also protects any other account, change it there too, and give each account its own unique password. Attackers routinely test stolen logins on other sites. A reused password can turn one breach into many.

That testing has a name: credential stuffing. Attackers take email-and-password pairs from a breached site and enter them on the login pages of other services. The attack succeeds only where a person used the same pair in more than one place. They do not need to break into the second site. If the same pair works there, they simply sign in as you.

The stakes of the breached site do not set the limit on the damage. A password first created for a recipe site, a game forum or a retailer's loyalty program may have spread to accounts that hold money or personal records. The breached site may never have stored anything sensitive. The accounts sharing its password might.

Start with your email account. Email is where password reset links arrive. Anyone who controls your inbox can reset the passwords on most of your other accounts. Next, move to banking, payment and brokerage accounts. Then cover shopping sites that store a card number or shipping address. Social media and cloud storage accounts come after that. Leave forgotten or rarely used accounts for last, but do not skip them.

Small variations do not count as unique. Adding a digit or swapping the year at the end of a known password leaves a pattern. Attackers can guess the new version from the leaked one. Each replacement should be unrelated to the old password and to every other password you use.

Few people can memorize dozens of unrelated passwords. A password manager handles that job. It generates long random passwords, stores them in an encrypted vault and fills them in on the matching site. Standalone options include 1Password and Bitwarden. Google $GOOGL Password Manager is built into Chrome and Android. Apple $AAPL builds a similar password tool into the iPhone and Mac.

Several of these tools can also flag passwords you have reused across sites. That report gives you a working checklist for this step. The only password you then need to remember is the one that unlocks the manager. It should be long, unique and used nowhere else.

Turn on two-factor authentication wherever a site offers it. With a second check in place, a password stolen in a breach is no longer enough on its own to open the account.

Two-factor authentication, often shortened to 2FA, asks for something beyond the password before it lets anyone in. That second factor is usually a code sent to a phone, a code generated by an app or a physical device the account owner holds. An attacker holding a leaked password still has to get past that extra step.

Start with the email account. Most other services send password reset links to an inbox. Whoever controls the email address can often take over everything connected to it. Banking, payment and shopping accounts come next, followed by any account that stores personal details or links to a real name.

The methods differ in strength. Text message codes are the most widely offered and the easiest to set up. They are still an improvement over a password alone, but they have known weaknesses. A criminal who persuades a mobile carrier to move a phone number to a new SIM card can receive those codes. That scam is known as SIM swapping. A person can also be tricked into typing an SMS code into a fake login page.

Authenticator apps such as Google $GOOGL Authenticator and Microsoft $MSFT Authenticator generate short codes on the phone itself, typically refreshing every 30 seconds. The codes never travel over the phone network. A SIM swap therefore does not hand them to an attacker.

Passkeys go a step further. A passkey replaces the typed password with a cryptographic key stored on a device and unlocked with a fingerprint, face scan or PIN. It is tied to the real website's domain. It will not work on a lookalike site. Physical security keys that plug into a computer or tap against a phone work on the same principle. Both authenticator apps and passkeys resist phishing better than SMS codes.

Setup usually sits in a site's security or account settings. Many services issue a set of single-use backup codes when 2FA is switched on. Store those somewhere safe and offline, or in a password manager. They are the way back into the account if the phone is lost or replaced.

Not every site offers a second factor. For accounts without one, a long, unique password remains the main defense against someone logging in with leaked credentials.

Have I Been Pwned is a free breach-lookup service. You type in an email address and see which known data breaches included it. Running that check after a breach notice shows whether the same address has turned up in other leaks too.

Security researcher Troy Hunt created the service. It collects data from breaches that have become public and indexes the email addresses they contain. A search returns a list of the breached sites tied to that address. Each entry typically describes what kinds of data the leak held, such as passwords, usernames, phone numbers or physical addresses.

Those descriptions matter. Each entry's list of exposed data shows which follow-up steps apply to that particular leak.

The results have limits. The service can show only breaches that have surfaced publicly and been added to its database. A clean result does not prove your data was never exposed. It means the address has not appeared in any breach the service knows about. An incident a company has not disclosed will not show up. Neither will a leak that never circulated.

The search can also turn up accounts you forgot you had. Old forum logins, retired shopping sites and abandoned apps often keep your data long after you stop using them. If one of those appears in the results, log in and change the password. Close the account entirely if the site allows it. Each dormant account you delete is one fewer place your details can leak from.

The service also lets you sign up for alerts. It emails you if your address appears in a breach it adds later. That gives you notice even when the affected company is slow to tell its users.

The results also show how widely a single email address has spread. An address that appears in several breaches is tied to accounts at each of those sites. That matters most on platforms built around pen names. On Archive of Our Own (AO3), the fan fiction archive, many writers publish under pseudonyms. Every account there still requires an email address. If a personal address registered on AO3 turns up in the results from another site's leak, that address is already circulating in breach data. Anyone who wants a pen name kept apart from a legal name can use that finding to choose a fresh address for the pseudonymous account.

Expect scam emails, texts and phone calls that mention a recent data breach, and never hand over a password or payment details in reply. A legitimate breach notice normally asks for neither.

Scammers watch breach headlines. Once a company announces a leak, fake notices can appear that copy its logo, tone and wording. Some claim your account will be locked unless you verify it. Others promise a refund, a settlement payment or free identity monitoring in exchange for personal information.

Treat every link in a breach-related message as untrusted. Instead of clicking, type the company's web address into your browser or open its official app. The same rule applies to phone numbers. Call the number printed on the company's website or on the back of your card, not the one in the message.

A few warning signs show up again and again. Pressure to act within hours is one. A sender address or link that resembles the real domain but differs by a letter, a hyphen or an extra word is another. A request to type a password, a one-time code or a full card number into a linked page is the clearest signal of all. Attachments that claim to contain breach details deserve the same suspicion.

Text messages follow the same pattern. A short text with a link and a warning about your account is a common format. A text can be harder to inspect than an email. On a phone screen, the full web address is often hidden.

Leaked data can make these messages more convincing. A scammer who holds your username, a pen name or an old order detail can drop it into a message so it looks official. On a pseudonymous fan site such as Archive of Our Own (AO3), a message that names your AO3 username is not proof that it came from the archive. Accurate personal details show only that the sender has some of your data.

If you already clicked a link or typed in a password, change that password from the real site right away. Then check the account for settings or contact details you did not change. Report the message through your email provider's phishing option, and delete it.

If a breach exposed your Social Security number or financial details, place a credit freeze at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze stops lenders from pulling your credit file, which blocks most new accounts opened in your name.

A fraud alert is a lighter option. Since September 2018, U.S. federal law has required the three nationwide credit bureaus to offer freezes free of charge. Fraud alerts cost nothing to place either.

A freeze restricts access to your credit report. Most lenders check that report before they approve a credit card, a loan or another line of credit. If they cannot see it, the application usually stalls. A thief holding your name, birth date and Social Security number then has a harder time turning them into new debt.

Each bureau handles its own freeze. A freeze placed at Equifax does not carry over to Experian or TransUnion. Full coverage means contacting all three. Each bureau takes requests online, by phone or by mail.

A freeze does not lock you out of your own credit. Before applying for a mortgage, a car loan or a new card, you can lift the freeze temporarily or remove it, then restore it afterward. Each bureau provides an online account or a PIN to manage this. Asking the lender which bureau it plans to check can spare you from lifting all three.

A freeze also has limits. It does not lower your credit score. It does not stop your existing creditors from reviewing your file. It does not block fraudulent charges on cards you already hold.

A fraud alert works differently. It flags your file and asks any business checking your credit to take extra steps to confirm your identity before opening an account. An initial fraud alert lasts one year. You request it from one bureau, and that bureau must notify the other two. Your credit stays fully available while the alert is active. Confirmed identity theft victims can request a longer extended alert.

A leaked Social Security number, bank account number or card number is the main reason to use either tool. Some people place a freeze and a fraud alert together.

Both tools belong to the U.S. credit system, and rules differ elsewhere. In the U.K., the fraud prevention service Cifas offers Protective Registration, which flags a person's details to its member organizations.

Pull your free credit reports from AnnualCreditReport.com, the federally authorized source, and read your bank and card statements line by line. Those two records show whether anyone has used exposed details to open accounts or spend money in your name.

AnnualCreditReport.com gives access to reports from all three nationwide credit bureaus: Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Each bureau keeps its own file. A lender may report to one bureau but not the others. A new account can show up on one report and be missing from the other two. Reading all three gives the fullest picture.

Start with the personal information section. An address you never lived at could be an early sign that someone has applied for credit with your details. A name variation you do not use or an employer you never worked for can point to the same thing.

Next, go through the list of accounts. Every credit card, loan and line of credit should be one you recognize. An unfamiliar account needs a closer look. So does a collections entry for a debt you never owed, or a balance that does not match your own records.

The inquiries section matters too. A hard inquiry appears when a lender reviews your file after a credit application. Hard inquiries from companies you never applied with can mean someone tried to borrow in your name. Checking your own report does not count as a hard inquiry and does not affect your credit score.

If an entry is wrong, the Fair Credit Reporting Act gives you the right to dispute it. You can file the dispute with the credit bureau and with the company that supplied the information. The bureau must investigate and correct or remove information that cannot be verified.

Credit reports list accounts and balances, not individual purchases. Bank and card statements fill that gap. Small charges from unfamiliar merchants need a closer look. Criminals sometimes test a stolen card with a minor purchase before attempting a larger one.

Contact the bank or card issuer as soon as you spot an unauthorized charge. Use the phone number on the back of the card or on the issuer's official website. The issuer can block the card and send a replacement with a new number. Many banking apps also offer alerts for each transaction. Those alerts make unfamiliar activity easier to catch between monthly statements.

If someone has used your stolen information to open an account, take out a loan or make purchases in your name, report it at IdentityTheft.gov. The Federal Trade Commission runs the site. It turns your report into a personalized recovery plan.

This step is for misuse, not exposure alone. A notice saying your email address or password leaked in a breach does not mean your identity has been stolen. Identity theft begins when someone acts on that data. Warning signs include a credit card you never applied for or a collection notice for a debt you don't recognize. A tax return filed under your Social Security number is another, as is a medical bill for care you never received. If nothing like that has happened, securing your accounts and watching them closely is the appropriate response.

Once misuse appears, the site walks you through questions about what happened. It asks which accounts were affected, when you noticed the problem and what information you believe was used. Your answers shape a checklist of next steps that fits your situation rather than a generic list.

The report has practical value beyond the record itself. Completing a report through IdentityTheft.gov produces an FTC Identity Theft Report. You can give that document to businesses and credit bureaus when you dispute fraudulent accounts or charges. It shows that you have formally reported the crime. Some people also file a report with their local police department. Certain creditors may ask for one.

Creating an account on the site lets you save your recovery plan and return to it later. You can mark steps as finished and update the report if new fraud turns up. Cleaning up identity theft can stretch over weeks or longer. One central plan keeps the work organized.

Contact each affected company directly. Call the fraud department of every bank, lender or retailer where a fraudulent account was opened or a charge was made. Ask them to close the account. Request written confirmation that you are not responsible for the debt.

Keep a written record of every step. Note the date of each call, the name of the person you spoke with and what they agreed to do. Save copies of letters, emails and any documents you send. Mailing important disputes by certified mail with a return receipt gives you proof that the company received them.

IdentityTheft.gov serves people in the U.S. and works within U.S. law. Readers in the U.K. and other countries should report fraud through their own national police or fraud reporting service instead.

On a pseudonymous site such as Archive of Our Own (AO3), the biggest breach risk is often personal rather than financial. A leaked email address can tie a pen name to the real person behind it. A separate email account used only for fan activity limits that exposure.

AO3 is a fan fiction archive run by the Organization for Transformative Works, a nonprofit. An account there needs a username and an email address. Many writers and readers post under pseudonyms. Some keep their fan work entirely apart from their professional or family lives.

That separation only holds if the details behind the account stay apart too. An email address built from a full name, or one also used for work, banking and social media, acts as a bridge. If any site's account records leaked, anyone holding the list could match that address to a public profile elsewhere.

A dedicated email address breaks that bridge. Create one that contains no part of your legal name, your birth year or your workplace. Reserve it for AO3 and similar community sites. Some email providers also offer alias addresses that forward to a main inbox, and those serve the same purpose.

Handles create a second link. A pen name reused on Tumblr, Discord, Reddit $RDDT or a personal blog lets someone connect accounts by searching a single word. A different handle on each platform makes that matching harder. At minimum, keep the AO3 name off any account that carries your real identity.

Profile details matter as well. Location, age, job title, school and photos can narrow a pseudonym down to one person even without an email leak. Leaving those fields blank reduces what a stranger can piece together. Keeping personal anecdotes out of author notes does the same.

These habits carry over to any hobby or community site, from craft forums to recipe boards. The risk is not limited to fan fiction. It exists wherever a person shares interests they would rather keep apart from their name.

AO3 has faced other kinds of incidents that differ from an account-data breach. The site has gone offline during distributed denial-of-service attacks, which flood servers with traffic rather than steal stored records. Its publicly posted works have also been scraped for AI datasets. Neither is the same as a breach of account data.

#5459. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

XRP whales are accumulating millions of tokens while US spot exchange-traded funds (ETFs) continue bleeding capital. Large holders added 65.32 million XRP worth $72 million at the current price over four days. Meanwhile, ETF investors withdrew roughly $18 million across two consecutive sessions.

The conflicting signals arrive as XRP trades near $1.04, struggling to recover from its latest correction. The token has fallen 35% from its October high at the $1.60 level, putting bullish expectations under serious pressure.

However, crypto analyst Dark Defender is sticking with an ambitious $10.11 XRP price target. His Elliott Wave projection outlines a potential recovery toward double-digit territory, despite deteriorating market conditions.

Data shows that large XRP holders accumulated 65.32 million tokens between November 7 and November 11. The purchases were worth nearly $72 million at prevailing market prices.

The accumulation stands in sharp contrast to institutional investment activity. US spot XRP ETFs recorded approximately $10.4 million in net outflows on November 9, followed by another $7.6 million on November 10. That brings combined withdrawals to $18 million across two sessions. Grayscale’s GXRP accounted for most of the November 10 outflow, shedding $7.2 million.

Are larger holders positioning for a recovery while ETF investors reduce their exposure? Maybe, but the growing appetite among large wallets shows that some investors are treating the correction as an opportunity, and not abandoning the XRP ship.

The technical picture remains difficult. XRP’s 14-day Relative Strength Index (RSI) has dropped to approximately 23, placing the token deep inside oversold territory. Its Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) also remains negative.

The next major support sits around $0.9852, corresponding with the August low. Losing that level could expose XRP to another wave of selling pressure.

Dark Defender’s bullish outlook offers a striking contrast to XRP’s current weakness. The analyst mapped out an Elliott Wave structure with a potential Wave 3 target of $10.1101. #5456. dnl Enters U.S. Market with AI-native U.S. GAAP Disclosure Checklist

The AI platform is trusted by 15,000 auditors globally at 140 firms, including the Big Four.

The U.S. GAAP checklist covers private and public companies, state and local governments, not-for-profit organizations and specialized industries.

NEW YORK, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- dnl today entered the U.S. market with a U.S. GAAP Disclosure Checklist, bringing American auditors an AI platform already used globally for high-quality, defensible audits.

dnl builds AI agents that do the hands-on work of an audit. Its agents read a company's annual reports, check every required disclosure, and verify that the numbers are accurate and consistent. The agents hand the auditor a checked result to review, in which every answer links to its source. The auditor reviews, approves and signs.

Founded in Berlin in 2019, dnl is trusted by 15,000 auditors globally at 140 audit firms worldwide, from independent practices to Big Four member firms. Customers include BDO, KPMG and Forvis Mazars. More than 60,000 audits have been completed on the platform. Auditors in the U.S. can now automate 90% of their audits, while improving audit quality and reallocate saved time to the work that matters: judgment calls.

"U.S. auditors face the same pressure we've seen in every market we serve: more disclosure requirements, tighter deadlines and no room for error," said Andreas Schindler, co-founder and CEO of dnl. "Our U.S. GAAP Disclosure Checklist does the checking and cross-referencing links every answer to its evidence, and leaves the judgment where it belongsâwith the auditor. Bringing it to the U.S. is the natural next step for a platform that thousands of auditors already trust."

"With most of the checklist already answered, U.S. audit teams get their hours back, to spend more time making judgment calls and client conversations," added Schindler. "Firms finish with a stronger, defensible file, where every conclusion can be traced and defended, ultimately ensuring the best outcomes for their clients."

#5455. Sumo Logic expands AWS Observability Solution with one-click deployment and new regions

Data analytics software firm Sumo Logic Inc. today released an expanded AWS Observability Solution, a monitoring package for Amazon Web Services Inc. users that can now be deployed in one click from AWS Marketplace.

Sumo Logic is pitching the update at cloud teams that would otherwise have to build their own dashboards before they can properly watch an AWS environment. Much of the company’s recent product work has gone into artificial intelligence agents that take on incident investigations.

Support for AWS regions in Zurich, Melbourne and New Zealand takes the number covered by the solution to 20. Workloads running in those three regions can now be watched with the same prebuilt alerts Sumo Logic offers elsewhere on 12 core AWS services. Lambda, DynamoDB and Application Load Balancer are among them.

Zurich has been on the company’s list since February, when Sumo Logic said its security products would come to the AWS Europe (Zurich) Region for customers bound by Switzerland’s Federal Act on Data Protection.

Anyone signing up through Quick Launch, the AWS Marketplace option behind the one-click deployment, can now do the whole thing — buying the package, setting it up and getting it deployed — without stepping outside their own AWS account. Sumo Logic says the deployments themselves are versioned, in Terraform and CloudFormation alike, which the company expects will mean less configuration drift over time.

Root Cause Agent, which Sumo Logic put into preview for operations teams on Oct. 13, is where much of the telemetry the package collects ends up. When an alert fires, the agent goes digging through the data on its own. A company blog post from the launch says every finding it turns up can be rerun as a search in one click.

The agent belongs to Dojo AI, the agentic AI platform Sumo Logic introduced for security operations teams in September 2025. Root Cause Agent carries that investigative work over into observability. Alongside it in October came new Dojo AI packages that bill all of a customer’s agent use, with Mobot, the SOC Analyst Agent and Root Cause Agent included, against one monthly credit pool.

“AI agents are only as good as the telemetry and context provided to them,” said Keith Kuchler, chief product and technology officer at Sumo Logic. Kuchler added that teams on AWS shouldn’t have to keep “working around regions their tools can’t reach.”

Back in September, Sumo Logic gave customers a way to trim telemetry before ingestion when it expanded its Data Pipelines service. The company, taken private by Francisco Partners in 2023 for $1.7 billion, will show the AWS package at AWS re:Invent in Las Vegas Nov. 30-Dec. 4.

Through Sumo Logic’s listings in AWS Marketplace, version 3.0.0 of the solution is available now to customers that monitor AWS infrastructure.

#5454. U.S.-Iran war by the numbers: 18 U.S. troops killed, oil swings, $38 billion cost

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The U.S.-Iran war by the numbers, from 18 U.S. troop deaths to Brent crude swings and a Congressional Budget Office cost estimate of $38 billion as of Aug. 1

U.S. forces have reported relatively few casualties in the war with Iran. That is one reason public attention has turned to the resources the conflict consumes, according to report R48887 from the Congressional Research Service. The report tracks figures through September 2026. Its numbers trace the war's reach into munitions stockpiles, federal budgets, crude futures and shipping lanes as well as casualty lists.

The fighting began on Feb. 28, 2026, when strikes opened Operation Epic Fury. A ceasefire followed on April 7. A memorandum of understanding was signed on June 17. The first U.S. strikes after that agreement came on June 26, and heavy U.S. strikes followed on July 7. President Trump declared the memorandum "over" on July 8. A 60-day window for a broader deal closed on Aug. 17 without a final agreement. The U.S. blockade of Iranian ports, which began April 13, ended June 18 and was reinstated July 14. As of September 2026, the two sides were trading limited strikes.

Tracking the U.S.-Iran war by the numbers means drawing on institutions that count different things over different periods. The Defense Department splits U.S. casualties across two separate tabs. The Congressional Budget Office and the Lead Inspector General each publish cost estimates with their own cutoff dates. Brent crude futures swung widely over the same months that shipping through the Strait of Hormuz stalled, then rose and fell. Each figure keeps its own date, and several cannot be added together.

The four slides below cover a selection of those measures. The first looks at the human cost, from U.S. troop deaths to Iranian and Israeli casualties and displacement in Lebanon. The second follows Brent crude prices alongside the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports. The third examines the fuel supply squeeze across Gulf producers, a Saudi pipeline and Red Sea shipping routes. The last tallies U.S.-Iran war costs, from Pentagon spending and arms sales to Iran's inflation and its record-low rial.

The U.S. military had 18 service members killed and 824 wounded in the war with Iran as of Sept. 15, 2026. Those totals come from the casualty summary in a Congressional Research Service (CRS) report on the conflict.

The headline count draws on two separate Defense Department casualty tabs. Each tab covers a different stretch of the fighting, and the report treats them as distinct counts rather than one running list.

The first tab is for Operation Epic Fury, the U.S. strike campaign that began on Feb. 28, 2026. It records 14 deaths and 418 service members wounded in action.

The second tab, labeled Overseas Operations, covers casualties from July 7, 2026, onward. That start date is the day of heavy U.S. strikes on Iran. This tab shows four deaths and 406 wounded in action.

Read side by side, the two tabs show that the April 7 ceasefire did not close the casualty count. Heavy fighting in July added a second set of U.S. losses.

The CRS timeline records an Iranian strike in Jordan on July 17 that killed three U.S. troops.

The toll inside Iran is far larger. The Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), a U.S.-based group that tracks rights abuses in Iran, counted 3,636 people killed as of April 7. That figure includes 1,701 civilians, or about 47% of the total.

The CRS report gives April 7 as the date for HRANA's count. The HRANA report it cites is dated May 18, 2026.

Iranian attacks also killed civilians in Israel. Reports cited by the CRS put that toll at 20 Israeli civilians before the ceasefire of April 7.

The war's human cost extended to Lebanon. Israeli operations there displaced more than 1 million people, or about 20% of the population, according to reports cited by the CRS. About 360,000 people remained displaced as of August.

Brent crude futures rose from $60.85 a barrel on Jan. 1, 2026, to $118.35 on March 31, according to the Congressional Research Service. The benchmark has moved sharply in both directions since then. It stood at $107.63 on Sept. 10.

Brent is the main global price reference for crude oil. The figures in the report are prompt-month futures prices. These track the contract for the nearest delivery month. They show where traders priced oil on specific dates, not an average across each period.

On Feb. 27, the day before U.S. strikes began, Brent stood at $72.48. Once the strikes began, Iranian threats and attacks on commercial vessels brought traffic through the Strait of Hormuz close to a standstill in the war's first days.

A ceasefire began on April 7, and Brent was at $94.74 the following day. The U.S. started a blockade of Iranian ports on April 13. By April 29, the price was back at $118.03, close to its March high.

The blockade has relied on about 20 Navy vessels, deployed for months at a time. Those ships have turned away hundreds of vessels. They have also disabled about 10.

The U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding on June 17. The blockade ended the next day. On June 21, the U.S. issued General License X $TWTR, which authorized transactions involving Iranian crude. Brent was down to $71.57 by July 1.

The U.S. later rescinded the license after further Iranian attacks on shipping. President Trump declared the memorandum "over" on July 8. The blockade was reinstated on July 14.

Ship movements through Hormuz have risen and fallen since the war's opening days. The flow has shifted as periods of fighting and periods of diplomacy have alternated. The September price of $107.63 came as the two sides exchanged limited strikes and the blockade of Iranian ports was back in force.

The Iran war squeezed fuel supplies by choking the routes that carry Gulf oil and natural gas to world markets. In the war's first days, Iranian threats and attacks on commercial ships brought Strait of Hormuz traffic close to a standstill, according to the Congressional Research Service.

The strait links the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea beyond it. Ship traffic through the passage has risen and fallen repeatedly since those opening days. Flows have tracked the conflict's swings between fighting and diplomacy.

The damage reached production as well as shipping. After Iranian missile and drone attacks, energy producers across the Gulf shut in part of their oil and gas output. Some also halted part of their exports. The CRS report says the trouble in Hormuz has hit natural gas markets as well as oil.

Iraq is one exporter caught in the bottleneck. Its oil exports have been held back by the Hormuz disruption, the CRS report notes.

Saudi Arabia's workaround ran through the Red Sea. Saudi cargoes had been routed from Yanbu, a port on the kingdom's Red Sea coast, north through the Suez Canal. That route kept those shipments clear of the Strait of Hormuz. It faced its own threats. The Houthis carried out attacks, and the Bab al Mandeb was closed to Saudi-linked vessels. The Bab al Mandeb is the strait at the Red Sea's southern end.

Pressure moved inland in September. Attacks that month struck Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, which carries crude across the kingdom toward Yanbu. The strikes forced the pipeline to close. The CRS report attributes them to Iran-backed groups based in Iraq.

Iran's own exports lean heavily on one site. Kharg Island, in the Gulf off Iran's coast, has handled 90% of the country's oil exports, according to the report. The island sits inside the Gulf. Tankers loading there must pass through the Strait of Hormuz to reach open ocean.

The Congressional Budget Office estimated in September 2026 that U.S. military operations against Iran had cost $38 billion as of Aug. 1, 2026. A separate estimate from the Lead Inspector General covers a shorter period and arrives at a different total.

The Lead Inspector General report, dated Sept. 14, puts the cost at $33.4 billion as of June 29. Spent munitions make up $22.3 billion of that figure. Incremental costs account for $7.4 billion, and lost equipment accounts for $3.7 billion. The total does not include damage to infrastructure.

The State Department carries its own costs. It reported $113 million in expenses, including money tied to evacuations. Damage to U.S. diplomatic facilities adds a separate $184 million. Most of that damage was in Iraq, at $157 million, with Kuwait accounting for $15 million.

The White House has asked Congress for more money. In June it requested $21 billion for munitions and $17.3 billion for operational costs. In July the House passed a budget resolution through the reconciliation process that included those funds.

Weapons sales to regional partners form another part of the ledger. The administration has notified Congress of more than $64 billion in sales to Israel, Kuwait, Jordan, Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Oman. Emergency sales make up $25.3 billion of that amount. Those emergency sales bypass the standard congressional review.

An April analysis from CSIS by Mark Cancian and Chris Park estimated that the U.S. had used roughly a third of its prewar Tomahawk stockpile. The same analysis put use at a quarter of its JASSMs and more than half of its Patriot and THAAD interceptors. A Pentagon assessment passed along in the Lead Inspector General report said munitions use had produced "strategic inventory shortfalls" and revealed "industrial base bottlenecks." In September, President Trump wrote that the U.S. has "virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition."

Equipment and logistics losses go beyond munitions. The U.S. has lost roughly 25% of its MQ-9 Reaper drones, according to an August report in The Washington Post. Iranian damage to Naval Support Activity Bahrain pushed Navy supply routes through Diego Garcia, more than 2,000 miles to the south.

Inside Iran, the toll shows up in prices and the currency. Iran's inflation rate reached 84% year-on-year in August. In September 2026 the rial hit a record low of 2.25 million to the dollar.

In Lebanon, Israel has occupied about 5% of the country's territory. The June 17 memorandum of understanding had envisioned a $300 billion regional plan to rebuild Iran as part of a "Final Deal." That deal never came together.

#5452. Bitcoin slides to as low as $62,000 as liquidations of leveraged bets accelerate

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A stronger dollar, rising Treasury yields and outflows from spot bitcoin ETFs are adding to pressure on the largest cryptocurrency

Bitcoin fell as low as $62,000 on Saturday as forced liquidations of leveraged bets accelerated, then recovered to about $64,000 on Monday morning.

The weekend low was the weakest level since July, according to Bloomberg, and the lowest since August, according to CNBC. Bitcoin has now fallen six weeks in a row.

Exchanges closed out more than $165 million in long positions on Saturday night, following Friday's $629 million and Thursday's near-$700 million, according to CNBC. The selling picked up after bitcoin dropped beneath the 200-day moving average, which sits near $73,000, during the week.

The dollar index climbed on Friday to a level not seen since April 2025, according to CNBC. That followed an inflation report earlier in the week that came in above forecasts and led traders to anticipate more Federal Reserve tightening. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield has risen past 5%, and the stronger dollar has weighed on bitcoin and gold alike.

U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds shed close to $3 billion on a net basis between Oct. 30 and Nov. 13, according to Bloomberg. Joshua Lim, co-head of markets at FalconX, pointed to stablecoin outflows of nearly $20 billion over the past month and to Anthropic's upcoming initial public offering as theories for the weakness.

Anthropic's expected listing is drawing strong interest, and investors may be raising cash for it by selling assets such as crypto, though it is unclear how much money has actually moved, according to Bloomberg. The $6.3 billion hack at Binance, along with fading demand from institutions for the ETFs, has also weighed on prices, according to CNBC.

The year's low is roughly $58,000, according to Bloomberg.

Bitcoin had already fallen below $70,000 last Friday as a technology stock selloff tied to the resignation of Nvidia $NVDA CEO Jensen Huang spread to cryptocurrencies. Nvidia is scheduled to report fiscal third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, Nov. 17.

#5451. Sonoma County Expands Panaptic Partnership, More Than Doubling Student Access to IMPACT Prevention Programs

Expansion more than doubles student access to evidence-informed substance use prevention education across Sonoma County

SANTA ROSA, Calif., Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Sonoma County Department of Health Services (DHS) is expanding its partnership with Panaptic to more than double access to the IMPACT Prevention Programs and reach thousands of eighth graders in schools across the county. Reach will grow from about 1,300 students to nearly 2,900, plus a family member for each student.

IMPACT is an online, empowerment-based substance use prevention program. It gives students current, evidence-informed information about cannabis, alcohol, opioids and fentanyl, building the knowledge, confidence and critical-thinking skills to make informed decisions.

Schools can launch IMPACT quickly and adapt it to local needs. Panaptic supports each rollout with hands-on implementation help, training guidance and ongoing collaboration with educators and community organizations.

An independent eight-year evaluation of IMPACT found that students' confidence in getting and using naloxone (Narcan) during an overdose grew 5.4 times more than the benchmark for meaningful attitude change in decades of prevention research.

Will Gayowski, Substance Use Disorders & Recovery Services Section Manager at Sonoma County DHS, said community demand and strong program outcomes drove the decision.

"There's a wealth of information, especially for youth cannabis use, and there is a strong foundation in statistical analysis of the program outcomes," Gayowski said. "Our vision, in a nutshell, is for evidence-based investments upstream to have downstream results that reverberate in the community for years to come."

"Input from school systems, internal program staff review of curriculum and strong statistical analysis of program data all contributed to this decision," he added. "IMPACT was also one of our more cost-effective solutions to reach youth, schools, teachers, parents and others. The Panaptic team has been reliable and impactful, and has shown they can scale up or down in accordance with community needs and preferences."

Richard Von Feldt, PsyD, a psychologist and co-founder of Panaptic, said the expansion shows the value of collaborative, community-centered prevention.

"We're grateful for Sonoma County's continued leadership in prevention," Dr. Von Feldt said. "Together, we're delivering prevention that is evidence-informed, sustainable and built around the needs of local schools and families."

As communities across California look for effective responses to youth cannabis, opioid and fentanyl use, Sonoma County and Panaptic aim to strengthen protective factors, support healthier decision-making and build long-term resilience among students and families.

Schools, districts, county health departments and community organizations interested in bringing IMPACT to their students can schedule a free consultation and program walkthrough with Panaptic at https://panaptic.com/contact/ Learn more at panaptic.com/impact-prevention.

Founded in 2009 by prevention experts Sarah Ferraro Cunningham, PsyD and Richard Von Feldt, PsyD, Panaptic partners with state agencies, counties, schools and community organizations nationwide to deliver scalable, evidence-informed prevention education. Its online IMPACT Prevention Programs address cannabis, alcohol, opioid and fentanyl use with practical, research-informed approaches designed for real-world implementation. Learn more at panaptic.com.

#5450. U.S. is closing cloud loophole on AI chips, adding five countries to license list

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The interim rule exempts U.S.-headquartered companies, with reporting requirements, and rescinds the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule

The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security on Sunday issued an interim final rule that will require licenses to export advanced AI chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. The rule also restricts remote access to U.S. chips through data centers overseas.

“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the bureau said in a statement, according to Bloomberg. It said the Treasury Department and the National Security Council wrote the rule and directed its release.

Under the rule text, a license will be required to send chips to data centers that supply significant volumes of computing power to companies headquartered in Macau or Country Group D:5. Data centers, foreign foundries and chip exporters must perform due diligence on customers' direct or indirect ownership or control. Data centers already providing such computing power must obtain a license within 90 days of the effective date or face future export restrictions. Commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers and social media companies, are exempt.

The five-country requirement applies in addition to existing license requirements, the rule says. It does not apply to chips destined for companies headquartered in the United States, or with a U.S.-headquartered ultimate parent, provided reporting requirements are met. Commerce will review applications case by case. The rule describes the five countries as presenting a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.

The rule also formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule, which it says was never enforced.

The rule takes effect on its publication in the Federal Register, with comments due 60 days after. It had not been posted as of 9 a.m. ET Monday, according to Bloomberg.

Nvidia $NVDA stock slid by as much as 2.9% on Monday, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index lost up to 5.5%.

The rule is meant to limit Chinese companies' access to advanced AI chips, according to Reuters. Reuters said it comes as President Donald Trump is set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday in Shenzhen, and as pressure grows on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to tighten export controls.

The rule follows weeks of scrutiny of chip exports. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down last week and acknowledged a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who is suspected of spying for China. Megaspeed is accused of illegally shipping export-controlled chips into China and has denied wrongdoing. Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott, a South Carolina Republican, has asked Jensen Huang to testify on Dec. 3 and Lutnick on Dec. 10. Lutnick has agreed to appear.

Before the rule, U.S. export controls covered the physical transfer of chips but not remote access to them, Cassia King, a senior researcher at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, said last week.

#5449. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

#5448. Supreme Court won't hear Trump's bid to cut $59 million in DEI research grants

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The justices left intact a 9th Circuit ruling that requires the NSF and NEH to keep funding University of California researchers

The US Supreme Court in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Nov. 4, 2025.(Pete Kiehart/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The Supreme Court declined on Monday to hear President Donald Trump's appeal in Trump v. Thakur, No. 26-210. The court listed the petition among those denied in its order list.

The denial preserves a 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruling that obligates the National Science Foundation and the National Endowment for the Humanities to keep paying out $59 million in grants, according to Bloomberg. The case was filed by a group of professors and scientists affiliated with the University of California. Bloomberg reported that no justice noted a dissent.

The appeals court found that the administration likely ran afoul of constitutional free speech protections by penalizing grantees over the views they hold, according to Bloomberg. The three-judge panel ruled unanimously. "Because the agencies' termination of grants is aimed at the suppression of viewpoints with which the government disagrees, it likely violates the First Amendment," the court said.

The grants support research projects that Trump said were "DEI programs," according to Bloomberg. Last year, Trump ordered agencies to cut off money for work touching on "gender ideology," "environmental justice" and diversity, equity and inclusion. Universities and researchers contend that the cancellations derailed work across the sciences, medicine and elsewhere.

In its appeal, the administration argued that the government may constitutionally pick which projects to bankroll, favoring those consistent with its own outlook. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices the 9th Circuit ruling would "hamstring every future administration" if left in place, according to Bloomberg.

"The First Amendment provides the government significant flexibility when it acts as patron to subsidize speech," Sauer argued, according to Bloomberg. "The government may itself promote favored viewpoints, including by disbursing public funds to private entities."

The 9th Circuit said the Supreme Court has separated choosing not to finance a program from turning down specific applicants over the opinions they express.

The University of California group urged the justices to leave the ruling alone, saying the 9th Circuit applied "clearly established law." "The stakes for the researchers, and for the public that benefits from their work, could not be higher," the group told the court.

The researchers also criticized the administration for flagging grants based on search terms like "diversity," according to Bloomberg. They said the method also caught projects whose titles referred to "Leaf Diversity" and "Diversity Within the Legume Rhizobia Mutualism."

#5446. PitchBook to give early-stage startups free access, using their data to feed a new tool for VCs

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:23 amNovember 10, 2026 at 7:25 am

PitchBook announced a new program to give early-stage startups free use of its private-market data, if they share their financials and other company details.

The Seattle-based company says the new program, dubbed PitchBook for Startups, will feed PitchBook Origin, a new deal-sourcing product that helps venture capitalists and other investors find startups before they raise their first institutional round.

PitchBook announced both offerings Tuesday morning at Web Summit in Lisbon. Owned by Morningstar since 2016, the company has more than 3,000 employees and sells subscriptions to venture firms, private equity investors and dealmakers.

The launches come as first-time startup financings hit a record. There were an estimated 8,625 such deals in the U.S. through the third quarter, already more than the 8,507 in all of 2021, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor. PitchBook attributes part of the surge to AI, which it says is making it easier to start companies.

The startup program is open to pre-seed and bootstrapped companies that haven’t taken money from a venture firm or other institutional investor, or raised a priced round, the type of funding round that sets a valuation.

Founders can use PitchBook to find investors who are active in their sector and stage, and to compare their valuation and growth against similar companies.

To keep their free access, startups must update their company information every quarter. PitchBook says that information can include financials, team growth and product milestones. Only “select portions” of that data will go into Origin, the company said, without saying which.

Origin covers about 25 million companies, including stealth, pre-funding and bootstrapped companies. About 15 million of them are new to PitchBook. It scores companies on how well they match an investor’s criteria and sends alerts when they show new activity.

“What’s been missing is visibility into the stage before a company raises, when the most important signals are the hardest to see,” said Paul Santarelli, PitchBook’s chief solutions officer, in a statement announcing the products.

PitchBook didn’t disclose pricing for Origin, and the product’s web page currently asks investors to join a waitlist.
