#5445. 10 Black Friday shopping tips for 2026, from price tracking to return policies

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These Black Friday shopping tips for 2026 cover online price comparisons, store return policies, TV timing, social media promo codes and ways to avoid holiday scams

Black Friday is no longer one day of doorbusters. It is a long weekend of competing retail tactics. Treating it as a research project rather than a race keeps the focus on what a deal is worth. A discount only means something when it is measured against a real price history, a fixed budget and the store's own fine print.

The shape of the event has changed. More stores have stayed closed on Thanksgiving. That leaves shoppers with more reason to hunt for deals on websites and apps that day. Retailers also tend to run more online-only promotions than in-store-only ones. Cyber Monday follows a few days later. The same product can therefore show up at different prices across several days and several sellers.

That spread creates room for mistakes as well as savings. A price labeled as a markdown may match what the item sold for weeks earlier. A doorbuster laptop may carry a model number that differs from the version reviewers covered. A shopping link in a text message may lead to a site built to collect card details. And a gift bought in a rush may come with a return window, a price-match exception or a restocking fee the buyer never checked.

The Black Friday shopping tips below are built around those pressure points. They start with planning — a spending limit and a named gift list set before the first sale email arrives. They move through price checking, including tools that chart how a product's price has moved over time. They cover payment safety, from the dispute rights that come with credit cards under U.S. law to the warning signs of fake storefronts and phishing messages. They finish with store policies and category timing, including why the largest TV markdowns tend to land on Black Friday itself.

Each of the 10 slides stands on its own. A reader looking only for return-policy guidance or for social media promo codes can jump straight to that slide. Read together, the slides form a plan for the whole holiday sales period. That plan runs from the first early access offer to the close of the return window, which most retailers extend into January.

Decide on a total spending limit and write down who you are buying for before any Black Friday sale opens. A fixed number and a named list turn each discount into a yes-or-no question about something you already planned to buy.

Start with the total. Look at what is left in your monthly budget after rent, utilities, debt payments and groceries. Set the holiday figure from that remainder. A holiday purchase that sits on a credit card as a carried balance can cost more in interest than the sale saved.

Then divide the total by person. Write each recipient's name next to a dollar limit. A per-person cap keeps one expensive gift from using up the money meant for everyone else on the list.

Add the costs that sit outside the price tag. Sales tax, shipping fees, gift wrap, batteries, cables and greeting cards all draw from the same pool. Holiday travel, hosting meals and year-end tips for service workers often fall in the same weeks. They belong in the plan too.

Attach specific items to each name where you can. "Headphones for my brother" is harder to shop for than a particular brand and model. The more precise the entry, the faster you can recognize a real deal and skip everything else.

Include a few things you need for yourself or the household. Black Friday is a common time to replace a worn mattress, vacuum or kitchen appliance. Putting those purchases on the list keeps them inside the budget instead of on top of it.

Black Friday sale pages lean on urgency cues such as countdown timers, "only a few left" banners and limited-quantity doorbusters. Those cues are designed to push a fast decision. A written list gives you a reason to close the tab when the item is not on it.

Track spending as you go. A simple spreadsheet or notes app can record the budgeted amount, the actual price paid and the retailer for each purchase. That record shows how much room remains at any point in the weekend. Saving order confirmations in one email folder also makes later returns and price adjustments easier to handle.

Leave a small cushion for a forgotten gift or a price that comes in higher than expected. If the cushion goes unused, it stays in your account.

Shopping online is one of the simplest ways to see more Black Friday deals and compare prices across retailers. Some promotions run only on a retailer's website or app. Those offers never reach a store shelf.

Price comparison is the larger advantage. A shopper can open the same product page at several retailers in separate browser tabs and see the differences in a few minutes. Doing that in person means driving from store to store on one of the busiest shopping weekends of the year.

The sticker price is only part of the comparison. Shipping fees, sales tax and delivery dates can change which offer costs the least in the end. A lower price at one retailer can lose its edge against a slightly higher price at a store that ships for free. Many large chains also offer buy online, pick up in store. That option removes shipping costs and delivery waits for items that are in stock locally.

Delivery timing matters most for gifts. An order placed during Thanksgiving weekend still has to clear warehouse processing and carrier transit. Holiday volume can stretch both. Checking the estimated arrival date before paying helps avoid a gift that lands after the occasion it was bought for.

Shopping online does not mean ignoring physical stores. In-store deals are still worth a look during research, if only to confirm that an online price is competitive. BlackFriday.com gathers brick-and-mortar holiday ads in one place. That saves a trip through dozens of individual retailer circulars.

Thanksgiving itself adds another reason to stay online. More stores have stayed closed on the holiday, according to Consumer Reports. Retailer websites and apps remain open even where store doors are not. Shoppers who want an early start on Thursday can still begin there.

The online push continues after the weekend. Shop.org, the digital division of the National Retail Federation, coined the term Cyber Monday in 2005. The name described the Monday after Thanksgiving as a day of heavy online shopping. Many retailers now run sales across the full stretch from Thanksgiving through that Monday.

A Black Friday price is only a deal if it beats what the item has recently sold for. Price-history trackers such as Keepa and CamelCamelCamel record how an Amazon $AMZN listing's price has changed. That record shows whether a holiday markdown is a real low or a routine fluctuation.

The two tools work in similar ways. Each logs a listing's price at regular intervals and plots it as a line graph. A shopper can paste in an Amazon link or search for an item by name. The chart then shows past lows, recent spikes and the price the item typically sells for.

Keepa offers a browser extension that places its price chart directly on Amazon product pages. The history appears alongside the listing, with no separate search needed. The service also tracks Amazon storefronts in several countries, including the U.S., U.K., Germany and Japan. Its basic charts are free. Keepa charges a subscription for more detailed data.

CamelCamelCamel runs a free website and a browser extension called the Camelizer. It also covers Amazon sites outside the U.S. Both services let users set a target price and receive an email alert when a listing drops to that level.

The chart answers a specific question. Is today's price lower than the item's usual price, and how does it compare with its lowest recorded price? A product that falls on Black Friday to a level it reached several times during the year is on a standard sale. A product whose price climbed in the weeks before the holiday and then fell back is being discounted from a raised starting point.

The second pattern is worth spotting. The "was" price on a sale tag is set by the seller. The Federal Trade Commission's Guides Against Deceptive Pricing cover these former-price comparisons. Under the guides, a former price should be one at which the item was actually offered to the public on a regular basis for a reasonably substantial period. A history chart lets a shopper check that claim independently.

These trackers follow Amazon listings, not every retailer. For items sold at Best Buy $BBY, Target $TGT or Walmart $WMT, an Amazon chart can still serve as a benchmark when the identical item is sold in both places. A target-price alert set a few weeks before Black Friday sends a notification if the price drops before holiday ads start running.

Paying with a credit card instead of a debit card for Black Friday purchases gives U.S. shoppers stronger legal protection. The Fair Credit Billing Act lets cardholders dispute billing errors, including charges for items that never arrived, and federal law caps liability for fraudulent credit card charges.

Congress passed the Fair Credit Billing Act in 1974 as an amendment to the Truth in Lending Act. It applies to open-end credit accounts, such as credit cards and revolving charge accounts like department store cards. It does not apply to debit cards, which fall under a different law.

The act defines a billing error broadly. It covers charges the cardholder did not authorize, charges for the wrong amount and math mistakes on a statement. It also covers charges for goods or services the buyer did not accept or that were not delivered as agreed. That last category fits common holiday problems, such as a package that goes missing or a retailer that ships the wrong item.

To use these rights, a cardholder sends a written dispute to the card issuer's billing-error address. The letter must reach the issuer within 60 days after it sent the first statement showing the charge. The issuer must acknowledge the dispute in writing within 30 days. It must then resolve the dispute within two billing cycles, and no later than 90 days.

While the dispute is open, the cardholder can withhold payment on the contested amount. The issuer cannot report that amount as delinquent during the investigation.

Liability for unauthorized credit card charges is capped at $50 under federal law. If a thief uses only the card number and not the physical card, the cardholder owes nothing for those charges.

Debit cards work differently. They are covered by the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, and the protection depends on how fast the account holder acts. Reporting a lost or stolen debit card within two business days limits liability to $50. Waiting longer raises the cap to $500. Failing to report unauthorized transfers within 60 days of the statement can leave the account holder with unlimited losses.

Cash flow is the other difference. A debit card purchase pulls money straight from a checking account. If that charge turns out to be fraudulent, the money can be missing while the bank investigates. With a credit card, the shopper can hold back payment on the disputed amount until the issuer finishes its review.

The dispute rights run on a deadline. Checking card statements in the weeks after Black Friday makes it easier to catch a duplicate charge or an undelivered order while the 60-day window is still open.

Social media feeds can surface Black Friday deals that never appear in a retailer's main holiday ad. Facebook $META, Instagram, Pinterest $PINS and TikTok can all point shoppers toward exclusive promotions and promo codes. Some companies advertise offers on these platforms that are not available anywhere else.

The most direct way to catch these offers is to follow the brands and retailers already on a gift list. Companies use their own accounts to announce sales and share codes with followers. A short list of followed brands makes those posts easier to spot in a crowded feed.

Influencers are a second channel. Creators who work with brands sometimes pass along inside information about upcoming sales. Others share special promo codes with their audiences. Those codes are usually entered at checkout. Some stores accept only one code per order. An influencer's code may not stack with a retailer's own sitewide Black Friday discount. Comparing the two before paying shows which one lowers the total more.

In the U.S., the Federal Trade Commission's Endorsement Guides require influencers to disclose material connections to the brands they promote. Payment and free products both count as material connections. Labels such as "#ad" or a platform's paid partnership tag signal that relationship. A disclosure says nothing about whether a code offers a good price. It tells the viewer that the post is advertising.

TikTok draws particular attention during the holiday season. Consumer Reports notes that TikTok's shopping platform is gaining popularity as a place to buy gifts. TikTok Shop launched in the U.S. in September 2023. It lets users buy products shown in videos and livestreams without leaving the app.

Pinterest works differently from the other three platforms. Its users save images of products and ideas to boards. Those boards can double as a visual gift list. Many pins link to a retailer's product page, where the current price can be checked.

A code shared in a video or post is only worth using if the final price beats what the same item costs elsewhere. Checking the order total at checkout, including shipping and tax, shows whether a social media offer actually saves money.

Avoid Black Friday scams by going straight to the retailer. Type a known web address or open the store's own app instead of tapping links in texts, emails or ads. Treat any unfamiliar site with prices far below every major retailer as suspect before entering payment details.

Fake shopping sites often copy a real brand's logo, product photos and page layout. The giveaway is usually in the address bar. Look for misspellings, extra words attached to a brand name, swapped letters or an odd domain ending in place of the company's usual one.

A padlock icon next to the address only means the connection is encrypted. It does not prove that the business behind the site is real or that it will ship anything.

Package-delivery texts are a common lure during the holidays, when many people are expecting shipments. A typical version claims a delivery failed or needs an address update. It then links to a page asking for card details or a small redelivery fee.

The U.S. Postal Service states that it does not send texts or emails unless a customer has first requested them. It also says those messages will not contain a link. When a delivery message arrives, check the tracking number on the carrier's own website rather than through the link.

The way a seller asks to be paid is another warning sign. The Federal Trade Commission warns that requests for payment by gift card, wire transfer, cryptocurrency or payment app are common markers of fraud. Legitimate retailers accept standard card payments at checkout. A seller who pushes for one of those other methods, particularly on a social media marketplace, should be treated with suspicion.

Social media ads can also lead to storefronts that take payment and never ship, or that ship a cheap imitation of the advertised product. Searching the store's name alongside words like "reviews" or "scam" before buying can turn up complaints from other shoppers. A site with no physical address, no phone number and only a contact form leaves buyers with little recourse.

If a purchase turns out to be fraudulent, act quickly. Contact the card issuer or bank to dispute the charge and, if needed, cancel the card. Report the scam to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Shoppers in the U.S. can forward scam texts to 7726, which spells SPAM on a phone keypad. The message then goes to their wireless carrier. Online fraud can also be reported to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov.

Read a retailer's price-match, return and restocking-fee policies before checking out on Black Friday. Those three rules decide whether a shopper can claim a lower price later, how long a gift can go back to the store and whether a refund arrives in full.

Nearly every major retailer offers some form of price matching, according to Consumer Reports. The outlet reports that most retailers have widened those terms for the holidays nearly every year. Price matching generally takes two forms. One matches a competitor's lower advertised price at checkout. The other refunds the difference if the store itself lowers the price after the sale. Each retailer writes its own conditions. The store's posted policy is the document that settles any disagreement at the register.

Black Friday weekend brings a specific exception. Some stores suspend price-match guarantees on certain items during those days. A doorbuster bought on Friday may not qualify for an adjustment if its price falls again on Cyber Monday. Where a match is allowed, retailers commonly require the identical item, down to the model number, from a competitor that has it in stock. Many also exclude prices from third-party marketplace sellers.

Return windows stretch for the holidays too. Most retailers move their deadlines into January. That gives gift recipients time to open items after the holidays rather than racing a standard 30-day clock. Some stores accept holiday returns through the first two weeks of January. Others extend the cutoff to Jan. 31. These extended windows usually apply only to purchases made within a defined holiday period. Items bought outside that period follow the standard return rules.

Restocking fees are the third thing to confirm. Shoppers should find out whether a store charges one on Black Friday returns and exchanges before buying. These fees most often apply to opened electronics and large items. They come out of the refund rather than blocking the return.

Paperwork makes each of these policies easier to use. Keep the receipt or order confirmation for every purchase. Ask for a gift receipt when buying for someone else. A gift receipt lets the recipient return or exchange an item without seeing the price. For price-match requests, a screenshot of the competitor's listing showing the price and date gives customer service something concrete to check.

The day after Thanksgiving is the date to target for a TV purchase. Consumer Reports reports that the largest TV markdowns land on Black Friday itself.

The outlet also reports that the steepest TV discounts arrive at this time of year. That applies across all screen sizes and price points.

Shoppers who miss Black Friday still have a short window. Some sale prices may hold through Cyber Monday, the Monday after Thanksgiving weekend. TV prices tend to rise after that.

Consumer Reports advises settling on a model and a budget before the day after Thanksgiving. A named model and a price ceiling make it possible to judge a listing quickly. Without them, a shopper ends up weighing unfamiliar sets while sale prices and stock change.

Narrowing the choice starts with display technology. OLED TVs light each pixel on its own. That lets them switch individual pixels fully off and show true black. LED-LCD sets rely on a backlight behind the panel instead. Mini-LED models use far more, and far smaller, backlight LEDs than standard LED-LCD sets. That allows finer control over which areas of the screen go dark.

HDR format support also varies by brand. Samsung TVs support HDR10+ but not Dolby Vision. LG's OLED TVs support Dolby Vision but not HDR10+.

Gaming needs can shorten the list further. A PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X $TWTR needs an HDMI 2.1 port on the TV to send 4K video at up to 120 frames per second. Not every TV on sale includes one. Many budget models leave it out. The spec sheet shows which ports a set has before checkout.

Physical fit is the final check. TV sizes are measured diagonally. The advertised number therefore does not describe the set's width. Measuring the wall space or the top of the media stand confirms the set will fit. Checking the spacing of the TV's feet confirms it will sit on the stand. For a wall bracket, the TV's VESA mounting pattern needs to match the mount.

Signing up for a retailer's loyalty program or email list before Black Friday can put its deals in front of you before the general public sees them. Many large chains reserve early access windows, member-only prices or extra rewards for shoppers who are already enrolled.

Timing matters here. Early access offers generally go to people who are members when the sale opens. Joining on the morning of the event can mean missing the first round of pricing. Enrolling a few weeks ahead leaves time to set up the account, install the store's app and receive any welcome offers.

Loyalty programs fall into two broad types. Free programs usually ask only for an email address or phone number. They reward purchases with points, store credit or occasional coupons. Paid memberships charge an annual or monthly fee and often bundle sale access with perks such as free shipping. A paid plan pays off only if a year of savings and perks exceeds what it costs. If a free trial covers the holiday weekend, note the date it converts to a paid charge.

The trade-off is volume. Holiday inboxes fill up fast once a shopper joins several lists. A separate email address set aside for retail sign-ups keeps promotions away from personal and work messages. It also makes unsubscribing in bulk easier once the season ends.

Retailer apps add another layer. Push notifications can flag app-only deals or the moment a members' sale goes live. Turning on alerts only for the stores tied to specific gifts keeps those notifications useful rather than constant.

A low Black Friday price on a laptop or appliance means something only if the product matches the one you researched. Before buying a doorbuster, check its full model number against the standard version. Some holiday deals involve variant models built with different parts or fewer features.

Manufacturers sometimes produce models for big sale events or for a single retailer. These versions can look nearly identical to a brand's regular lineup. The difference can sit in a few extra characters at the end of the model number. A familiar brand or series name on the box does not confirm which configuration is inside.

Laptops show the gap clearly. A heavily discounted machine may share a series name with a well-reviewed model but ship with less memory. It may also have a slower or older processor or a smaller storage drive. Some entry-level laptops use eMMC flash storage instead of a solid-state drive. That choice affects both speed and capacity. Screen resolution, battery size and port selection can also differ between configurations. Reviews written about one configuration do not automatically apply to another.

Appliances follow a similar pattern. Two dishwashers or washing machines from the same brand can carry nearly matching model numbers. They can still differ in cycle options, tub material, finish or noise rating. A variant may lack the feature that drew a shopper to the line in the first place, such as a steam setting or a stainless steel interior.

The check is short. Find the exact model number on the retailer's listing or the store tag. Then search for it on the manufacturer's website to pull up its specification sheet. Compare that sheet line by line with the model you originally wanted. Use the exact model number again when reading reviews, so the feedback matches the unit for sale.

For major appliances, the Energy Star product finder lets shoppers look up whether a specific model number carries certification. Checking a variant there can reveal differences in energy use that a sale tag will not show.

A model with lower specs is not automatically a poor buy. It may suit someone who needs a laptop only for email, documents and streaming. The point is to know which version is in the cart. That way, the discount gets measured against the right product.

#5444. McKinsey Global Institute: Trade’s $4 trillion Achilles’ heel is also an opportunity

Shubham Singhal is a senior partner at McKinsey & Company and chair of the McKinsey Global Institute, where Jeongmin Seong is a partner and Tiago Devesa is a senior fellow. This piece draws on the McKinsey Global Institute’s new research on trade’s Achilles’ heel.

On Nov. 6, the U.S. Defense Logistics Agency announced up to $2 billion to buy strategic and critical materials for the National Defense Stockpile. DLA aims to create targeted demand signals to enable domestic production. In fact, the United States produces a small fraction of many of the critical minerals it uses, including less than 1% of the most common type of rare-earth magnet it uses. In other words, these products are among America’s “Achilles’ Heels.”

The global market for solving these vulnerabilities is huge. More than $4 trillion of global imports, nearly a quarter of the total, sit in what our new research calls the Achilles’ heel of global trade: products that face at least two of three vulnerabilities. They are critical to economic activity, they come from a handful of suppliers, or they come from geopolitically distant partners. For business, they can also be a map of where the next growth opportunities lie.

Companies are moving, for example by finding ways to have alternative sources of rare earths outside of China and by pooling purchasing commitments for generic drugs. Software companies now sell visibility into suppliers several tiers upstream.

The next era of globalization is not about retreat; it is about reconfiguration. In 2025, U.S.–China goods trade fell nearly 30%, yet total U.S. imports and Chinese exports reached new highs, and trade is now traveling shorter geopolitical distances as economies shift toward more closely aligned partners. So businesses need to understand where that reconfiguration is most likely to happen, and much of it could center on the Achilles’ heel.

The Achilles’ heel runs through the foundations of the global economy, from crude oil to critical minerals. It also includes the value chains of the future. Electronics carries the largest share: 43% of electronics imports face two or more vulnerabilities, and five of the sector’s products make up about a fifth of the global imports, including smartphones, high-bandwidth memory chips that power AI and lithium-ion batteries.

Other products fly under the radar: not just rare earths but rare gases; not just batteries for electric vehicles but marine engines for large ships; not just laptops but also the transformers and copper cables that deliver electrons to them.

The routes that deliver products matter, too. Roughly 80% of maritime trade (around $10 trillion) passes through at least one chokepoint, and a single blockage is costly. The 2021 Suez blockage held up an estimated $10 billion of trade a day. This year, Strait of Hormuz closures cut transits by as much as 95% at their peak, and prices of commodities from oil to urea spiked.

Chips, batteries, and energy, all central to the Achilles’ heel, are where companies and governments are moving. Since 2022, three-quarters of cross-border investment announcements have gone to industries such as semiconductors and batteries, AI infrastructure, and energy and mining, up from about half before 2020. Our McKinsey Global Institute analysis of greenfield foreign direct investment announcements through June 2026 found that, since 2017, their average geopolitical distance had contracted roughly twice as fast as that of trade. When compared to pre-pandemic averages, advanced economies’ investment in China fell from 10% to 2% of total FDI announcements by value, while flows among advanced economies rose from 35% to 50%.

Industrial policy is putting money behind these moves and could speed them up. Japan’s support for TSMC’s first Kumamoto plant later unlocked more than $20 billion of investment in its semiconductor ecosystem. Efforts to diversify rare-earth magnet supply are drawing public and private capital through direct investment, long-term offtake, and price guarantees. The money is targeting the Achilles’ Heels.

This does not mean a quarter of trade will relocate, but it shows where customers and governments may place greater value on alternatives.

The first opportunity is new production capacity that builds resilience for companies and their customers. Long-term purchasing commitments can make that capacity investable.

More broadly, alternative capacity could create demand for equipment, infrastructure, logistics, financing, and insurance. A company does not have to own a semiconductor factory to benefit from the ecosystem around it. Opportunities often lie upstream: 38% of smartphones’ first- and second-tier upstream inputs are exposed to the Achilles’ heel. The question for a supplier is not just where to build the next assembly plant but what that plant, and its customers, will still struggle to source.

The second opportunity lies in product design. In a more geopolitically contested era, economic security needs to shape what companies make. Suppliers can offer automakers electric-vehicle motors that eliminate heavy rare earths such as dysprosium and terbium. Resilience doesn’t just call for alternative supply, but also for alternative technologies.

A vulnerability is not automatically a business opportunity.

By our estimates, producing advanced semiconductors in Germany or the United States costs about 40% to 50% more than in Taiwan or mainland China. Businesses need to know whether productivity, execution, customer access, or targeted policy support can narrow that gap.

That argues for selectivity: looking first for opportunities close to existing capabilities, rather than assuming every vulnerable product can be made, and distinguishing lasting demand for resilience from a temporary response to disruption.

For management teams, that means examining customers’ vulnerabilities alongside their own, such as which dependencies could interrupt their business, which they could help others resolve, and where their technologies, skills, or supplier relationships give them an edge.

Seen this way, resilience belongs on the growth as well as the risk agenda. With more than $4 trillion of imports at stake, the next opportunity may begin with a question companies too rarely ask: Whose Achilles’ heel could we help solve?

The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune.

#5443. Allen Family Philanthropies gives $10M to hundreds of small arts groups across Washington state

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 9, 2026 at 2:56 pm

Allen Family Philanthropies and Seattle nonprofit ArtsFund awarded $10 million to 745 small arts and culture organizations across Washington state, and renewed the grant program for another $10 million next year.

The latest Community Accelerator Grant awards range from $2,500 to $25,000 and reach organizations in 37 of the state’s 39 counties. The 2027 renewal brings the program’s total to $50 million over five years.

For 2026, the program focused on groups with annual budgets under $1 million, which raised the average award by about 25%, from $10,753 last year to $13,423.

The change followed a sector analysis by Allen Family Philanthropies and SMU DataArts. It found that smaller arts groups lost an average of one staff position between 2023 and 2024, while organizations with budgets over $1 million added an average of five.

“The incredible reach of this program across our state, along with the significant findings from our report, show just how much this type of flexible support is needed to bolster Washington’s rich and diverse arts and culture sector,” said Lara Littlefield, executive director of Allen Family Philanthropies.

Of this year’s grantees, 496 are in Northwest Washington, 132 in Southwest, 67 in Eastern and 50 in Central Washington. Recipients include 12 of the state’s 29 federally recognized tribes, and more than 22% are in rural counties.

A handful of the organizations blend art and technology, including Tacoma’s Fablab Nonprofit ($25,000), Seattle-based Simulated Immersive Experimental Realities ($15,000) and Bellingham Makerspace ($2,500).

The Old Hotel Art Gallery in Othello, in Adams County, has received a $25,000 grant each year since 2024. The gallery used the money to pay staff a living wage, to keep operating until its annual fundraiser, and to renovate its historic building, which now brings in rental income.

Gallery director Samantha Copas said the 2025 award “truly kept our doors open.”

Allen Family Philanthropies, formerly known as the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation, was founded in 1988 by the late Microsoft co-founder and his sister, Jody Allen. Arts and culture is one of its core program areas, along with youth and the environment. Last year the foundation committed nearly $7 million to eight Seattle Center nonprofits, including KEXP and the Museum of Pop Culture, to expand youth access to the arts.

ArtsFund will hold a virtual webinar in the spring for organizations interested in applying for 2027 grants. Details will be posted here.

#5442. 12 generator safety tips to prevent carbon monoxide poisoning and fires

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 12 generator safety tips cover carbon monoxide, placement, refueling, fuel storage and wiring to help you run a portable generator more safely through a storm outage

A portable generator can solve one problem during a power outage and create a more dangerous one. After a storm, a compact generator can feel like a real rescue, Consumer Reports notes. It can get a refrigerator running again, power a few lights and keep phones and laptops charged until the grid comes back.

That relief comes with a serious hazard. A generator burns fuel and releases exhaust the entire time it runs. Running one indoors or too close to living space can cause carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning. Touching a hot unit can cause burns. Consumer Reports warns that both injuries occur too often during outages and storms.

The Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) identifies CO poisoning as the biggest hazard tied to generators. The gas has no color, no smell and no taste. Someone inside a home where it is building up gets no warning from sight, smell or taste.

Federal data show the toll. CPSC figures record nearly 900 nonfire CO poisoning deaths associated with generators alone between 2012 and 2022. That count covers poisonings only and excludes deaths from fires.

The guidance in this list centers on a handful of practical choices. Where the generator sits matters, along with which way its exhaust points. So do how it gets refueled and how it connects to the home's wiring.

The generator safety tips below take those choices one at a time. They draw on Consumer Reports, the CPSC and National Institutes of Health safety guidelines. Some cover placement, including the minimum distance between a generator and a house and why a garage or basement is never a safe spot. Others cover fuel, from what to do before adding gasoline to how to store extra for a long outage. The rest cover electricity and detection. That includes what a transfer switch does and which extension cords can handle a generator's load. It also includes what a built-in CO shutoff sensor can and cannot catch.

The 12 practices here are a selection from Consumer Reports' generator advice, not a ranking.

A portable generator belongs outdoors, not inside a house, garage or basement. Carbon monoxide from generators run indoors or in partly enclosed spaces causes most generator-related injuries and deaths, according to Consumer Reports.

That finding ties most of the harm to where a generator runs rather than to the machine itself. A generator that is a hazard inside an enclosed room is built to run in open air.

The rule covers more than the rooms where people sleep and eat. Consumer Reports singles out basements and garages as spaces that can hold deadly concentrations of carbon monoxide. Neither one is a safe middle ground between the living area and the yard.

Partly enclosed spaces carry the same risk. Consumer Reports groups them with indoor use as the setting for most generator injuries and deaths. A location that is only partly closed in does not count as outdoors.

A portable generator should sit at least 20 feet from your home, with its engine exhaust pointed away from the building. Consumer Reports gives 20 feet as the minimum distance.

The guidance has two parts, and each does a separate job. Distance puts open space between the running engine and the walls of the house. Exhaust direction controls where the fumes go once they leave the engine.

One part does not replace the other. A unit parked 20 feet out but aimed at the house still sends its exhaust toward the people inside. A unit pointed the right way but set up beside a wall still releases fumes close to the living space.

That exhaust carries carbon monoxide (CO). Consumer Reports warns that running a generator too close to living space can lead to CO poisoning.

The 20-foot figure is a minimum, not a target. A generator placed closer than that falls short of the guidance, even if it sits outdoors.

Generator exhaust needs to stay clear of any path into the house, and a working carbon monoxide detector inside the home adds a second layer of protection. Placement limits how much gas reaches living space. The detector warns people indoors about a threat their own senses cannot pick up.

Open doors and windows are the weak points. Exhaust that drifts through an open doorway or window can carry carbon monoxide into a room even while the machine itself stays outdoors. Setting the generator up so that no opening sits in the path of its exhaust keeps the gas moving away from the building rather than into it.

A detector covers what placement misses. An alarm mounted inside the home sounds where people are, not out where the generator sits. That warning counts most in rooms where people may not be alert to their surroundings, such as a bedroom at night.

The two measures guard against different failures. Careful placement keeps exhaust out of the house in the first place. The indoor detector is the backstop if some of that gas still reaches the rooms where people are sleeping, working or cleaning up.

An inverter generator can put out lethal concentrations of carbon monoxide (CO), just as a standard portable generator can. The Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) applies that warning to both types of portable generator.

The CPSC warning makes no exception for inverter models. Either type can produce enough CO to kill.

The choice between a standard unit and an inverter unit does not change the carbon monoxide risk. The precautions that apply to a standard portable generator apply to an inverter model in the same way. An inverter unit belongs outdoors and away from the home, under the same rules as any other portable generator.

Switch a gas-powered generator off and give it time to cool before adding fuel. Gasoline that spills onto a hot engine can catch fire, Consumer Reports warns.

The fire risk is concentrated in the moment of pouring. A tank filled while the engine is running, or seconds after shutdown, puts any stray fuel right next to hot engine parts. A splash or an overfill that would do no harm on a cold engine becomes a fire hazard on a hot one.

The cooling period also protects the person doing the refueling. Letting the unit cool cuts the chance of a burn, according to Consumer Reports. Refueling brings hands and arms close to the engine. A generator that has been switched off can still be hot.

The same shutdown-and-wait step applies every time the tank needs more fuel during an outage. One pause before each refill addresses both the fire risk and the burn risk.

Spare gasoline for a portable generator should go only into an ANSI-approved container and be stored somewhere cool with good ventilation. Consumer Reports recommends keeping extra fuel on hand in case a power outage runs long.

A gas-powered generator runs only as long as its fuel supply lasts. Fuel already in storage lets the unit keep running through an extended outage without a trip to find more.

ANSI stands for the American National Standards Institute. Consumer Reports names an ANSI-approved container as the only acceptable place to keep spare generator fuel. An improvised jug or other unapproved vessel does not meet that guidance.

The storage spot needs to be cool and well-ventilated, according to Consumer Reports.

A fuel reserve does not last forever. Gasoline kept for too long can degrade, Consumer Reports notes. An emergency supply set aside for outages does not stay usable indefinitely.

A portable generator should never be brought inside the home during storm or flood cleanup. Consumer Reports gives this rule without exception for households dealing with water damage.

The guidance targets a specific moment in recovery. Consumer Reports notes that homeowners caught up in cleanup after water damage may feel pulled to set a generator up inside the living space. Its answer is direct: this should never be done.

Bringing the machine indoors for the job exposes the people doing the cleanup to two separate hazards. The first is carbon monoxide poisoning from the engine's exhaust. The second is burns from touching the hot unit.

The risk does not depend on the generator sitting in the middle of a room. Running one too close to the living space can also cause carbon monoxide poisoning, according to Consumer Reports. A unit set just inside a doorway or tucked against the house to be near the work falls into the same danger zone.

Both injuries occur too often during storms and outages, according to Consumer Reports. Those are the same conditions that send households looking for backup power in the first place.

For recovery work, the generator stays outside the living space for the entire cleanup. Moving it in, even briefly to run lights for the job, puts everyone in the house at risk.

A portable generator with an automatic carbon monoxide (CO) safety shutoff adds built-in protection against the hazard that the Consumer Product Safety Commission ranks as the biggest danger of generator use. Consumer Reports discusses this CO-shutoff technology in its guidance on getting through storm outages safely.

The feature relies on a sensor built into the generator itself. The sensor is part of the machine, not a separate device placed inside the house. When it detects carbon monoxide building up, the shutoff stops the engine.

The response is automatic. The generator does not need an owner to notice a problem before it acts. Generator exhaust carries CO, and the shutoff is designed to act on that exhaust at the source.

A shutoff adds to safe placement rather than replacing it. The generator still belongs outdoors, away from the home.

A generator's built-in carbon monoxide shutoff sensor responds only to the air around the machine, according to Paolo Fu, the engineer who heads generator testing at Consumer Reports. That limit means the feature does not make running a generator indoors or near a home safe.

Fu explains that the sensor is built into the generator itself. In his account, it reacts to the conditions surrounding the unit and nothing beyond them.

That leaves a gap whenever exhaust travels away from the machine. Fu describes the risk this way: "If the generator is spewing exhaust to another part of your home, CO levels there may rise to dangerous levels before the sensor registers much of anything."

The sensor and the people inside a house can be breathing very different air. Exhaust can collect in a room the sensor never reaches, while the air next to the generator gives it little to register.

A generator with a shutoff still belongs outdoors, away from the house. The feature works at the machine. It does not replace safe placement.

A transfer switch is the link between a portable generator and a home's circuit panel. Consumer Reports describes it as equipment made for portable generators of 5,000 watts or more. With one in place, the generator can run hardwired appliances.

Hardwired appliances are wired into the home's circuits rather than plugged into an outlet. A generator can reach them only through a connection to the circuit panel. The transfer switch provides that connection.

The switch also changes how plug-in appliances get power. Once a generator feeds the panel through a transfer switch, plug-in devices no longer need extension cords running out to the generator.

The point where a generator meets a home's wiring also carries a separate electrical hazard. A portable generator that is the wrong size, or that is set up or run incorrectly, can push electricity back into the power lines. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention describes this as backfeed or feedback.

When a generator is connected to a household circuit, current can travel backward through that circuit and out into the power grid. Its voltage can rise along the way. That current could electrocute a worker repairing the lines.

The risk extends beyond utility crews. Backfeed can also seriously injure or kill people in nearby buildings.

Line workers are expected to treat power lines as live until the lines have been de-energized and grounded.

Without a transfer switch, a portable generator should power appliances only through its own outlets. Consumer Reports advises plugging each appliance directly into the generator whenever possible.

A direct connection isn't always practical. An appliance may sit too far from the spot outdoors where the generator has to run. In that case, Consumer Reports calls for a heavy-duty extension cord rated for outdoor use.

A heavy-duty build is only part of the requirement. Every extension cord carries a rating, expressed in watts or amps. That rating needs to be at least as high as the combined electrical load of every appliance plugged into the cord.

The key word is combined. A cord running a refrigerator and a few lamps has to handle all of them at once, not just the single largest appliance. Totaling the wattage or amperage of everything on the cord gives the figure to match against the cord's rating.

Plugging straight into the generator takes the extension cord out of the setup entirely. With no cord in the chain, there is no cord rating to check.

The approach also keeps the generator off a home's wiring. A portable generator that is the wrong size, or is set up or run incorrectly, can push electricity back into the power lines. This is known as backfeed, or feedback.

Connecting a generator to a household circuit is one way it happens. Current can flow in reverse through that circuit and into the power grid, rising in voltage as it goes. At that point it could electrocute a worker repairing the lines.

Backfeed carries a risk of serious injury or death for utility repair crews. People in nearby buildings face that risk too. Utility workers should treat any power line as live unless it has been de-energized and grounded.

A household with no transfer switch keeps its own wiring out of the picture this way. Appliances go into the generator's outlets, or onto a properly rated outdoor cord, and nowhere else.

Carbon monoxide from a generator can kill in as little as five minutes if levels are high enough. Consumer Reports cites that timeline from National Institutes of Health safety guidelines.

The figure comes with a condition. The five-minute window applies only when carbon monoxide concentrations are high enough. It shows how fast a poisoning can turn fatal. It does not describe how every exposure unfolds.

The gas gives off no odor. That leaves the people inside a home without the cue they would normally rely on to notice engine fumes.

Those two facts work together. A poison that can act within minutes, and that a person cannot smell, can reach a fatal level before anyone in the house realizes something is wrong. The time between a safe room and a dangerous one can be shorter than the time it takes to recognize a problem.

Dangerous concentrations come from exhaust collecting in an enclosed or partly enclosed space. The five-minute timeline is the reason that matters so much. Once the gas is inside, there may be little or no time left to respond.

That is why generator safety centers on keeping exhaust out of living space from the start. Noticing carbon monoxide after it has built up is not a dependable defense against a gas that can kill this quickly.

#5441. Most work doesn’t need the Ferrari of AI, Wharton and Accenture find, but companies may be paying for it anyway

When companies unleash AI agents, they like to reach for the shiniest, newest, and most powerful model and use it for every job task. A new joint report from the Wharton School and Accenture published Monday suggests that might be overkill.

The landmark new report, What Does Agentic AI Really Cost?, studied more than 18,000 tasks and work activities across 923 occupations. More than 90% of tasks in the framework that AI agents could take over are routine enough for the less expensive models. Moreover, in each of the 19 industries studied, only 6% to 11% of the work AI agents could do is complex enough to typically need a bleeding edge “frontier” model, according to the research findings. Meaning, complex tasks that need frontier models are a small portion of the workflow.

Yet, Eric Bradlow, vice dean of AI and analytics at Wharton and a coauthor of the report, said he doubts most companies are making that distinction.

“I don’t even think most companies are thinking about deploying differential models for different parts of the workflow,” Bradlow told Fortune. “I think they’re taking possibly their most sophisticated model and applying it to all of the workflow.”

That may not deliver the best return, he said, “because certain tasks, a large fraction of tasks, just do not require the more sophisticated models.”

Bradlow said people often seek out the latest—and usually marketed as the greatest—model.

“Most people tend to want to have, I’ll call it the shiniest object,” he said. “But for most tasks, actually, you don’t.”

To reach their findings, the researchers classified which tasks an AI agent could undertake, weighing how much human interaction and physical activity each task involved. That left 11,339 tasks. They scored each on five measures of complexity including how many interdependent steps it involves; whether legal, regulatory, or audit requirements apply; how many computer systems it affects; whether it needs sensitive data; and, how much data it needs.

James Crowley, Accenture’s Americas industry and enterprise lead and a coauthor, said complexity isn’t only about raw-computing difficulty. A task can be complex because of “the workflow navigation, or the number of systems you touch, or the regulations,” he said.

For instance, in life sciences, tasks that scored as complex included developing quality-control systems for production and drafting legal documents like patent applications. Tasks that ranked lower included enrolling people in programs and drafting copy.

“It’s not an argument against frontier models,” noted Crowley. “They remain essential for complex, specialized, high-stakes work.”

In the capital markets, tech, and aerospace, the report found that higher-volume tasks tend to be more complex and a better fit for frontier models more often. Crowley pointed to aerospace and defense companies trying to raise production rates, which requires close tracking of certifications, quality, and the availability of huge amounts of parts across complicated supplier networks. That’s “an extremely complex task, super high value,” he said.

Bradlow pointed to research and development in health care, where AI can help detect promising mixes of molecules. Those tasks are complex and expensive, said Bradlow, but the return for a company could lead to billions in revenue.

The choice of model is an important one because AI compute is among the largest costs in most of the report’s industry estimates and one of the main reasons cost can differ dramatically between industries. For a company with 100,000 employees running 35 agents, estimated five-year costs range from about $155 million in health care to about $520 million in insurance.

And while AI models are getting cheaper, total spending is on its way up, said Bradlow.

“If I ask it to do something from a year ago, it’s cheaper to do it today,” he said. “But I’m asking it to do 100 different things I wasn’t asking it to do a year ago. So my total cost is going up” even as “my per-task cost is going down.”

Crowley and Bradlow emphasized that companies should track what AI costs alongside the value it generates, in what the report calls an AI P&L, or profit and loss statement.

“The minute you start thinking of a P&L, it changes,” said Bradlow. It can also do away with the thinking that using an LLM isn’t an expense. People think, “I’ll just use this LLM because it’s quote-unquote free,” he explained. “No, it’s not. It’s not free.”

The report recommends deciding what model capability each agent needs at the design stage, before it is built. Dynamic model routing, in which tasks are sent to different models as the work runs, is difficult to track in live operations and few enterprises can run it at scale, wrote the authors. The report is the third in a series published jointly by Wharton and Accenture.

Crowley said switching between models is technically doable. The challenge, however, is that “the model choice often happens too late.”

“People tend to use the model that they already have access to rather than what’s best suited to the task,” said Crowley.

Bradlow expects that to change. He envisions AI systems that can take in a request, break it into parts, and send each part to the right model on their own.

“We’re not 100% there yet,” he said. “It’s coming, and it’s coming sooner than later” because “the customer’s going to demand greater ROI, and one way to do it is to lower costs by using less sophisticated models.”

Amanda Gerut is the west coast editor at Fortune, overseeing publicly traded businesses, executive compensation, Securities and Exchange Commission regulations, and investigations.

#5440. Data center developers brace for new reality as election backlash sinks in

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 10, 2026 at 10:25 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:41 am

Data center developers already knew they had a public relations problem. This month’s midterm elections showed how much of a political problem it has become.

Voters approved data center restrictions in 44 of 45 local measures across a dozen states. Candidates who support stronger regulation of the facilities won 32 of the 34 gubernatorial races called so far. And political campaigns reportedly spent more than $380 million on TV ads referencing data centers, according to the Associated Press.

The results capped a year of accelerating resistance as tech giants plan to spend hundreds of billions of dollars on new facilities.

So what comes next? More outreach, more transparency and the expectation that states and local governments will pass data center rules, said leaders in the Pacific Northwest.

“We’ve been working and adapting our approach to meet the moment,” said John Wilson, chief financial officer of Sabey Data Centers, in an interview. “There used to be a time where we would say that our track record could speak for itself, and that’s clearly no longer the case.”

Communities nationwide have raised concerns about the facilities’ effect on rising electric bills, their water use for cooling electronics and the noise they generate.

Broader fears about artificial intelligence are also stoking the pushback, including worries that it will replace workers and appropriate human-created content, and that it can provide erroneous information, foster unhealthy relationships with users, or facilitate scams or terrorist attacks.

A renewed effort to regulate data centers is expected in January in Washington state — home to the headquarters of Sabey, Microsoft and Amazon.

Earlier this year, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, pushed legislation that included ratepayer protections, transparency on environmental impacts and clean energy requirements. Microsoft and the national Data Center Coalition opposed the bill, which failed.

“It’s going to be a very tech-heavy session,” Doglio said.

Before voters weighed in this month, tech companies launched efforts to assuage public fears.

In January, Microsoft released its “Community First AI Infrastructure” initiative, which includes promises to pay the company’s full power costs, reject local property tax breaks, replenish more water than it uses, train local workers and fund AI education and community programs.

Last month, Amazon announced its “Built Together” program, pledging to invest $1 billion over five years in the U.S. communities where it operates data centers, including support for education and civic projects. The initiative offers similar commitments to Microsoft’s on transparency and covering its energy costs.

Wilson said Sabey also works with communities to understand and meet their needs. When a proposed campus in Indianapolis triggered significant pushback, the company brought community members to Quincy, a central Washington data center hub, to tour a Sabey facility and hear from locals about their experience.

“It requires a lot of patience. It requires a lot of transparency in our communication,” Wilson said. Sabey’s Decatur Technology Park in Indianapolis is moving ahead, and the company aims to bring it online in 2030.

But the even bigger challenge now is statewide moratoriums and data center bans — a scale of resistance that is difficult to address even when there is local support.

Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. Umatilla, where Sabey is developing its first Oregon campus, declared a local state of emergency over the potential loss of investment and revenue, the Oregon Capital Chronicle reported.

Even with the surge in resistance, “we’ve been able to find our way through on every project that we’ve had,” Wilson said. “I’m knocking on wood as I say that.”

Corporate commitments alone may no longer be enough to win public confidence, said Brad Smith, Microsoft vice chair and president, in a GeekWire interview. Communities increasingly want laws requiring all data center developers to build responsibly — a shift he called a “watershed” moment, “but one we anticipated.”

“[P]eople want to see everyone who builds a data center do it in a responsible way,” Smith added, “and they feel that the only way that one can obtain that result is to have some new laws that are put in place.”

Come next year, that could include Washington and impact local tech giants, Sabey and others. Baxtel, a data center industry research firm, lists 29 Microsoft facilities operating in Washington and four under construction, with Sabey operating eight facilities.

Amazon plans to build its first large-scale data centers in Washington, with proposed campuses in Walla Walla County and the Tri-Cities. Amazon did not respond to repeated requests for comment on this story.

Doglio said the next version of her bill will be more stringent. “We have to have a strong bill,” she said, adding that the public and members of her party are calling for it. Microsoft did not publicly specify which provisions triggered its opposition to the previous bill.

Wilson hopes any legislation, in Washington or elsewhere, allows flexibility and recognizes that data centers vary widely in size, impact and application. Sabey provides data center space and infrastructure for customers ranging from major cloud companies to corporations and community organizations.

“Describing all data centers as one thing is just not accurate,” Wilson said, “and it doesn’t understand the realities of the industry itself.”

Smith expressed optimism that U.S. lawmakers can find a middle ground that meets the needs of communities and tech companies.

“There’s plenty of room to draft laws that enable people to go forward and build responsible data centers without chilling the economic contributions these data centers make, especially to local communities,” he said.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5439. Gen Z and millennials will make up half of holiday spending just in time for the great consumer tradedown

American shoppers are hunting for cheaper stores harder than at any point since the pandemic-throttled period of early 2021, according to Bank of America card data. By BofA’s measure, they’re trading down more now than at any point since 2022, including June of that year, when inflation peaked at 9.1%, the biggest jump in more than 40 years.

It should make for a particularly diminished holiday spending season, as millennials and Gen Z come of age in the economy of the 2020s. The two cohorts now account for 50% of holiday spending, a first in Deloitte’s annual holiday survey, and both groups are planning double-digit increases this year.

At the same time, BofA finds that since 2022, millennials have been trading down faster than Gen X or baby boomers, particularly in apparel and groceries, “suggesting greater sensitivity to rising costs.” Apparel shows some of the clearest trading down overall, and the bank said some households may be putting off clothing purchases and “shopping closer to need.”

BofA Institute’s Spending Tier Composite, built from card and deposit data on apparel, dining, groceries and travel, tracks how much spending goes to value-tier merchants. It “suggests consumers are trading down at the highest level since 2021,” the bank wrote Nov. 9. “Rather than spending less, many appear to be changing where – and how – they spend.”

Hunting for deals doesn’t mean spending less. Deloitte classifies 38% of shoppers as “holiday value seekers” who chase promotions, redeem rewards and buy store brands. They expect to spend 12% more than other shoppers. Gen Z and millennials also report better household finances than a year ago, after pulling back last year, Deloitte said.

In Deloitte’s survey, households earning $200,000 or more plan to spend $3,607 on the holidays, more than five times the $693 planned by households under $50,000. Goldman Sachs economist Pierfrancesco Mei recently wrote that benefit cuts, softer nominal wage growth and bigger exposure to gas prices weighed disproportionately on lower-income households in 2026. Middle- and higher-income households held up better because they captured most of the boost from last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

The National Retail Federation expects November and December retail sales to grow 4.2% to $1.01 trillion, after a 3.1% gain last year. NRF chief economist Mark Mathews said “inflation, rising gas prices and pressure on household spending will affect consumers differently across income groups.”

Mastercard SpendingPulse forecasts 5.5% growth from Nov. 1 to Dec. 24, excluding autos and gas. It estimates “about half the growth in spending will be due to higher prices.” In other words, it’s only bigger on paper; it won’t be a holiday season full of more stuff, just more expensive stuff.

In NRF’s October survey of 8,094 adults, 56% said the economy will affect their holiday spending. Among those, 43% plan to shop sales more often. Discount stores are on the list for 43% of all holiday shoppers.

Real disposable income fell 0.3% in September, and PCE prices were up 3.6% from a year earlier, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis.

Goldman expects spending to hold up anyway. In a Nov. 9 note, Mei estimated spending will rise 2.5% in 2026 (fourth quarter over fourth quarter) and 2.2% in 2027. He called the consumer “more resilient than looked likely when the Iran war began and energy prices spiked.” Higher inflation hasn’t been matched by faster wage growth this year, so Goldman forecasts real disposable income growth of just 1.4% in 2026. It expects that to pick up to 2.3% in 2027 as price pressure from tariffs, energy and AI-related costs fades, and as higher net interest income and cost-of-living adjustments to Social Security and other transfers kick in.

The cushion is thinner than in 2021. The personal saving rate hit 26.2% in March 2021, the month the third round of stimulus checks began going out, and was still 6.8% that December, according to BEA data compiled by the St. Louis Fed. It was 3.8% in September. Goldman estimates the true rate is “closer to 5%” once timelier source data are counted.

Spending has also had help from the stock market. Goldman estimates the wealth effect added over 0.4 percentage point to spending growth in 2026. It expects about half that next year, and says the effect “could weigh on spending if AI-related stocks continue to decline.”

Travel is the exception in BofA’s data. There, some households “may be opting out of trips entirely rather than shifting to lower-cost options.”

#5437. AI companies are putting technologists in charge of HR. A Wharton professor says that’s a mistake

OpenAI is doing it. Anthropic is, too: Putting technologists and product operations people in charge of HR is the latest trend among AI-native companies. But Wharton professor of management Peter Cappelli has a warning for companies looking to follow suit: Give the general counsel a heads-up, because “they’re going to be busy.”

His concern? Companies are betting that technical expertise will translate into better people management, when the two require fundamentally different skills.

“I think [organizations] are expecting that technologists will come in there and sprinkle some pixie dust, and then in a little while, all the problems will be gone,” Cappelli says.

While researching his book, Our Least Important Asset, Cappelli examined why companies struggle to manage their people. One culprit, he found, is that many executives are engineers by training, and companies have largely abandoned the management development programs that once taught them how to lead.

Engineers and technologists tend to approach problems through optimization, Cappelli says. But when applied to managing people, that mindset can prioritize cutting headcount over developing and supporting employees—an approach that risks creating more problems than it solves.

That doesn’t mean technologists can’t become effective HR leaders, Cappelli says. But they need to learn the fundamentals of people management first, perhaps through a rotational assignment on an HR team before taking the top job.

For HR leaders worried about being replaced by technologists, Cappelli recommends demonstrating value by helping companies navigate the AI transition and positioning oneself as an expert in change management.

“If you show them a couple of successes, then they’re going to think you’re doing fine,” Cappelli says. “But if you can’t do anything and you’re wringing your hands, then you probably will get replaced.”

This week, Kai Werner, CHRO at software company TeamViewer, answers your burning workplace questions. Responses have been edited for length and clarity.

Q: I’ve been in the same role at my company for about two years. Recently, my boss told me he’s overhauling my position by moving me to a new project, changing nearly all of my day-to-day tasks, and adding more responsibilities.

I don’t feel I have the skills for this new work. What’s more, I’m not interested. It isn’t something I’m passionate about, and I don’t see how it will help my career grow. What recourse do I have? Do I have to accept this new role, or can I push back and keep things as they are?

A: The most helpful first step is to have an open and honest conversation with your boss. Changes like this rarely come out of nowhere, and you may not have the full picture. Ask why he chose you for this role and what strengths he sees in you. It’s also worth discussing what success would look like. Then, share your concerns openly, including any skills you'd need to develop and questions about how this could shape your career.

Your company has a genuine interest in helping you do work you feel good about and finding a role where you can thrive. Hiring and training someone new takes time, so most managers would prefer to explore a solution that works for everyone. That might mean training, a gradual transition, or expanding responsibilities while keeping some of the work you enjoy. Bringing ideas along with your concerns shows that you care about finding a positive solution.

You're absolutely free to push back; however, work circumstances can change. It's helpful to keep in mind that things may not stay exactly as they are.

I'd also encourage you to stay open minded. Your boss may see strengths in you that you haven't recognized yet, and work that doesn't feel exciting right now could become a valuable opportunity that opens unexpected doors.
