#5422. I helped grow a steel company from $750 million to $12 billion. CEOs should use AI before they grade employees on it

Geoff Woods is the founder of AI Leadership, which helps companies accelerate growth by aligning strategy and execution with AI, and the author of The AI-Driven Leader. He was previously chief growth officer at Jindal Steel & Power, where he helped grow the company’s market cap from $750 million to over $12 billion in four years. AI Leadership sells the kind of AI training this piece recommends.

“Raise your hand if your executive team has mandated the use of AI.”

I was standing on stage at the annual Great Places to Work convention in Las Vegas, and every one of the 500 CHROs I was in front of put their hands up. These were all HR leaders in mid-market and enterprise companies.

“Now, keep your hands up if every single person on your executive team is using AI to make themselves more valuable.”

I ask this question at every speaking engagement, and I’ve seen a pattern–and a problem. Company leaders are mandating the use of AI. With that mandate, they’re expecting increases in the productivity of their workforce. But they’re not holding themselves to the same standard.

Executives often think that “leading AI” in their organizations means delegating the adoption and strategy of it to IT, a Chief AI Officer, or an outside consultant. That’s not delegation–that’s abdication.

CEOs and executive teams need to learn to use AI, and become AI-driven leaders, before they can build AI-driven organizations.

I say this as I’m starting to see companies increasingly tying AI goals and skills directly to employee raises and promotions. Should compensation be tied to AI skill? It depends on the company. If you’re an organization that typically ties performance to specific skills that will grow in value, it makes sense. If you don’t, it’s a break from precedent–but it doesn’t mean it’s the wrong move.

What does concern me is when a CEO who doesn’t use AI is the one making the call. And by “use AI,” I don’t mean to help them write better emails–I mean truly leveraging it to think strategically and make themselves more valuable. Without that experience, a leader will limit their vision for what AI can actually do for their organization. It’s tough to describe color when you’ve only seen black and white.

The first time I saw AI, it was December 2022. I was the Chief Growth Officer at Jindal Steel, and ChatGPT had been out for about two weeks.

And like most leaders, I said to myself, “I’m really busy. I’ll revisit this later.”

Like any good executive, I then thought about delegation. “I have a huge IT department,” I thought. “I’ll delegate this to them. Or maybe we will hire a consulting company to do it for us.”

Then I remembered a quote from my college mentor: “Focus on mastering the skills that are so valuable, they’ll serve you no matter where you go.” At that moment, I knew AI would be one of those skills.

That cemented my thinking. I needed to learn more about this myself, not delegate it.

I started with a simple commitment. Use AI once a day, every day. Very quickly, I realized I was using it for things that really didn’t matter, like writing better emails. Last time I checked, I never received a promotion for the quality of my emails. I had this realization that I was using AI to major in the minors. Then I started to wonder, what would it look like to major in the majors?

I started thinking about the skills I had that truly enabled me to deliver the most value. One of them was the ability to ask leaders the right strategic questions to unlock new levels of growth. In that moment, I realized I was asking AI questions like it was Google. I wondered what it would look like if I had AI ask me questions instead as a thought partner to elevate how I think and shift how I lead.

That was the game changer. I started using AI to elevate how I think, which shifted how I was leading within Jindal Steel.

A few months into my AI use, I was talking with Naveen Jindal, the Chairman of Jindal Steel. I told him how I was using AI for strategy instead of tactics, and he asked to see an example. I opened up my AI tool using the CRIT framework I’d developed, which stands for “Context,” “Role,” “Interview,” and “Task.”

CONTEXT Attached is our annual strategic plan. (Which I attached into a secure instance of ChatGPT). ROLE Your role is to act as an aggressive, growth-minded board member with deep expertise in the steel industry, vertically integrated from distribution to mining.

INTERVIEW Interview me. Ask me one question at a time, up to five questions, to understand where our plan may be insufficient to deliver results to the market.

TASK Tell me where our plan may be insufficient to deliver the expected results and the actions we can take over the next 30 days to deliver on our next earnings call.

AI started asking one sharp question at a time. Questions that only someone who knew our industry would ask. It pulled out all of the context that was in our heads. Then it laid out a real analysis of where the plan could break.

Naveen’s mind was blown. “This is incredible,” he said. I agreed and suggested we should drive it through the whole company and that he should lead it as Chairman.

The problem was, I knew almost nothing about AI. But I knew the power of asking the right questions. I asked, “Who could I get into a relationship with that could enable me to drive this across our company?”

That led to a partnership with Google, where I learned a lot about the tech–and the more I learned about it, the less I realized how much the tech mattered. You can have the greatest technology in the world, but if you don’t win the hearts and minds of your people to harness the technology, you’ll never unlock the value. It became clear that AI adoption was about leadership.

Over my time at Jindal, the market cap grew from $750 million to $12 billion over a four year period. This was done with the right strategic thinking—thinking that AI directly supported throughout the company.

That is not about AI. It’s about the right strategic thinking. AI became supportive of that

I went all-in on the leadership aspect of AI, to the point where I resigned from Jindal Steel, wrote a book about what I learned, and turned it into a company.

One of the questions I get asked often is, “If a CEO wanted to start this week, what’s the first piece of their own work they should test with AI?”

Start by asking yourself something you’re already asking anyway: “What’s the biggest problem facing our company–the one that would unlock huge growth if you solved it?”

That question gets you focused on the 20% of work that drives 80% of your results.

Then, ask how AI can help. Write a prompt using CRIT: Describe the context in detail, tell AI what kind of expert you wish could advise you, have it interview you one question at a time, and give it a task, like, “Give me the top three high-impact, non-obvious strategies I could deploy to solve this problem.”

Here’s the biggest piece of advice: Don’t take the AI response at face value. Tell AI what you like, don’t like, and would change about the response, and keep iterating on it until you’re confident enough to act.

When you’re using AI as a thought partner, it becomes much easier to judge whether your people are using it in a way that improves how they think and moves the business forward.

Most companies are measuring AI adoption through usage metrics (i.e. “80% of our workforce is using AI every week”). That’s a good place to start, but it doesn’t tell you whether people are actually using AI for high-value work. If you look closer, you’ll probably find that most of that usage is small tasks that don’t make anyone valuable to the company.

The better test is to inspect what you expect. When your team walks you through how they solved a problem, ask how they used AI as part of the process. The ones who have bought into AI as a thought partner will be able to tell how it sharpened their thinking, or helped them see blind spots they would have missed.

If all they can describe is time saved on emails and summarizing meeting notes, they’re complying with your adoption mandate, but haven’t really seen what AI can do for them.

You can only coach people if you’ve done the work–and the learning–yourself.

If your company has already tied compensation or raises to AI, take another look at what you’re measuring. If it’s just usage, you’re not tracking the skill that matters. The AI skills worth rewarding are the ones that will keep growing in value: the strategic thinking, or the great line of questioning.

And if you’re a leader, be honest about whether your own pay is being held to the same standard as everyone else’s.

The next time I ask the question about whether an executive team is using AI to make themselves more valuable, I’m looking for every hand to stay up.

#5421. This Popular Wearable Now Has Its Own Social Network. Every Account Has a ‘Verified Heartbeat.’

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Bots are barred from this social network.

Whoop, the consumer technology company making screenless fitness bands, wants to track more than just your heart rate.

The fitness tracker company launched a social network this week called Whoop Humans, and claims in a recent press release that the feature is “the most verifiably human social network.”

“In a world that’s becoming increasingly artificial, we’re building something deeply human,” said Will Ahmed, founder and CEO of Whoop, in the press release. “Every account represents a real person with a verified heartbeat. They have real goals, challenges, and achievements. That’s what makes Whoop Humans different, and it’s a big area of investment for us.”

Here’s how it works: Whoop members can follow friends, family and other Whoop-wearing people on the wearable’s accompanying app. They can share workout, sleep and recovery milestones in posts. Members can write comments and express reactions within the app.

Whoop designed the network to help customers cheer on each other’s progress and check in with each other if the data is concerning.

Whoop Humans rolled out earlier this week on the app. It’s all up to the user if they want to participate.

Whoop member Mika Bublitz said that the social network allows members to give their friends a boost.

“Sometimes people don’t tell you when they’re not feeling their best,” Bublitz said in the press release. “If I see a friend’s Recovery is low, I can check in and say, ‘Hey, it’s okay to take it easy today.’ That’s what I like about Whoop Humans. It gives us another way to look out for each other.”

Whoop’s fitness bands have become popular. According to the company, more than three million members are part of Whoop’s network and own a wearable. The press release adds that members open the Whoop app more than eight times per day, an indicator of the app’s popularity among people who own a Whoop device.

Whoop sells annual memberships ranging from $199 to $359, each bundled with a wrist-worn fitness tracker. The device monitors sleep, heart rate and stress, with the aim of helping users improve their health and athletic performance. Its battery lasts two weeks on a single charge.

Ahmed has been building the company for 14 years.

“It took a very long time to be an overnight success,” he said in an interview on the All-In Podcast last month. “It took about 12 years for us to get to a million members, and then another 18 months or so to two million, about six months to three million. We expect to end the year around four million members.”

Research published by Whoop last year in the journal Sensors found that people who wore the Whoop wearable every day clocked in more than 90 additional minutes of exercise per week. Daily wearers also logged about 20 extra minutes of sleep per night, or over two extra hours of sleep per week. The study analyzed 12 weeks of data from nearly 12,000 Whoop members.

Whoop faces competition from Google, which released a screenless wearable earlier this year for $100 called the Fitbit Air. Apple is also reportedly developing a similar screenless device.

#5420. Warren Buffett is giving $5.4 billion to his family foundations for Thanksgiving. His advice to everyone else: ‘Be a benefactor for someone else’

Warren Buffett kept his Thanksgiving message short this year, but the amount he gave was anything but small.

The 96-year-old Berkshire Hathaway chairman emeritus is converting 6,150 Class A shares into 9,225,000 Class B shares and donating them to four of his family’s foundations, according to a Berkshire release published Monday. At the latest Class B price, the donation is worth an eye-popping $5.4 billion.

The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation (named in honor of Warren’s first wife) will receive shares worth about $2.2 billion. The Sherwood Foundation (led by Warren’s daughter, Susan), the Howard G. Buffett Foundation (run by Warren’s son), and the NoVo Foundation (run by Warren’s other son, Peter) will each get shares worth a little more than $1 billion.

“Today’s gift is consistent with the plan I have previously described,” Warren Buffett wrote in his annual Thanksgiving letter. “All my Berkshire shares will be donated to the four foundations, with the goal of growing the grants each year.”

He said whether he reaches that goal will largely depend on how the stock market performs between now and his target date. He also said he has full confidence in his three children: “I trust 100% both their abilities and their fidelity.”

After this gift, Buffett will still own 182,140 Class A shares and 1,162 Class B shares, according to the release. That’s still worth more than $160 billion, assuming the most recent price.

Buffett said shareholders heard “plenty” from him in September, when he stepped down as Berkshire’s chairman and handed the role to Howard. So he kept this year’s letter brief, writing that his confidence in the company “is as strong as ever.”

Instead, he returned to one idea from last year’s message: Kindness is “costless but also priceless.” A year later, Buffett added that it “compounds, and at a better rate than anything Charlie and I ever bought,” a reference to his late business partner Charlie Munger. He said both men received enormous benefits at no cost from teachers such as economist Ben Graham, lawyer and businessman Joe Rosenfield, and longtime Capital Cities CEO Tom Murphy. Those benefits helped them prosper and let them pass many of them on.

“Much of my good fortune has come in the form of people who were kind to me and expected nothing in return,” Buffett wrote. “I’m grateful to every one of them.”

“This Thanksgiving, thank one of those selfless people in your own life,” he continued. “Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else.”

This is the second time this year Buffett has sent a major round of giving to his family’s foundations. In July, he left the Gates Foundation out of his summer donation for the first time since 2006 and directed roughly $6 billion in Berkshire shares to the four family foundations instead. Over two decades, he had given the Gates Foundation about $48 billion.

The break came as more details emerged about Bill Gates’ relationship with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. In June, the Wall Street Journal reported Buffett was holding off on his Gates gift until an external review of the foundation’s dealings with Epstein was finished. Buffett later told CNBC Gates’ actions with Epstein were “distasteful.”

That review, conducted by law firm WilmerHale, found the foundation met with Epstein about 30 times between 2011 and 2014, even though staff had raised concerns. It found no evidence the foundation paid Epstein or knew of his criminal activity.

To be sure, Buffett hasn’t framed the change in his philanthropic giving as purely a response to the Epstein-Gates ties. He told CNBC in July that his children are getting older and are ready to distribute his wealth, and he sped up his giving timeline. In his July announcement, he wrote his remaining shares will go to the four foundations “one way or the other by December 31, 2034.” He had also said in 2024 that the Gates Foundation wouldn’t receive money from his estate after his death.

That means billions more will flow through his family’s foundations in the coming years, which could have an outsized effect in Buffett’s hometown in Omaha, Neb. Steve Isom, COO and CFO of nonprofit software company Bloomerang, who is also based in Omaha, previously told Fortune that family foundations such as Sherwood already fund a large share of Nebraska’s nonprofits.

“This is this example where it’s going to be this hyper, hyper concentrated [giving] in a populace of like roughly a million people,” Isom said.

Isom said Sherwood has been bringing in consultants and running feasibility studies with nonprofits to gauge “how much money could you ingest and actually still be productive.”

Sydney Lake is an associate editor at Fortune, where she writes and edits news for the publication's global news desk.

#5419. AWS gives developers a free local stand-in for its cloud, built from scratch by AI agents

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 10:51 amNovember 11, 2026 at 10:52 am

AWS says its engineers didn’t write or review a single line of code in its newest developer tool, and the company is touting that as a selling point.

AWS Emulator, released Wednesday, simulates AWS services on a developer’s own machine. It’s built from more than 400 API models covering more than 200 AWS services. Developers and AI coding agents can use it to test code without a network connection and without paying for the real cloud.

The tool addresses a problem that coding agents such as Amazon’s Kiro and Anthropic’s Claude Code have made worse. Agents can write code faster than teams can test it against the real cloud. Agents check their work by running the code and reading the results, over and over, and doing that in the cloud adds delays and costs.

The emulator lets them run that loop on a developer’s own machine.

In an ironic or perhaps appropriate twist, AWS used AI agents to build the emulator. Agents also maintain it, testing it against real AWS and fixing the gaps they find.

“The emulator was written entirely by autonomous agents. Our team hasn’t written or reviewed any of the code,” wrote Matt Goldberg, the AWS senior principal engineer behind the project, in a blog post.

Goldberg compared his agents to himself as a kindergartner, too young to hold a crayon properly, who got yelled at by classmates for ruining a group drawing of dinosaurs. The problem wasn’t bad intent, he wrote, just a lack of competence. The answer, for agents, is clearly defined areas to fill in.

“I think agents also need coloring books,” he wrote.

The agents work from AWS’s public API models, which describe how each service should behave, and check their work against the real AWS cloud.

The agents run on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in three teams. One writes “fidelity tests” — real-world scenarios such as creating a queue, sending a message and deleting the queue — and checks each against real AWS. A second runs those tests against the emulator and files issues for failures, and a third fixes them, one agent per issue.

Every change passes through an automated gate where other agents check coding standards and security. Goldberg wrote that hundreds of agents now fix thousands of issues a day.

The project started as a weekend experiment, inspired by Anthropic’s demonstration earlier this year in which a team of Claude agents built a C compiler. Goldberg gave Kiro a three-step prompt and got a passable first version of Amazon SQS, AWS’s message queuing service, in 15 minutes.

By the end of the weekend, Goldberg wrote, Kiro had built a rough version of the rest of AWS, with obvious gaps, and his team started using it to test its software that Monday.

Swami Sivasubramanian, AWS vice president of agentic AI and emerging tech, tied the project to a lesson he described to GeekWire in June. He spent four nights babysitting Kiro as it tried to rebuild a replication engine he and Allan Vermeulen built by hand nearly 20 years ago.

Once he gave the agent a spec and a way to test its work, the job took about two hours.

“When agents write the code and check their own work, the engineer’s job is to give them room to work on their own and to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct,” Sivasubramanian wrote in a guest post on CTO Werner Vogels’ blog.

It’s the same idea behind Amazon’s recent move to rewrite its engineering playbook for an era when AI writes the code.

The emulator has limits. Devin Pratt, an IDC analyst, told InfoWorld that it doesn’t yet simulate throttling, outages or differences in which services and features are available by region, and that it doesn’t sandbox the code it runs. The agents’ backlog of known gaps is public, in a GitHub folder called “things-that-do-not-work.”

Other AWS emulators exist, most notably LocalStack, which this year put its free version behind an account requirement and limited it to noncommercial use. AWS released its emulator for free under CC0, a public domain dedication, with the full commit history on GitHub.

The company says it will share more at its upcoming re:Invent conference.

#5418. Your Success Might Be Creating Problems You Can’t See. Here’s What to Ask Yourself.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Your business may be growing, but what is that growth really costing you?

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In the early 1920s, car manufacturers faced a frustrating problem: They wanted to build more powerful engines, but “engine knocking” kept getting in the way. Fuel igniting unevenly inside an engine created violent vibrations that damaged its components. The finest minds scratched their heads over how to get more power without sacrificing reliability.

Meanwhile, refrigerator manufacturers faced a problem of their own: Some chemicals used in early refrigerators were toxic or highly flammable. A leak could turn a household appliance into a serious hazard. Finding a safer refrigerant could make refrigeration more practical for homes and businesses.

Enter Thomas Midgley Jr., an American engineer who was working at General Motors.

Midgley discovered that adding lead to the fuel could suppress engine knocking. Later, he’d help develop Freon, a refrigerant far less toxic and flammable than many alternatives in use at that time. And just like that, two stubborn engineering problems appeared to be solved.

Manufacturers respected him and adopted his work, and both products became commercial successes. For his work, the American Chemical Society awarded him the Priestley Medal, their highest honor.

You could look at that record and reasonably conclude he had done an excellent job. Entire industries were growing because of him, and he’d earned recognition from his peers.

Would you agree that by the usual measures, Midgley had an extraordinary career? Well … then the other shoe dropped.

Leaded petrol was found to spread toxic lead through the exhaust, exposing generations of people to a metal whose harmful effects we now know better about. Decades after Freon and related chemicals became widespread, scientists discovered that chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) damaged the Earth’s ozone layer.

Midgley died in 1944, before scientists discovered the damage to the ozone layer. In Midgley’s defence, he could not have predicted every consequence, but his story begs the question for anyone who has built a successful business: What if the very thing that made you successful is also creating costs you haven’t accounted for?

Warning signs around leaded petrol had already appeared during its early production, but the “cost” was ignored, and it remained in widespread use for decades. Freon seemed safe and harmless at first glance, and CFCs were widely used in refrigeration and elsewhere before scientists truly understood how they were damaging the ozone layer.

I think there’s a shared lesson in this about the limits of the original measure of success: A product can work as intended while creating consequences its original purpose never required anyone to consider.

Business owners can fall into a similar pattern. You find something that works, so you do more of it. Being available at all hours helps win customers, so you keep answering calls. Making every important decision helps the business move quickly, so you stay involved as the team expands and you keep accepting work because demand is strong.

Each decision may have solved a problem and helped you get where you are. The costs can emerge later, as the business grows and when you know better.

Early in a company’s life, personal involvement can be exactly what it needs.

The difficulty comes when those habits continue long after the circumstances that made them useful have changed. The founder who once needed to approve every important decision may now be bottlenecking the team. The availability that once won clients leaves no room to switch off. The behavior that helped build the business can become expensive as the business grows.

Sometimes, getting personally involved is exactly what a business needs. You step in, solve a problem, establish a process or build a relationship that gets things moving. But was your involvement meant to be permanent? What began as a short-term solution can quietly become an ongoing responsibility, until you’re spending more time operating the business than leading it.

So now, you have more customers bringing more revenue, but also more complexity. A new market opens up, but demands more travel and attention. The business becomes more profitable while the owner’s time and energy become harder to protect, and their family is neglected.

In my coaching conversations with entrepreneurs, I often return to the difference between what a business produces and what it demands from the person running it. Revenue, profit and growth are easy to track. The cost to a founder’s health, relationships, judgment or freedom can be harder to quantify, so it may go unexamined for years.

A business can be winning by its own measures while the person who built it pays a price they never intended to pay.

None of this is the business owner’s fault, because it’s particularly easy to miss when the numbers look good. A crisis forces you to take a step back and review, but who stops to question continued success? Nobody.

When revenue is growing, and customers are happy, why feel pressured to question the way you’re running the business, even if the arrangement is becoming harder to sustain?

You don’t need to become suspicious of every ambitious decision; building a business requires risk, investment and choices whose consequences cannot be predicted perfectly. But you do need to ask whether your measures of success account for enough of the picture.

Imagine reviewing a new business initiative. You’d probably examine the expected revenue, costs, staffing, return, etc. Would you also ask what it will demand from you personally, what it might displace or whether the business will become more dependent on your involvement?

Tomorrow, choose one part of your business that is performing well. It might be your fastest-growing service, a major client relationship or a process that depends on you being constantly available.

Write down three things: what it produces, what it demands and what it displaces. Then consider whether the arrangement remains sustainable as the business grows. Is it delivering the results you need today at the expense of what the business will need to sustain those results over the longer term? Or can it continue producing the same results without placing increasing demands on you, your team or the resources the business needs elsewhere?

Time spent managing one opportunity is time unavailable for another. Energy spent resolving routine decisions cannot also be spent thinking about the future. An arrangement that works financially may place demands on family life that nobody intended when it began.

Then ask yourself what has changed since you first made that decision. Perhaps the business has grown, your responsibilities have shifted, regulations have changed, or a risk you once considered acceptable now deserves another look. Would you make the same decision today, knowing what you know now?

If the answer is yes, carry on with a clearer understanding of the exchange. If something has changed, you have an opportunity to reconsider the arrangement while you still have options. You might choose to delegate a decision, renegotiate a client relationship or stop doing something that no longer justifies the demands it places on you.

The point is to make that choice while you still have options, rather than waiting for circumstances to make it for you.

You worked hard to build the business you have. You deserve to understand what it gives you, what it asks of you and whether that exchange still makes sense. Success deserves examination even when everything appears to be going well. Sometimes the most important decision a business owner makes is to look beyond the results that got them here.

In the early 1920s, car manufacturers faced a frustrating problem: They wanted to build more powerful engines, but “engine knocking” kept getting in the way. Fuel igniting unevenly inside an engine created violent vibrations that damaged its components. The finest minds scratched their heads over how to get more power without sacrificing reliability.

Meanwhile, refrigerator manufacturers faced a problem of their own: Some chemicals used in early refrigerators were toxic or highly flammable. A leak could turn a household appliance into a serious hazard. Finding a safer refrigerant could make refrigeration more practical for homes and businesses.

Enter Thomas Midgley Jr., an American engineer who was working at General Motors.

#5417. Rand Fishkin’s Seattle game studio serves up first trailer for ‘The Snackbar at the End of the World’

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 11, 2026 at 11:21 amNovember 11, 2026 at 11:21 am

If the eventual release of “The Snackbar at the End of the World” is a full-on meal for video game fans, news this week of the game’s first trailer should at least suffice as an appetizer.

Seattle-based Snackbar Studio, co-founded by SparkToro founder Rand Fishkin and his wife, writer Geraldine DeRuiter, unveiled its debut title and Steam page on Tuesday. The hand-drawn narrative adventure RPG puts players in the role of a chef trying to save a struggling family restaurant in a magical version of 1960s Italy.

The studio now plans to launch the game late next year, after originally targeting the second half of 2026. Snackbar raised $2.15 million from 38 angel investors two years ago, and the project began four years ago, according to Fishkin. The team includes five co-founders (Fishkin, DeRuiter, game designer Nicolas Kraj, lead programmer Miriam Cabrera and art director Francesco Mazza) plus about 10 contractors.

In the studio’s description on Steam, players forage for ingredients in the “forbidden wilds” outside town, battling explosive tomatoes, chaotic zucchini and vendetta-driven poultry. They then cook dishes back at the restaurant before a tyrannical mayor known as the Sindaco can shut it down. The game mixes combat and stealth with cooking mini-games based on real-world recipes.

The trailer is set to “’O surdato ’nnammurato,” a classic Neapolitan song performed by professional musicians recruited by the studio’s music director. Fishkin said he and DeRuiter both cried the first time they heard it.

Fishkin is best known in Seattle tech circles as co-founder of SEO software company Moz and audience research startup SparkToro, and he more recently launched Alertmouse, a tool for tracking online mentions. DeRuiter, a writer and author, is Snackbar’s head writer.

In a LinkedIn post this week, Fishkin recalled telling DeRuiter during the COVID lockdown that he wanted to fulfill a childhood dream of making a video game. Her reply: “Don’t wait. Do it now. I’ll do it with you.”

In the same post, he said the game’s themes include found family and fighting fascism “even when there’s no hope you’ll win.” He called it a love letter to DeRuiter’s small family village in the mountains outside Naples, to that era of Italy, to video games, and to the many people both of their families have lost in recent years.

Moments like hearing that song come often in the work, Fishkin said, such as when a new feature clicks or a new animation brings DeRuiter’s characters to life. He has always loved art without being good at any form of it. “I may not be able to create art, but I can enable it,” he said. “What a wonderful feeling.”

There have been lows, too. The team spent its initial 18 months on the project with a contract agency that didn’t work out, losing money with nothing to show for it. Fishkin is glad they kept going, “even when it felt financially irresponsible.”

The game is entirely human-made, and Snackbar’s no-AI stance is firm. “Geraldine hates AI with the fury of a thousand suns,” Fishkin said. He once suggested, just once, that she use Google’s AI Mode to find a synonym, and she was mad at him for the rest of a six-hour flight home from Philadelphia. Even if players, the rest of the team and the games media were fine with AI (and they’re not), DeRuiter alone would make it a no-go, he said.

Still ahead are 10 to 12 months of finishing the game’s content, playtesting, bug fixing, marketing and launch prep. Fishkin called it daunting, but said team members have done it many times before, “even though it’s our first rodeo.”

Fishkin is still juggling Snackbar with SparkToro and Alertmouse, and describes his role at the studio as mostly oversight and management. SparkToro is growing again, and Alertmouse recently hit a big milestone in annual renewals with high retention. He and his Alertmouse co-founders are putting more money into the company to fund growth.

Balancing the three roles is a challenge, he said, but only rarely completely overwhelming. “Like this week.”

#5415. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#5414. Lila Bio lands $3.65M grant to fight pulmonary hypertension with AI-designed proteins

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:31 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 2:31 pm

Lila Bio, a startup spun out of Nobel laureate David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington, has received a $3.65 million grant from the National Institutes of Health to develop a treatment for pulmonary hypertension.

The condition causes high blood pressure in the arteries that carry blood from the heart to the lungs. It forces the heart to work harder and can lead to heart failure.

The Small Business Innovation Research fast-track award supports Lila’s efforts to develop a protein-based treatment for pulmonary hypertension that could be given by injection a few times a year.

“Most approved therapies only manage symptoms, such as vasodilators,” Lila CEO Jake Kraft said in a LinkedIn post, referring to drugs that widen blood vessels. “Lila Bio is pursuing clinically-validated, disease-modifying mechanisms that treat the underlying disease.”

The funding comes from the NIH’s National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and is divided into two phases. The initial $605,981 will support early testing in mice, rats and non-human primates. The second phase, totaling $3,049,462, will support further animal testing and studies using lung tissue from patients.

Kraft and chief scientist Anindya Roy co-founded Lila in 2023. Both worked as postdoctoral fellows at UW’s Institute for Protein Design, which Baker directs. Lila raised $10 million in seed funding the year it was founded. Last year, it announced a collaboration with pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly to develop treatments for solid tumors.

The startup uses AI and machine learning to design therapeutic proteins through two platforms. One supports the pulmonary hypertension project, creating long-acting injectable drugs designed to remain active in the body for weeks or months. The other focuses on targeted radiotherapy, using proteins to deliver radioactive isotopes to tumors.

“We want to bring medicines to patients,” Kraft told GeekWire in an earlier interview. “We don’t want to just say we’ve designed a protein, but we actually want to be able to say we’ve saved lives.”

#5413. Why Tech and Crypto Sold Off After the Blue Wave

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The reversal of the post-election rally offers founders a practical lesson in financing growth, managing risk and separating political expectations from business fundamentals.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The first market reaction to an election can make a poor foundation for a business plan. On Nov. 4, stocks and Bitcoin recovered after the Democratic sweep of Congress. By the next U.S. trading morning, that relief rally was coming apart.

During morning trading on Nov. 5, the Nasdaq Composite fell nearly 4%. Bitcoin also reversed course: Bitcoin.com reported a Bitstamp low of $75,468 by 10:55 a.m. Eastern, after the cryptocurrency had traded above $81,000 the previous day.

The reversal makes a simple political explanation difficult. The election result had not changed. Investors were reassessing what it might mean for businesses and assets whose valuations depended on continued growth, access to financing and confidence in the future.

For entrepreneurs, the useful question is how much of a business plan still works when those assumptions become less generous.

The blue wave introduced another uncertainty for the AI buildout. Reuters reported concern that Democratic victories could bring closer scrutiny of data-center expansion. Chipmakers, data-center operators and companies supplying that expansion came under pressure as investors considered the possibility of slower development.

These were concerns about possible future restrictions. Markets can mark down a company because a project might face delays, long before an agency or legislature acts. Expectations can change a valuation before a rule changes an operating plan.

For a developer, even a temporary delay can change the economics. Equipment has to be financed, contracts carry obligations and interest can accumulate before customers start paying. A project can remain technologically promising while becoming less attractive at its original cost and timetable.

Those concerns were already building before election night. A separate Reuters report described investors questioning returns on enormous AI investments and the use of debt to fund them. The political shift added another uncertainty to that existing debate; it did not create every weakness in the trade.

Company results mattered, too. In its November 4 earnings release, Qualcomm reported quarterly handset revenue of $5.137 billion, down 26% from a year earlier. It also warned of rising semiconductor input costs. These were operating pressures with their own implications for earnings, irrespective of which party won Congress.

For a founder selling an ambitious growth story, that is the uncomfortable part. Investors may still believe in the technology while demanding stronger evidence that expansion will produce an acceptable return.

Bitcoin’s decentralized design does not make its price independent of financial markets. Its network operates without a central owner, but people still buy and sell it with finite capital, changing risk preferences and sometimes borrowed money.

When investors become more defensive, assets with very different underlying purposes can fall together. A trader reducing exposure does not need to abandon a long-term belief in Bitcoin to sell it. The immediate priority may simply be to reduce losses or free up cash.

Leverage can make that process faster. Coinbase International Exchange’s trading rules, for example, provide for automatic liquidation when account equity falls below maintenance requirements. Closing leveraged positions can add further pressure to an existing move. The mechanism helps explain how selling can accelerate without a new piece of political news arriving each time prices fall.

There was evidence of forced closures across crypto. Bitcoin.com cited Coinglass figures showing roughly $839 million in liquidations over the preceding 24 hours, including approximately $741 million in bullish positions. That window spans two trading days, and the figures measure positions liquidated rather than an equivalent amount of cash withdrawn.

The simultaneous sell-off is consistent with investors cutting risk, with leverage amplifying the pressure. It does not establish that the same investors sold both markets, or that the blue wave alone caused Bitcoin’s decline.

The most useful response to this kind of volatility is a closer look at the operating plan. A changing market can reveal dependencies that were easy to overlook when financing was available and valuations were rising.

Start with funding. If the next equity round takes six months longer, which commitments still have to be paid? If a loan becomes more expensive or a project approval takes longer, does the business have enough cash to reach its next meaningful milestone?

Then examine demand. An AI company should be able to show what customers pay for, how often they return and whether delivering the service produces a sustainable margin. A crypto business should understand how lower asset prices, thinner liquidity or increased withdrawals would affect its operations.

Political assumptions deserve the same treatment. An expected approval, friendly administration or proposed law may improve the outlook. Put those benefits in a scenario that can be tested, and identify how the business operates if they arrive later than expected.

This exercise can produce specific decisions: stage a capital project, negotiate more flexible supplier terms or prioritize a product customers already pay to use. It is more useful than trying to predict the next market rebound.

The post-midterm reversal does not settle the long-term case for AI or digital assets. It does show how quickly market enthusiasm can disappear while a company’s spending obligations remain.

The blue wave was part of the context. Earnings, financing costs, expectations for infrastructure growth and leveraged trading also shaped the environment. Assigning the entire move to one election result would leave founders with an incomplete explanation.

A company cannot control the next election or the next wave of selling. It can control how much of its future depends on a favorable outcome. That is where the work should begin.

The first market reaction to an election can make a poor foundation for a business plan. On Nov. 4, stocks and Bitcoin recovered after the Democratic sweep of Congress. By the next U.S. trading morning, that relief rally was coming apart.

During morning trading on Nov. 5, the Nasdaq Composite fell nearly 4%. Bitcoin also reversed course: Bitcoin.com reported a Bitstamp low of $75,468 by 10:55 a.m. Eastern, after the cryptocurrency had traded above $81,000 the previous day.

The reversal makes a simple political explanation difficult. The election result had not changed. Investors were reassessing what it might mean for businesses and assets whose valuations depended on continued growth, access to financing and confidence in the future.

#5412. AI voice company WellSaid retools for agents while keeping its commitment to human actors

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:56 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 3:09 pm

WellSaid, the AI voice company that spun out of Seattle’s Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence in 2019, is reinventing itself for the era of AI agents.

The company this week launched WellSaid Producer, which connects its voiceover direction tools directly to AI assistants such as Claude and Microsoft Copilot.

Instead of logging into WellSaid’s app, corporate users can ask the AI assistant for a voiceover to accompany a training or marketing video, for example. The assistant then sends the script to WellSaid, which generates the audio using its licensed voices.

It’s part of a broader overhaul and refocusing of WellSaid’s business. The company has spent the past two years moving away from individual users to focus on businesses. It now has about 30 employees, down from more than 70 in late 2024.

Along the way, WellSaid has turned profitable, CEO Benjamin Dorr told GeekWire.

“We’ve been calling this adventure Act II, so I guess Producer is Scene I,” Dorr said. Extending the metaphor, he acknowledged that “the cast is a lot smaller,” and noted that many of the company’s leaders are new, recruited from his own network.

Dorr joined WellSaid as CFO in 2024 and became CEO in spring 2025. He was previously chief operating officer of Cordial, a San Diego marketing software company, and earlier worked in tech investing and banking at The Carlyle Group, Morgan Stanley and Citi.

He succeeded Brian Cook, the former Nintex CEO who led WellSaid for about 16 months. Co-founder Matt Hocking, who was CEO until early 2024, remains on WellSaid’s board and is now chief product officer at Type, an AI startup for creative writers.

Dorr’s leadership team includes three executives who also worked at Cordial and joined WellSaid since last fall: Natalia Holts, senior vice president of finance and accounting; Jeni Bishop, vice president of marketing; and Bryan Keefer, vice president of product.

Chris Johnson, the chief product and technology officer, and co-founder Mixail Petrochuk, the chief technology officer, remain from the earlier leadership team.

The company is maintaining its longstanding practice of building its AI voices from recordings of professional voice actors, who are paid royalties when businesses use their voices to narrate training courses, marketing and other videos.

WellSaid drew widespread attention in 2023 when it created a spot-on synthetic version of former NPR “Planet Money” host Robert Smith’s voice, with his permission, as part of a special series by the popular radio show and podcast.

Its customers include nearly half of the Fortune 100, according to WellSaid. The company’s licensing approach stands out in a sector that remains a wild west, with models trained on audio scraped from the internet and tools used to fake the voices of public figures.

“We view [Model Context Protocol], and agents in general, to be as disruptive to software as the Web once was twenty years ago.”

How it works: Producer uses Model Context Protocol, or MCP, a standard way for AI assistants to connect to other software. It works with Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot and Atlassian’s Rovo, and Dorr said AI agents that work on their own will be able to use it by the end of the year.

Companies using WellSaid Producer can set up style guides so brand names, acronyms and technical terms are pronounced the same way in every file. When a product name or script changes, Producer can update every affected voiceover in one pass, and each finished file carries a record of its license.

WellSaid also says it’s the first voiceover platform to generate audio natively at 48 kHz, the standard for film and video. Producer is sold as a platform, with customers committing to buy credits for minutes of finished, licensed audio. WellSaid’s licenses today are mostly one-time buyouts, but Dorr said the company wants to price more like the traditional voiceover industry, where an ad voiceover is priced by its length, reach and how long it runs. WellSaid will continue to offer its Studio app for customers who want to work there directly.

The strategy: Dorr said voiceover is just one step in a larger production process, and many creative tools now include basic AI speech that is sometimes good enough. He sees AI agents letting companies combine specialized tools from vendors they trust, instead of settling for one all-in-one app.

“We view MCP, and agents in general, to be as disruptive to software as the Web once was twenty years ago,” he said.

Voice actors: Actors’ revenue share rates won’t change when their voices are used through AI assistants, Dorr said. One of his first moves as CEO was to open the company’s stock option pool to its top 20 voice actors, and WellSaid is building a voice actor advisory board, with more details expected to be released in December. Dorr said WellSaid plans to add custom royalty structures, “potentially all the way up to union rate cards.”

Customers will also be able to use voice models from other companies alongside WellSaid’s own, for features its models lack, such as one voice speaking several languages. The voices still come from WellSaid’s actors under its licensing terms. “We’re not moving from our position on commercial licensing,” Dorr said.

The business: WellSaid has about 1,000 business customers, and its top 25 customers each spend more than $100,000 a year, Dorr said. Moving away from individual users “did flatten our growth compared to a lot of AI companies growing at astronomical rates,” he said.

By comparison, rival ElevenLabs, which has offered voice generation through Claude since 2025, was valued at $22 billion in a recent employee tender offer.

WellSaid raised venture debt from Multiplier Capital in March but didn’t disclose the amount. Its most recent disclosed equity funding was a $10 million Series A round in 2021 that valued the company at $65 million, according to PitchBook.

Dorr said debt was a better fit than equity for a “modestly growing and, now, profitable company,” at a time when investors’ growth expectations “have become extreme.” He said WellSaid will consider other financing in 2027 “if our ambitions outstrip our ability to reinvest.”

#5411. 5 Businesses I Wouldn’t Start in 2027 — and 5 Models I’d Look at Instead

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

These are the businesses I would think twice about starting, plus alternatives that offer better leverage, scalability and income potential.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Search “best businesses to start” and you’ll see the same ideas on repeat: dropshipping, influencing, a generic marketing agency, something on Amazon. Technically, they can all still work. But “can work” and “where I’d put my time and money today” are two very different things.

After nearly a decade in ecommerce and online business, I’ve learned that the business model matters almost as much as the entrepreneur. A great operator can fight through a difficult model, but why choose one that demands enormous time, has razor-thin margins or depends on constantly finding your next customer?

Heading into 2027, I’m drawn to three things: leverage, recurring revenue and systems. Here are five businesses I’d think twice about starting from scratch, and what I’d consider instead.

A few years ago, the playbook was simple: land a few local clients at $1,000 or $2,000 a month, outsource the work and scale. But everyone got the memo. Generalist agencies now compete with freelancers, offshore teams, in-house hires and increasingly capable AI tools.

Solve one expensive problem for one type of business. Help dental practices follow up with leads who never scheduled. Build AI customer-service workflows for ecommerce brands. Automate reminders and customer reactivation for home-service companies.

The opportunity isn’t selling AI; businesses can access that themselves. It’s knowing what to automate and connecting it to a real outcome. “Social media management” is a vague line item, while recovering thousands of dollars in lost leads is easy to understand. Sell the outcome, not the technology.

The idea that you can open a Seller Central account, list a few products after work and enjoy effortless income is increasingly disconnected from reality. Sourcing, pricing, Buy Box competition, inventory, customer service and account health all demand attention. For someone who wants to become an operator, that’s fine. But many professionals want ecommerce exposure without creating a second full-time job.

For people with more capital than time, a professionally managed ecommerce storefront may be worth a look. The owner funds and owns the store, while an experienced team handles day-to-day operations for a fee or a share of profits, much like a property owner hiring a property manager. These investors aren’t looking for something else to do. They’re looking for something else to own.

It isn’t risk-free. Marketplaces shift, sales fluctuate and projected income is never guaranteed income, so vet who actually operates the store and how profits are calculated before you commit.

The pitch is irresistible: no inventory, your supplier ships the order and you pocket the difference. But acquiring the customer is the hard part. A store selling products that hundreds of other websites also sell has little competitive advantage, and you’re often dependent on paid advertising and on finding products before competitors pile in.

Think beauty, pet products, specialty foods, personal care or hobby consumables. The category matters less than the economics. Ask yourself: If I spend $40 acquiring this customer today, can they be worth $200 to me over the next two years?

An ad stops producing the moment you turn it off. A loyal customer base, an email list and a recognizable brand can become more valuable every year.

Expertise used to be nearly enough: record six hours of video, build a landing page, charge $997. Today, information is abundant, including through AI, and people are reluctant to pay premium prices for it. Information isn’t scarce anymore; real results are.

Build several specific products that solve narrow problems, such as a template, calculator, workflow, database, paid community or small software tool, and create content for the audience they serve. Someone who knows Airbnb could skip the “$997 Masterclass” and offer a profitability calculator, a cleaning-checklist system, guest-message templates and a paid newsletter on market changes. That ecosystem is much harder to replace with a single AI prompt.

Personal brands are powerful, but they can become cages. If revenue disappears when you stop posting or showing your face online, you’ve created income, not necessarily an independent business. You might love posting three videos a day at 25. Will you still want to at 35?

This is the filter I’d apply to almost any opportunity: Can this eventually work without me? It doesn’t need to be hands-off on day one, but there should be a path from founder-dependent to system-dependent. Can someone else handle customer service? Can sales become repeatable? Can procedures be documented? Can customers keep buying while you’re on vacation?

If every important function leads back to you, that’s not freedom. It’s self-employment with a nicer title.

The business I’m watching in 2027 isn’t really an idea. It’s leverage. AI gives one employee leverage. Software gives a small company leverage. Recurring revenue gives customer acquisition leverage. A management team gives an owner leverage. Capital gives an investor leverage. And systems give entrepreneurs perhaps the most valuable form of all: time.

So instead of asking, “What’s the hottest business to start?” ask: What can I build or own today that becomes less dependent on my time as it grows? If you have little capital but plenty of time, an AI automation service may fit. If you understand products and branding, consider a niche consumer brand. If you have expertise but don’t want to become an influencer, digital products can turn it into an asset. And if you have capital but little spare time, a professionally managed business may deserve a closer look.

The best business isn’t always the one that makes the most money today. It may be the one that eventually stops needing you to make every dollar. After all, your time is precious.

Search “best businesses to start” and you’ll see the same ideas on repeat: dropshipping, influencing, a generic marketing agency, something on Amazon. Technically, they can all still work. But “can work” and “where I’d put my time and money today” are two very different things.

After nearly a decade in ecommerce and online business, I’ve learned that the business model matters almost as much as the entrepreneur. A great operator can fight through a difficult model, but why choose one that demands enormous time, has razor-thin margins or depends on constantly finding your next customer?

Heading into 2027, I’m drawn to three things: leverage, recurring revenue and systems. Here are five businesses I’d think twice about starting from scratch, and what I’d consider instead.

#5409. Ex-Seattle startup DeltaGen acquired by new AI company backed by Veeam co-founder

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 12, 2026 at 5:51 amNovember 12, 2026 at 5:51 am

DeltaGen, an AI startup that got its start in Seattle before moving to San Francisco this year, has been acquired by Worker.ai, a new small-business software company backed by Veeam founder Ratmir Timashev.

Worker, which launched Thursday, acquired all of DeltaGen for an undisclosed price that included a substantial cash component and equity in Worker, DeltaGen co-founder and CEO Rene Bystron told GeekWire.

Bystron joins Worker as co-founder and COO, and nine other DeltaGen employees are coming with him, including co-founders Michal Studnicka and Matus Ondreicka.

Worker, led by co-founder and CEO John Roberts, a former private equity operator based in Raleigh, N.C., is building software that lets small businesses hand off recurring work to AI agents. DeltaGen’s voice technology captures decisions made in conversations and turns them into assigned tasks.

Roberts had been a DeltaGen customer before Worker needed voice technology, Bystron said. “We could have raised another round and kept building independently, but this gave us the capital and experience to move faster with people we trusted,” he said.

Launched in 2024, DeltaGen raised a $1.2 million pre-seed round in early 2025 to build generative AI tools for financial professionals, with a focus on streamlining mergers and acquisitions. The company relocated from Seattle to San Francisco earlier this year.

“I still love Seattle and miss it like crazy,” said Bystron, who is keeping his apartment in Belltown. “But being closer to the AI founders, customers and investors in San Francisco makes a real difference at this stage. It also didn’t help that Washington has been chipping away at its tax advantage.”

Timashev, who co-founded data backup giant Veeam, is backing Worker to help small businesses such as manufacturers, service companies and family businesses grow.

“AI can now give small businesses more capacity without asking already stretched owners to work longer days,” he said in a statement. “Worker is my bet on that shift.” The size of his investment was not disclosed.

DeltaGen’s current product is an AI voice platform, which will continue as it’s integrated into Worker. DeltaGen’s AI voice platform will continue as it’s integrated into Worker, which is opening access gradually through a waitlist.

#5408. The Leadership Skills You Think You’ve Outgrown May Be the Ones You Need Most

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

It’s easy to get caught up in complicated answers to problems and forget to go back to the fundamental skills. But here’s why you need them.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

So often in leadership circles we look for the complicated answer — the one that requires input from all team members and takes scrutiny from every angle. And, to be honest, sometimes that is exactly what’s needed. But I’ve found that more often than not, what’s really required to make sense of a situation or find direction is a return to basics.

The fundamental unit of work is a conversation. Part of working well together means learning and practicing these fundamental skills such as active listening, presence, asking open, honest questions and deciding who makes decisions and how they are made in any conversation. In your business, these are the skills that give you an edge and foster healthy collaboration, clear speaking, making sure that the vision is well understood and that good commitment hygiene is tended to.Many leaders learn to be patient, make decisions, move forward by weighing pros and cons and — if you’re lucky — trust their intuition. The best leaders can identify overthinking, confer-and-defer tendencies and conflict avoidance in themselves as well as in their teammates. Healthy teams can surface these in the group when they arise by recognizing and naming them so they don’t bog down their considerations. But when the essentials of good leadership are lost, I see leaders get caught up trying to solve difficult problems by reaching for the most complex solutions. Teams, then, get trapped in a mire.

Sophisticated solutions tend to masquerade as expertise, and reaching for a basic skill can feel almost shameful when you’re trying to wear the mask of an infallible leader. It’s hard to set ego aside and use the tools you started with. It’s a lesson in humility that’s not easy to learn. ‘I’ve learned so many new things since I first began, so why would I do something so simple?’ This is a question a client brought to me when I suggested drawing on listening skills to work through a team dispute.

Sure, you have new skills and knowledge, and you’re most certainly not the person you were when you started your career, but that doesn’t mean those core skills of good leadership you learned a long time ago are baseless. Returning to what you know at your core is often the advice I give to my clients. It’s also frequently the advice they need to hear.

There are some ways to tell if your efforts to solve a problem are caught in an endless loop. If you find yourself stuck in over-consulting, endless information gathering, solutions nobody can explain, decisions that keep getting deferred and problems that never seem to be solved, it’s time to follow the breadcrumbs back to basics.

Some ways to get back to what works when no other solution seems to be helping can include:

​It’s important to let go of the mindset that returning to basic skills means regression. Those fundamental skills aren’t something you learn once and put aside. Fundamentals aren’t the beginner stage you graduated from; they’re the thing you consistently get better at. Basics steeped in experience look like listening before diagnosing, presence over performance, intuition as experience rather than guesswork and knowing when and how to be present.

​Go back to the problem you’re grappling with — the one you built the framework for, the one you scheduled three meetings about before you scheduled the work. Ask yourself what you would have done if you’d trusted yourself with it on day one. Complexity is often where we go to feel safe. If it will take months of models and matrices to find a solution, the outcome is delayed (and then not your fault if it fails).

Sitting with a problem and trusting your own judgment leaves you holding it alone, and that can be frightening. But it’s also how you grow. It’s how those basic skills evolve, and it’s how you’ll move past this problem and to the next one with confidence. Going back to basics asks more of us than frameworks do. It asks us to stop, think, listen and remember how and why it all started.

So often in leadership circles we look for the complicated answer — the one that requires input from all team members and takes scrutiny from every angle. And, to be honest, sometimes that is exactly what’s needed. But I’ve found that more often than not, what’s really required to make sense of a situation or find direction is a return to basics.

The best leaders can identify overthinking, confer-and-defer tendencies and conflict avoidance in themselves as well as in their teammates. #5407. Seattle’s Allen Institute helps create a ‘Rosetta Stone’ for brain cells to unlock clues to disease

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 11, 2026 at 5:15 pm

A coalition of 56 institutions across nine countries is publishing groundbreaking research today on the basal ganglia — a group of brain structures that help control movement, emotions, motivation and habits. The region is linked to psychiatric and degenerative disorders, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and Parkinson’s disease.

The scientist have produced a biological Rosetta Stone that creates a shared system for naming and describing cells in the basal ganglia across species. The goal is to help researchers compare findings, collaborate and accelerate their understanding of this essential brain region.

“This is groundwork that is necessary to really make progress,” said Michael Hawrylycz, principal investigator with the Seattle-based Allen Institute who helped organize the consortium.

The project, called the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network, or BICAN, produced a basal ganglia atlas that is publicly available for basic researchers, clinicians and others to use.

The research is being presented in a package of 26 articles in a special issue of the journal Cell. The data comes from humans, macaques, marmoset and mice. One of the benefits of comparing the basal ganglia between species is understanding which components are uniquely human, providing potential insights into neurological diseases.

Despite the critical and wide-ranging roles, the basal ganglia is relatively small — it’s about 2% of the brain with a volume roughly the size of a large gumball.

For the project, the researchers pulled information from 25.5 million brain cells, including 21 million human cells. They used a variety of techniques to tease out insights, including RNA sequencing to identify gene activity from single cells in precise locations; epigenomic studies revealing where genes are switched on or off; and measurements of electrical activity combined with cell shape and genetic information.

It’s a lot of data to stitch together and make sense of, Hawrylycz said. “AI is a perfect tool” for the job, he said, because it excels at finding patterns.

The findings could help guide future treatments, but the work remains basic research rather than clinical research, Hawrylycz said.

The new research is the first major installment of the third phase of a brain-mapping effort that began in 2014. The first phase demonstrated that scientists could analyze individual cells on a large scale. The second produced an atlas of the mouse brain.

BICAN aims to create a standardized atlas describing cells throughout the brains of humans and other primates. Hawrylycz said the work is expected to take another two or three years.

#5406. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.
